$$

context.statement:
We first fix the notation used throughout the paper. Scalars are written as lower case letters and vectors as bold lower case letters, e.g. w. For two vectors u and v, $\langle{\pmb u},{\pmb v}\rangle$ is their inner product. The p-norm of a vector x is written $\| \pmb{x}\|_{p}$, and ||x|| abbreviates $\| \pmb{x}\|_{2}$.

$$
f({\pmb w})+r({\pmb w}),\tag{1}
$$

in which f and r are both convex and bounded below (so that, with no loss of generality, they are taken to map into $\mathbb{R}_{+}$). Typically f is an empirical loss of the form $\textstyle\sum_{i\in S}\ell_{i}(w)$ built from loss functions $\ell_{i}: \mathbb{R}^{n}\to \mathbb{R}_{+}$, and $r(w)$ is a regularizer that penalizes overly complex vectors, e.g. $r(\mathbf{w})=\lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|_{p}$. Such tasks are common in machine learning, where learning problems for decision and prediction are formulated as convex optimization problems. With this in mind, we study a general and intuitive algorithm called forward-backward splitting for minimizing Eq. (1), with particular emphasis on derivations for, and the use of, regularization functions that are not differentiable.

context.name: Definition: subgradient set
context.statement:
For a function f and a point w, write $\partial f ({\boldsymbol{w}})$ for the subgradient set of f at w, that is,

$$
\partial f(w)=\{g\mid\forall v:f(v)\geq f(w)+\langle g,v-w\rangle\}.
$$

context.name: Algorithm: FoBoS update and forward-looking subgradient, Eqs. (2)-(5) (Section 2)
context.statement:
Our version of Forward-Backward Splitting is driven by the wish that the iterates ${\pmb w}_{t}$ be able to reach points where r is not differentiable. For problems such as $\ell_{1}$-regularization, the method sidesteps the difficulties caused by non-differentiability by alternating subgradient steps with analytical minimization steps. Informally, FoBoS resembles the projected subgradient method, except that the projection step is replaced or augmented by an instantaneous minimization problem whose solution can be derived in closed form. The method is compact: every iteration is made of the two steps below,

$$
\begin{array}{r l r}{{\bf w}_{t + \frac{1}{2}}}&{{}=}&{{\bf w}_{t}- \boldsymbol \eta_{t}{\bf g}_{t}^{f},}\end{array}\tag{2}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r c l}{{\pmb w}_{t+1}}&{=}&{\displaystyle\operatorname*{argmin}_{{\pmb w}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\left\|{\pmb w}-{\pmb w}_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\right\|^{2}+\eta_{t+\frac{1}{2}}r({\pmb w})\right\}\ .}\end{array}\tag{3}
$$

Here $g_{t}^{f}$ is an element of $\partial f ({\pmb w}_{t})$, and $\eta_{t}$ denotes the step size used by the algorithm at time step t. What value $\eta_{t}$ takes depends on the particular setting and analysis. The first step is thus nothing more than an unconstrained subgradient step for the function $f$. The second step produces a new vector that balances two aims: (i) remaining near the interim vector $w_{t + \frac{1}{2}}$, and (ii) having small complexity as measured by r. Observe that r is multiplied by an interim step size, written $\eta_{t + \frac{1}{2}}$. The analyses later in the paper fix the particular value of $\eta_{t + \frac{1}{2}}$, which is either $\eta_{t}$ or $\eta_{t + 1}$.

An important property of the solution of Eq. (3), which also explains the name FoBoS, is the necessary optimality condition: at the optimum ${\pmb w}_{t + 1}$, the subgradient set of the objective must contain the zero vector, i.e.

$$
\mathbf{0}\in\partial\left\{\frac{1}{2}\left\|w-w_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\right\|^{2}+\eta_{t+\frac{1}{2}}r(w)\right\}\bigg|_{w=w_{t+1}}.
$$

As $\pmb{w}_{t + \frac{1}{2}}= \pmb{w}_{t}- \eta_{t}\pmb{g}_{t}^{f}$, this condition reads

$$
\mathbf{0}\in\pmb{w}_{t+1}-\pmb{w}_{t}+\eta_{t}\pmb{g}_{t}^{f}+\eta_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\partial r(\pmb{w}_{t+1}).\tag{4}
$$

From $\mathbf{0}\in\pmb{w}_{t+1}-\pmb{w}_{t}+\eta_{t}\pmb{g}_{t}^{f}+\eta_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\partial r(\pmb{w}_{t+1})$ it follows that, as long as ${\pmb w}_{t + 1}$ is taken to be the minimizer of Eq. (3), there is guaranteed to be a vector $\pmb{g}_{t+1}^{r}\in\partial r(\pmb{w}_{t+1})$ with

$$
{\bf 0}={\pmb w}_{t + 1}-{\pmb w}_{t}+ \eta_{t}{\pmb g}_{t}^{f}+ \eta_{t + \frac{1}{2}}{\pmb g}_{t + 1}^{r}\mathrm{~ . ~}
$$

This identity may be read as an update rule in which the new weight vector ${\pmb w}_{t + 1}$ is a linear combination of three vectors: the previous weight vector ${\pmb w}_{t}$, an element of the subgradient set of $f$ at ${\pmb w}_{t}$, and an element of the subgradient of r at the not-yet-known ${\pmb w}_{t + 1}$; this is the origin of the name Forward-Looking Subgradient. In summary, ${\pmb w}_{t + 1}$ can be written as

$$
\pmb{w}_{t + 1}= \pmb{w}_{t}- \eta_{t}\pmb{g}_{t}^{f}- \eta_{t + \frac{1}{2}}\pmb{g}_{t + 1}^{r},\tag{5}
$$

with ${\pmb g}_{t}^{f}\in \partial f ({\pmb w}_{t})$ and $\pmb{g}_{t+1}^{r}\in\partial r(\pmb{w}_{t+1})$. Solving Eq. (3) with r as above brings two main advantages. First, algorithmically, it produces sparse solutions at almost no extra computational cost. Second, thanks to the forward-looking gradient we can reuse existing analyses and prove that the resulting framework inherits the formal convergence guarantees of many existing gradient-based and online convex programming algorithms.

context.name: Setup: choice of the interim step size eta_{t+1/2} (Section 3)
context.statement: At first sight FoBoS appears quite different from subgradient and online convex programming methods. Yet because FoBoS in fact uses a forward-looking subgradient of the regularizer, existing analyses carry over well. In this section we adapt known results, exploiting the forward-looking property of FoBoS, to obtain convergence rate analyses for FoBoS. This requires choosing $\eta_{t + \frac{1}{2}}$ appropriately. As shown below, to get convergence and low regret bounds it suffices to take $\eta_{t + \frac{1}{2}}$ equal to $\eta_{t}$ or to $\eta_{t + 1}$, according to whether the optimization is online or batch. context.name: Assumption: bounded subgradients, Eq. (6)
context.statement:
In this section $w^{\star}$ always denotes the minimizer of $f ({\pmb w}) + r ({\pmb w})$. Below we set $\begin{array}{r}{\|\partial f(\pmb{w})\|\triangleq\operatorname*{sup}_{\pmb{g}\in\partial f(\pmb{w})}\|\pmb{g}\|}\end{array}$. Our first convergence results are derived under the rather general assumption (see, for instance, Langford et al. 2008 or Shalev-Shwartz and Tewari 2009) that the subgradients obey the bounds

$$
\begin{array}{r}{\|\partial f(\pmb{w})\|^{2}\leq Af(\pmb{w})+G^{2},\quad\|\partial r(\pmb{w})\|^{2}\leq Ar(\pmb{w})+G^{2}.}\end{array}\tag{6}
$$

(6) with $G = 0$ and $A = 4$. The following lemma is technical, but it is the central tool behind every convergence result in this paper.

context.name: Lemma 1 (Bounding Step Differences)
context.statement:
Lemma 1 (Bounding Step Differences) Suppose the subgradient norms of f and r obey the bounds of Eq. (6):

$$
\|\partial f(\pmb{w})\|^{2}\leq Af(\pmb{w})+G^{2},\quad\|\partial r(\pmb{w})\|^{2}\leq Ar(\pmb{w})+G^{2}.
$$

Let $\eta_{t + 1}\leq \eta_{t + \frac{1}{2}}\leq \eta_{t}$, and assume $\eta_{t}\le 2 \eta_{t + \frac{1}{2}}$. Then, when the FoBoS update of Eqs. (2) and (3) is used, for a constant $c \leq 4$ and every vector $\pmb{w}^{\star}$,

$$
\begin{array}{r l r}{{2\boldsymbol\eta_{t}\big(1-cA\boldsymbol\eta_{t}\big)f\big(\boldsymbol{w}_{t}\big)+2\boldsymbol\eta_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\big(1-cA\boldsymbol\eta_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\big)\boldsymbol{r}\big(\boldsymbol{w}_{t+1}\big)}}\\ &{\leq}&{2\boldsymbol\eta_{t}f\big(\boldsymbol{w}^{\star}\big)+2\boldsymbol\eta_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\boldsymbol{r}\big(\boldsymbol{w}^{\star}\big)+\|\boldsymbol{w}_{t}-\boldsymbol{w}^{\star}\|^{2}-\|\boldsymbol{w}_{t+1}-\boldsymbol{w}^{\star}\|^{2}+7\boldsymbol\eta_{t}\boldsymbol\eta_{t+\frac{1}{2}}G^{2}\quad .}\end{array}
$$

context.name: Setup: online learning and regret R_{f+r}(T) (Section 4)
context.statement:
This section gives a regret analysis of FoBoS in online settings. An online learning problem supplies a sequence of functions $f_{t}: \mathbb{R}^{n}\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}$. The aim is that the predictions ${\pmb w}_{t}$ incur low regret relative to one fixed optimal predictor $w^{\star}$. Precisely, $f_{t}({\boldsymbol{w}})$ is the loss incurred on the $t^{t h}$ input loss function by the predictor w. For an online algorithm whose predictors are $\boldsymbol{w}_{1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{w}_{t},\ldots$, the regret with respect to a fixed predictor $\pmb{w}^{\star}$ under a regularization function r is

$$
R_{f+r}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[f_{t}(\pmb{w}_{t})+r(\pmb{w}_{t})-\left(f_{t}(\pmb{w}^{\star})+r(\pmb{w}^{\star})\right)\right].
$$

The ideal would be zero regret against a stationary $\pmb{w}^{\star}$ for sequences of any length.

To get an online bound for a sequence of convex functions $f_{t}$, we adapt the arguments of Zinkevich (2003). With the bound of Lemma 1 at hand, a theorem on the online regret of FoBoS can be stated and proved directly. The boundedness assumptions in the proof could be dropped (yielding a regret analogue of the bound in Theorem 2), but we do not consider this notably more interesting. Apart from its use of Lemma 1, the proof closely follows Zinkevich's, and so it is postponed to Appendix A.

namespace ResearchLevel

variable {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]

def HasSubgradientAt (f : E → ℝ) (g x : E) : Prop :=
  ∀ y, f y ≥ f x + @inner ℝ _ _ g (y - x)

def IsFoBoSRun (f r : E → ℝ) (w gf gr : ℕ → E) (η ηhalf : ℕ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  (∀ t, HasSubgradientAt f (gf t) (w t)) ∧
  (∀ t, HasSubgradientAt r (gr t) (w t)) ∧
  (∀ t, w (t + 1) = w t - η t • gf t - ηhalf t • gr (t + 1))

def IsFoBoSOnlineRun (f : ℕ → E → ℝ) (r : E → ℝ) (w gf gr : ℕ → E) (η : ℕ → ℝ) :
    Prop :=
  (∀ t, HasSubgradientAt (f t) (gf t) (w t)) ∧
  (∀ t, HasSubgradientAt r (gr t) (w t)) ∧
  (∀ t, w (t + 1) = w t - η t • gf t - η t • gr (t + 1))

def Regret (f : ℕ → E → ℝ) (r : E → ℝ) (w : ℕ → E) (wstar : E) (T : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ t ∈ Finset.Icc 1 T, (f t (w t) + r (w t) - (f t wstar + r wstar))

def sqL2 {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ i, (x i) ^ 2

noncomputable def linftyNorm {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ := ⨆ i, |x i|

def l1Norm {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ i, |x i|

noncomputable def l2Norm {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ := Real.sqrt (sqL2 x)

def IsProxNorm {n : ℕ} (N : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (x xm : Fin n → ℝ) : Prop :=
  IsMinOn (fun u => sqL2 (u - x) / 2 + lam * N u) Set.univ xm

context.name: Setup: online learning and regret R_{f+r}(T) (Section 4)
context.statement:
This section gives a regret analysis of FoBoS in online settings. An online learning problem supplies a sequence of functions $f_{t}: \mathbb{R}^{n}\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}$. The aim is that the predictions ${\pmb w}_{t}$ incur low regret relative to one fixed optimal predictor $w^{\star}$. Precisely, $f_{t}({\boldsymbol{w}})$ is the loss incurred on the $t^{t h}$ input loss function by the predictor w. For an online algorithm whose predictors are $\boldsymbol{w}_{1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{w}_{t},\ldots$, the regret with respect to a fixed predictor $\pmb{w}^{\star}$ under a regularization function r is

$$
R_{f+r}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[f_{t}(\pmb{w}_{t})+r(\pmb{w}_{t})-\left(f_{t}(\pmb{w}^{\star})+r(\pmb{w}^{\star})\right)\right].
$$

The ideal would be zero regret against a stationary $\pmb{w}^{\star}$ for sequences of any length.

To get an online bound for a sequence of convex functions $f_{t}$, we adapt the arguments of Zinkevich (2003). With the bound of Lemma 1 at hand, a theorem on the online regret of FoBoS can be stated and proved directly. The boundedness assumptions in the proof could be dropped (yielding a regret analogue of the bound in Theorem 2), but we do not consider this notably more interesting. Apart from its use of Lemma 1, the proof closely follows Zinkevich's, and so it is postponed to Appendix A.

context.name: Definition: H-strong convexity and Eq. (17)
context.statement:
FoBoS also admits an improved regret bound when the loss functions $f_{t}(\cdot)$ or the function $r(\cdot)$ are strongly convex. Hazan et al. (2006) showed that, for the projected gradient method with strongly convex functions, regret of order ${\cal O}(\log T)$ is attainable by exploiting the curvature of the functions $f_{t}$ instead of relying only on convexity and linearity as in Theorems 2 and 6. These results extend to FoBoS whenever $f_{t}({\pmb w}) + r ({\pmb w})$ is strongly convex, at least on the region $\| \pmb{w}- \pmb{w}^{\star}\| \leq D$. For the sake of completeness we restate some definitions and give the logarithmic regret bound for FoBoS. A function f is said to be H-strongly convex when

$$
f(\pmb{w})\geq f(\pmb{w}_{t})+\langle\nabla f(\pmb{w}_{t}),\pmb{w}-\pmb{w}_{t}\rangle+\frac{H}{2}\|\pmb{w}-\pmb{w}_{t}\|^{2}.
$$

Hence, when r and the functions $f_{t}$ are strongly convex with constants $H_{r}\geq 0$ and $H_{f}\geq 0$ respectively, we get $H = H_{f}+ H_{r}$, and H-strong convexity yields

$$
f_{t}({\boldsymbol{w}}_{t}) - f ({\boldsymbol{w}}^{\star}) + r ({\boldsymbol{w}}_{t}) - r ({\boldsymbol{w}}^{\star}) \leq \left\langle{\boldsymbol{g}}_{t}^{f}+{\boldsymbol{g}}_{t}^{r},{\boldsymbol{w}}_{t}-{\boldsymbol{w}}^{\star}\right\rangle - \frac{H}{2}\|{\boldsymbol{w}}_{t}-{\boldsymbol{w}}^{\star}\|^{2}~ .\tag{17}
$$

It is not necessary for both $f_{t}$ and r to be strongly convex; it is enough that at least one of the two has a positive strong convexity constant. For instance, with $\begin{array}{r}{r ({\bf w}) = \frac{\lambda}{2}\|{\bf w}\|^{2}}\end{array}$ we have $H \geq \lambda$ provided the functions $f_{t}$ are convex. Using Eq. (17), we can build directly on Hazan et al. (2006) to prove a stronger regret bound for the online learning case. Because the proof resembles that of Hazan et al., it too is deferred to Appendix A.

context.name: Eq. (36), from the proof of Theorem 6
context.statement:
Proof of Theorem 6 When $\| \partial f \|$ and $\| \partial r \|$ are bounded by G, Lemma 1 gives at once

$$
f_{t}(\boldsymbol{w}_{t})-f_{t}(\boldsymbol{w}^{\star})+r(\boldsymbol{w}_{t+1})-r(\boldsymbol{w}^{\star})\leq\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\left(\|\boldsymbol{w}_{t}-\boldsymbol{w}^{\star}\|^{2}-\|\boldsymbol{w}_{t+1}-\boldsymbol{w}^{\star}\|^{2}\right)+\frac{7}{2}G^{2}\eta_{t}.\tag{36}
$$

context.name: Theorem 6 (another result of the same paper)
context.statement:
Theorem 6 Suppose that $\| \pmb{w}_{t}- \pmb{w}^{\star}\| \leq D$ holds at every iteration, and that G is an upper bound on the norms of the subgradient sets $\partial f_{t}$ and $\partial r$. Fix an arbitrary scalar $c > 0$. Then FoBoS run with step sizes $\eta_{t}= c / \sqrt{t}$ has a regret bound of the form

$$
R_{f+r}(T)\leq 2GD+\left({\frac{D^{2}}{2c}}+7G^{2}c\right)\sqrt{T}.
$$

  ∀ y, f y ≥ f x + @inner ℝ _ _ g (y - x)

def IsFoBoSRun (f r : E → ℝ) (w gf gr : ℕ → E) (η ηhalf : ℕ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  (∀ t, HasSubgradientAt f (gf t) (w t)) ∧

$$
\mathcal{P}.1:~{\pmb w}_{t}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{{\pmb w}}\frac{1}{2}\|{\pmb w}-{\pmb w}_{t-1}\|^{2}+\lambda_{t}\|{\pmb w}\|_{q}\enspace .\tag{28}
$$

and let $\pmb{w}_{T}$ be the vector obtained at the end. Denote by $\pmb{w}^{\star}$ the optimal solution of the problem

$$
\mathcal{P}. 2:\pmb{w}^{\star}=\underset{\pmb{w}}{\mathrm{argmin}}\frac{1}{2}\|\pmb{w}-\pmb{w}_{0}\|^{2}+\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\lambda_{t}\right)\|\pmb{w}\|_{q}.
$$

Then, for $q\in\{1,2,\infty\}$, the two vectors $\pmb{w}_{T}$ and $\pmb{w}^{\star}$ coincide.

context.name: Setup and notation: objective f + r, convex and nonnegative (Section 1)
context.statement:
We first fix the notation used throughout the paper. Scalars are written as lower case letters and vectors as bold lower case letters, e.g. w. For two vectors u and v, $\langle{\pmb u},{\pmb v}\rangle$ is their inner product. The p-norm of a vector x is written $\| \pmb{x}\|_{p}$, and ||x|| abbreviates $\| \pmb{x}\|_{2}$.

The paper studies an algorithmic framework for regularized convex programming whose aim is to minimize a sum of two functions,

$$
f({\pmb w})+r({\pmb w}),\tag{1}
$$

in which f and r are both convex and bounded below (so that, with no loss of generality, they are taken to map into $\mathbb{R}_{+}$). Typically f is an empirical loss of the form $\textstyle\sum_{i\in S}\ell_{i}(w)$ built from loss functions $\ell_{i}: \mathbb{R}^{n}\to \mathbb{R}_{+}$, and $r(w)$ is a regularizer that penalizes overly complex vectors, e.g. $r(\mathbf{w})=\lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|_{p}$. Such tasks are common in machine learning, where learning problems for decision and prediction are formulated as convex optimization problems. With this in mind, we study a general and intuitive algorithm called forward-backward splitting for minimizing Eq. (1), with particular emphasis on derivations for, and the use of, regularization functions that are not differentiable.

context.name: Definition: subgradient set
context.statement:
For a function f and a point w, write $\partial f ({\boldsymbol{w}})$ for the subgradient set of f at w, that is,

$$
\partial f(w)=\{g\mid\forall v:f(v)\geq f(w)+\langle g,v-w\rangle\}.
$$

context.name: Algorithm: FoBoS update and forward-looking subgradient, Eqs. (2)-(5) (Section 2)
context.statement:
Our version of Forward-Backward Splitting is driven by the wish that the iterates ${\pmb w}_{t}$ be able to reach points where r is not differentiable. For problems such as $\ell_{1}$-regularization, the method sidesteps the difficulties caused by non-differentiability by alternating subgradient steps with analytical minimization steps. Informally, FoBoS resembles the projected subgradient method, except that the projection step is replaced or augmented by an instantaneous minimization problem whose solution can be derived in closed form. The method is compact: every iteration is made of the two steps below,

$$
\begin{array}{r l r}{{\bf w}_{t + \frac{1}{2}}}&{{}=}&{{\bf w}_{t}- \boldsymbol \eta_{t}{\bf g}_{t}^{f},}\end{array}\tag{2}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r c l}{{\pmb w}_{t+1}}&{=}&{\displaystyle\operatorname*{argmin}_{{\pmb w}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\left\|{\pmb w}-{\pmb w}_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\right\|^{2}+\eta_{t+\frac{1}{2}}r({\pmb w})\right\}\ .}\end{array}\tag{3}
$$

Here $g_{t}^{f}$ is an element of $\partial f ({\pmb w}_{t})$, and $\eta_{t}$ denotes the step size used by the algorithm at time step t. What value $\eta_{t}$ takes depends on the particular setting and analysis. The first step is thus nothing more than an unconstrained subgradient step for the function $f$. The second step produces a new vector that balances two aims: (i) remaining near the interim vector $w_{t + \frac{1}{2}}$, and (ii) having small complexity as measured by r. Observe that r is multiplied by an interim step size, written $\eta_{t + \frac{1}{2}}$. The analyses later in the paper fix the particular value of $\eta_{t + \frac{1}{2}}$, which is either $\eta_{t}$ or $\eta_{t + 1}$.

An important property of the solution of Eq. (3), which also explains the name FoBoS, is the necessary optimality condition: at the optimum ${\pmb w}_{t + 1}$, the subgradient set of the objective must contain the zero vector, i.e.

$$
\mathbf{0}\in\partial\left\{\frac{1}{2}\left\|w-w_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\right\|^{2}+\eta_{t+\frac{1}{2}}r(w)\right\}\bigg|_{w=w_{t+1}}.
$$

As $\pmb{w}_{t + \frac{1}{2}}= \pmb{w}_{t}- \eta_{t}\pmb{g}_{t}^{f}$, this condition reads

$$
\mathbf{0}\in\pmb{w}_{t+1}-\pmb{w}_{t}+\eta_{t}\pmb{g}_{t}^{f}+\eta_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\partial r(\pmb{w}_{t+1}).\tag{4}
$$

From $\mathbf{0}\in\pmb{w}_{t+1}-\pmb{w}_{t}+\eta_{t}\pmb{g}_{t}^{f}+\eta_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\partial r(\pmb{w}_{t+1})$ it follows that, as long as ${\pmb w}_{t + 1}$ is taken to be the minimizer of Eq. (3), there is guaranteed to be a vector $\pmb{g}_{t+1}^{r}\in\partial r(\pmb{w}_{t+1})$ with

$$
{\bf 0}={\pmb w}_{t + 1}-{\pmb w}_{t}+ \eta_{t}{\pmb g}_{t}^{f}+ \eta_{t + \frac{1}{2}}{\pmb g}_{t + 1}^{r}\mathrm{~ . ~}
$$

This identity may be read as an update rule in which the new weight vector ${\pmb w}_{t + 1}$ is a linear combination of three vectors: the previous weight vector ${\pmb w}_{t}$, an element of the subgradient set of $f$ at ${\pmb w}_{t}$, and an element of the subgradient of r at the not-yet-known ${\pmb w}_{t + 1}$; this is the origin of the name Forward-Looking Subgradient. In summary, ${\pmb w}_{t + 1}$ can be written as

$$
\pmb{w}_{t + 1}= \pmb{w}_{t}- \eta_{t}\pmb{g}_{t}^{f}- \eta_{t + \frac{1}{2}}\pmb{g}_{t + 1}^{r},\tag{5}
$$

with ${\pmb g}_{t}^{f}\in \partial f ({\pmb w}_{t})$ and $\pmb{g}_{t+1}^{r}\in\partial r(\pmb{w}_{t+1})$. Solving Eq. (3) with r as above brings two main advantages. First, algorithmically, it produces sparse solutions at almost no extra computational cost. Second, thanks to the forward-looking gradient we can reuse existing analyses and prove that the resulting framework inherits the formal convergence guarantees of many existing gradient-based and online convex programming algorithms.

context.name: Setup: proximal step notation, Eq. (18) and [z]_+ (Section 5)
context.statement:
We begin by adjusting the notation. To make the derivations simpler, we write v for the vector $w_{t + \frac{1}{2}}= w_{t}- \eta_{t}g_{t}^{f}$ and write $\tilde{\lambda}$ for $\eta_{t + \frac{1}{2}}\cdot \lambda$. In this notation the problem of Eq. (3) becomes

$$
\operatorname*{minimize}_{\pmb{w}}\frac{1}{2}\|\pmb{w}-\pmb{v}\|^{2}+\widetilde{\lambda}r(\pmb{w}).\tag{18}
$$

We use $[ z ]_{+}$ for $\max\{0,z\}$. Although full derivations are given for every regularization function we consider, to save space we do not formally state well-known technical lemmas. Many of the results below were stated implicitly by Wright et al. (2009).

context.name: Update: l1 regularization (soft thresholding), Eq. (19) (Section 5.1)
context.statement:
Taking $r(\pmb{w})=\lambda\|\pmb{w}\|_{1}$ leads to a simple and intuitive update. To begin with, the objective decomposes, since Eq. (18) can be rewritten as

$$
\operatorname*{minimize}_{\boldsymbol{w}}\ \sum_{j=1}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{2}(w_{j}-v_{j})^{2}+\tilde{\lambda}|w_{j}|\right).
$$

Fix one coordinate of w and, to shorten notation, drop the index $j$. Let $w^{\star}$ be the minimizer of $\frac{1}{2}(w-v)^{2}+\tilde{\lambda}|w|$. Plainly $w^{\star}\cdot v \geq 0$. Otherwise $w^{\star}\cdot v < 0$, but then ${\scriptstyle{\frac{1}{2}}}v^{2}<$ $\begin{array}{r}{\frac{1}{2}v^{2}-w^{\star}\cdot v+\frac{1}{2}(w^{\star})^{2}<\frac{1}{2}(v-w^{\star})^{2}+\tilde{\lambda}|w^{\star}|}\end{array}$, which contradicts the assumed optimality of $w^{\star}$. Since the objective is symmetric in v, we may also take $v \geq 0$; it then remains to minimize $\frac{1}{2}\left(w-v\right)^{2}+\tilde{\lambda}w$ subject to $w \ge 0$. Attaching a Lagrange multiplier $\beta \geq 0$ to this constraint gives the Lagrangian $\frac{1}{2}(w-v)^{2}+\tilde{\lambda}w-\beta w$. Differentiating the Lagrangian in w and equating to zero shows that the optimum is $w^{\star}= v - \tilde{\lambda}+ \beta$. When $w^{\star}> 0$, complementary slackness, which requires the optimal pair $w^{\star}$ and β to satisfy $w^{\star}\beta = 0$ (Boyd and Vandenberghe, 2004), forces $\beta = 0$, hence $w^{\star}= v - \tilde{\lambda}$. When $v < \tilde{\lambda}$, we have $v - \tilde{\lambda}< 0$, so β must be positive and, again by complementary slackness, $w^{\star}= 0$. The case $v \leq 0$ is the same up to a change of signs. Putting this together and returning to the full notation, the coordinates of the optimal solution $\pmb{w}^{\star}= \pmb{w}_{t + 1}$ are obtained from $w_{t + \frac{1}{2}}$ by

$$
w_{t+1,j}=\mathrm{sign}\Big(w_{t+\frac{1}{2},j}\Big)\left[|w_{t+\frac{1}{2},j}| -\widetilde{\lambda}\right]_{+}=\mathrm{sign}\Big(w_{t,j}-\eta_{t}g_{t,j}^{f}\Big)\left[\Big|w_{t,j}-\eta_{t}g_{t,j}^{f}\Big| -\eta_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\cdot\lambda\right]_{+}.\tag{19}
$$

This update can produce sparse solutions: any component of ${\pmb w}_{t +{\frac{1}{2}}}$ whose absolute value is below $\tilde{\lambda}$ yields a zero in the corresponding component of ${\pmb w}_{t + 1}$. Eq. (19) therefore provides a simple online and offline method for minimizing a convex $f$ under $\ell_{1}$ regularization.

context.name: Update: l2^2 regularization, Eq. (20) (Section 5.2)
context.statement:
With $\begin{array}{r}{r(\pmb{w})=\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\pmb{w}\|_{2}^{2}}\end{array}$ the optimization problem is very simple:

$$
\operatorname*{minimize}_{\boldsymbol{w}}\frac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol{w}-\boldsymbol{v}\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{\lambda}\|\boldsymbol{w}\|^{2},
$$

where, to make the solution more concise, $\tilde{\lambda}$ has been replaced by $\frac{1}{2}\tilde{\lambda}$. Setting the derivative of this objective to zero gives $\pmb{w}^{\star}- v + \tilde{\lambda}\pmb{w}^{\star}= 0$, and in the original notation this is the update

$$
\pmb{w}_{t + 1}= \frac{\pmb{w}_{t}- \pmb{\eta}_{t}\pmb{g}_{t}^{f}}{1 + \tilde{\lambda}}.\tag{20}
$$

context.name: Update: l2 regularization (Section 5.3)
context.statement:
The $\ell_{2}$ norm of the weight vector is a less commonly used choice of regularizer. Taking $r(\boldsymbol{w})=\tilde{\lambda}\|\boldsymbol{w}\|$, we arrive at the problem

$$
\operatorname*{minimize}_{\boldsymbol{w}}\frac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol{w}-\boldsymbol{v}\|^{2}+\widetilde{\lambda}\|\boldsymbol{w}\|.\tag{21}
$$

Any solution of Eq. (21) points in the direction of v, i.e. it has the form $\pmb{w}^{\star}= s \pmb{v}$ with $s \geq 0$. To verify this form, suppose for contradiction that $\pmb{w}^{\star}= s \pmb{v}+ \pmb{u}$, where u lies in the null space of v (should u have components parallel to v, these can be added to v, leaving an orthogonal $\pmb{u}^{\prime}$) and s is allowed to be negative. As u is orthogonal to $v$, the objective can be written in terms of $s$, $v$ and u as

$$
\frac 12(1-s)^{2}\|{\pmb v}\|^{2}+\frac 12\|{\pmb u}\|^{2}+\widetilde{\lambda}(\|{\pmb v}\|+\|{\pmb u}\|)\ge\frac 12(1-s)^{2}\|{\pmb v}\|^{2}+\widetilde{\lambda}\|{\pmb v}\|.
$$

So u has to be the zero vector, ${\pmb u}={\bf 0}$, and the optimization problem can be written as

$$
\operatorname*{minimize}_{s}\frac{1}{2}(1-s)^{2}\|\pmb{v}\|^{2}+\widetilde{\lambda}s\|\pmb{v}\|\enspace .
$$

Moreover, no negative s can be optimal. Indeed, when $s < 0$,

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-s)^{2}\|\pmb{v}\|^{2}+\tilde{\lambda}s\|\pmb{v}\|<\frac{1}{2}\|\pmb{v}\|^{2}.
$$

Hence the choice $s = 0$ attains a smaller objective value, which rules out negative s as an optimal solution. We are thus led once more to a constrained scalar problem, $\operatorname*{minimize}_{s\geq 0}\frac{1}{2}(1-s)^{2}\|\pmb{v}\|^{2}+\tilde{\lambda}s\|\pmb{v}\|$, whose Lagrangian is

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-s)^{2}\|\pmb{v}\|^{2}+\tilde{\lambda}s\|\pmb{v}\|-\beta s\ ,
$$

with $\beta \geq 0$. Differentiating the Lagrangian in s and setting the derivative to zero gives $(s-1)\|{\pmb v}\|^{2}+\tilde{\lambda}\|{\pmb v}\|-{\beta}=0$, and hence the closed form $s = 1 - \tilde{\lambda}/ \| v \| + \beta / \| v \|^{2}$. If $s > 0$, complementary slackness gives $\beta = 0$, and s simplifies to $s = 1 - \tilde{\lambda}/ \| v \|$. This quantity is positive if and only if $\| v \| > \tilde{\lambda}$. If $\| v \| < \tilde{\lambda}$, then β has to be positive and complementary slackness yields $s = 0$.

In summary, with $\ell_{2}$ regularization the second step of the FoBoS update is

$$
w_{t+1}=\left[1-\frac{\tilde{\lambda}}{\lVert w_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\rVert}\right]_{+}w_{t+\frac{1}{2}}=\left[1-\frac{\tilde{\lambda}}{\lVert w_{t}-\eta_{t}g_{t}^{f}\rVert}\right]_{+}(w_{t}-\eta_{t}g_{t}^{f})\ .
$$

Consequently, $\ell_{2}$ regularization gives the zero weight vector exactly under the condition $\| \pmb{w}_{t}- \pmb{\eta}_{t}\pmb{g}_{t}^{f}\| \le \tilde{\lambda}$. As a requirement for sparsity this is considerably stronger than the one for $\ell_{1}$ (there a single weight becomes sparse depending only on its own value, whereas here sparsity occurs only when the whole weight vector has $\ell_{2}$-norm below $\tilde{\lambda}$), so in high dimensions it is unlikely to be met. It is nonetheless a key building block when a mixed $\ell_{1}/ \ell_{2}$-norm serves as the regularizer, as shown later.

context.name: Update: l-infinity regularization via its dual (l1-ball projection), Eqs. (22)-(25) (Section 5.4)
context.statement:
Next we consider a regularizer that has received less attention, the $\ell_{\infty}$ norm of w. On its own this regularizer cannot offer a strong guarantee against overfitting, because many of the weights of w may go unpenalized. There are, however, settings in which one wants to treat blocks of variables as a group, as in $\ell_{1}/ \ell_{\infty}$ regularization. We postpone the discussion of mixed norms once more and concentrate on the $\ell_{\infty}$ norm alone, since it is a building block. Concretely, we want an efficient solution of the problem

$$
\operatorname*{minimize}_{\boldsymbol{w}}\frac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol{w}-\boldsymbol{v}\|^{2}+\tilde{\lambda}\|\boldsymbol{w}\|_{\infty}\textrm{.}\tag{22}
$$

An efficient algorithm for the minimizer of Eq. (22) could be derived from properties of the subgradient set of $\| \boldsymbol{w}\|_{\infty}$. The dual form of Eq. (22), however, has a well-known solution. Since the conjugate of a quadratic function is quadratic and the conjugate of the $\ell_{\infty}$ norm is the $\ell_{1}$ barrier function, the dual of the problem in Eq. (22) is immediately seen to be

$$
\operatorname*{maximize}_{\alpha}-\frac{1}{2}\left\|\alpha-\pmb{v}\right\|_{2}^{2}\mathrm{s . t .}\left\|\pmb{\alpha}\right\|_{1}\leq\tilde{\lambda}\mathrm{~.~}\tag{23}
$$

In addition, the dual variables $\pmb{\alpha}$ are related to the primal by ${\pmb{\alpha}}={\pmb{v}}-{\pmb{w}}$. Solving the dual form in Eq. (23) therefore readily gives a solution of Eq. (22). Problem Eq. (23) is the same as Euclidean projection onto the $\ell_{1}$ ball, which many authors have studied. The solution summarized here follows recent work of Duchi et al. (2008). The maximizer of Eq. (23), written $\alpha^{\star}$, has the form

$$
\alpha_{j}^{\star}=\mathrm{sign}(v_{j})\left[|v_{j}| -\theta\right]_{+}\ ,\tag{24}
$$

with θ a non-negative scalar. A linear-time algorithm for computing θ is given by Duchi et al. (2008). We therefore do not analyze that algorithm and instead concentrate on the core properties that affect the solution of the problem in Eq. (22). Computing θ requires finding a pivot element of v, namely the $\rho^{t h}$ order statistic $v_{(\rho)}$ (with $v_{(1)}$ the entry of v of largest magnitude), characterized as follows: $v_{(\rho)}$ is the element of v of smallest magnitude for which

$$
\sum_{j: |v_{j}| > |v_{(\rho)}|}\bigl(|v_{j}| - |v_{(\rho)}|\bigr)<\tilde{\lambda}\ .
$$

When every element of v (with an extra element equal to 0 appended to take care of the smallest entry) satisfies this requirement, θ = 0 is the optimal choice. In the remaining case,

$$
\theta=\frac{1}{\rho}\left(\sum_{j: |v_{j}| > |v_{(\rho)}|}|v_{j}| -\tilde{\lambda}\right).
$$

So θ = 0 is optimal exactly when $\sum_{j = 1}^{n}| v_{j}| \leq \tilde{\lambda}$ (not by coincidence, this is just the subgradient optimality condition for the zero vector in Eq. (22)).

Combining the linear relation $\pmb{\alpha}= \pmb{v}- \pmb{w}\Rightarrow \pmb{w}= \pmb{v}- \pmb{\alpha}$ with the dual solution provided by Eq. (24), the solution of Eq. (22) is

$$
w_{t+1,j}=\mathrm{sign}\Big(w_{t+\frac{1}{2},j}\Big)\operatorname*{min}\left\{\Big|w_{t+\frac{1}{2},j}\Big|\ ,\ \theta\right\}\ .\tag{25}
$$

As noted above, $\theta = 0$ if and only if $\| \pmb{w}_{t + \frac{1}{2}}\|_{1}\leq \tilde{\lambda}$, and otherwise $\theta > 0$ and θ can be computed in $O(n)$ steps. Put in words, the components of ${\pmb w}_{t + 1}$ are obtained by capping every component of ${\pmb w}_{t}$ at θ, with θ equal to zero when the 1-norm of $w_{t + \frac{1}{2}}$ is below $\tilde{\lambda}$. This property mirrors, through duality, the $\ell_{2}$-regularized update, which gives a zero weight vector when the 2-norm (which is self-dual) of v is below $\tilde{\lambda}$. These properties can be used with mixed-norm regularization to obtain sparse solutions for complex prediction problems; this is described later, and preliminary results are given in Sec. 7. Before turning to it, we present one further norm-related regularizer.

Lemma 5 (Weighted-Regret Bound for EXP3). Let $\{\eta_{t}\}$ be a non-increasing step-size sequence such that $\eta_{t}\leq\frac 12e^{-2}$ for all t. Let $\left\{l_{t}^{\left(i\right)}\right\}$ be a cost sequence such that $l_{t}^{(i)}\in [0,1]$ for every $t,i.$ Let $\{d_{t}\}$ be a delay sequence such that the cost from round t is received at round $t + d_{t}$ . Define the set $\mathcal{M}^{\ast}$ of all samples that are not received before round T or that were delayed by $\begin{array}{r}{d_{t}\geq \frac{1}{e^{2}\eta_{t}}- 1}\end{array}$ . Then using EXP3 (Algorithm 3) guarantees:

1. With an oblivious adversary and $\gamma_{t}= 0$ for all t:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(a_{t})}-\operatorname*{min}_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(i)}\right\}\leq\log K+\frac{e^{2}}{2}K\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}^{2}+4\sum_{t\notin\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}^{2}d_{t}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}.\tag{42}
$$

2. With an adaptive adversary and $\gamma_{t}= \eta_{t}$ for all t:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(a_{t})}-\operatorname*{min}_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(i)}\right\}\leq 2+2\log K+(1+\frac{e^{2}}{2})K\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}^{2}+4 e^{2}K\sum_{t\notin\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}^{2}d_{t}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}.\tag{43}
$$

context.name: Setup: problem formulation, adversaries, delays, missing samples (Section 2)
context.statement:
Consider a player that in each round t from 1 to $T$ picks an action $\pmb{a}_{t}\in \mathcal{K}$ from a set $\mathcal{K}$ . The cost at round t from playing $\pmb{a}_{t}$ is $l_{t}\left(\boldsymbol{a}_{t}\right)\in\left[0,1\right]$ . We consider two types of adversaries:

1. Oblivious Adversary: chooses the cost functions $l_{1},...,l_{T}$ before the game starts.

2. Adaptive Adversary: chooses the cost function $l_{t}$ after observing $\{a_{1}, \ldots a_{t - 1}\}$ , for each t.

With full information and no delays, the player gets to know the function $l_{t}$ immediately after playing $\pmb{a}_{t}$ . In the bandit delayed feedback scenario, the player only gets to know the value of ${l}_{t}\left(\pmb{a}_{t}\right)$ at the beginning of round $t + d_{t}$ . (i.e., after a delay of $d_{t}\geq 1$ rounds). The adversary (oblivious or adaptive) chooses the delay sequence $\{d_{t}\}$ before the game starts.

We assume that the cost feedback includes the timestamp of the action that incurred this cost. This is indeed the case in many applications, such as when robots take physical actions, a recommendation is made to a customer or a treatment is given to a patient. If the delays are bounded by d, Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2018) have shown that EXP3 can still be implemented even with no timestamps, with expected regret $O(\sqrt{dTK\log K})$ instead of $O\left({\sqrt{\left(d+K\right)T\log K}}\right)$ . For our unbounded delays case, it is not clear if FKM or EXP3 can be implemented without timestamps.

The set of costs (feedback samples) received and used at round t is denoted $\mathcal{S}_{t}$ , so $s \in \mathcal{S}_{t}$ means that the cost of $\pmb{a}_{s}$ from round s is received and used at round t. Since the game lasts for $T$ rounds, all costs for which $t + d_{t}> T$ are never received. Of course, the value of $d_{t}$ does not matter as long as $t + d_{t}> T$ , and these are just samples that the adversary chose to prevent the player from receiving. We name these costs the missing samples and denote their set by $\mathcal{M}$ .

While the rounds of the game are indexed by t, it will be useful to our analysis to index a finer time scale that counts the steps of the algorithm for every such t. We define $s_{-}, s_{+}$ as the steps a moment before and after the algorithm uses the feedback from round s, respectively. These steps are taking place in round t if $s \in S_{t}$

context.name: Setup: multi-armed bandit special case (Section 2)
context.statement:
We analyze two widely applied algorithms for the two central special cases of the scenario above:

2. Multi-Armed Bandit - $\mathcal{K}=\{1,...,K\},\ l_{t}:\{1,...,K\}\to [0,1].$ With no delays, the EXP3 algorithm (Auer et al., 2002) achieves an expected regret of $O \left({\sqrt{T K \log K}}\right)$ for this problem.

context.name: Setup: EXP3 with delays, mixed actions and the filtration F_t (eq. 41, Section 6)
context.statement:
Consider a player that at each round t picks one out of K arms. Let $a_{t}$ be the arm the player chooses at round t. The cost at round t of playing arm i is $l_{t}^{(i)}\in [0,1]$ , and let $l_{t}=\left(l_{t}^{(1)},...,l_{t}^{(K)}\right)$ be the cost vector. At round t, the EXP3 algorithm, detailed in Algorithm 3, chooses an arm at random using a distribution that depends on the history of the game. The variant when $\gamma_{t}\neq 0$ , as we use against an adaptive adversary, is known as EXP3-IX (see Neu (2015)). We denote the vector of probabilities of the player for choosing arms at round t by $\pmb{p}_{t}\in \Delta^{K}$ , where $\Delta^{K}$ denotes the K-simplex. This is also known as the mixed action of the player. We also define the following filtration

$$
\mathcal{F}_{t}=\sigma\left(\left\{a_{s}\vert s+d_{s}\le t\right\}\cup\left\{l_{s}\vert s\le t\right\}\right)\tag{41}
$$

which is generated from all the actions for which the feedback was received up to round t and all cost functions up to round t. Note that the mixed action $\pmb{p}_{t}$ is a $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ -measurable random variable since $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ includes everything that could affect the algorithm up to round t. With a slight abuse of notation, we use $\mathcal{F}_{s_{-}}$ to denote the filtration induced from all actions for which the feedback has been received and used up to step $s_{-}$ and all the cost functions up to round t.

context.name: Algorithm 3 (EXP3 with delays, eqs. 44-45)
context.statement:
Algorithm 3 EXP3 with delays   
Initialization: Let $\{\eta_{t}\}$ and $\{\gamma_{t}\}$ be non-negative non-increasing sequences such that $\eta_{1}\leq \frac{e^{- 2}}{2}$ and   
set $\tilde{L}_{1}^{(i)}=0$ and $\begin{array}{r}{p_{1}^{(i)}=\frac{1}{K}}\end{array}$ for $i=1,...,K.$   
For $t=1,...,T$ do   
1. Choose an arm $a_{t}$ at random according to the distribution $\pmb{p}_{t}$ .   
2. Collect in $S_{t}$ all the rounds s for which $l_{s}^{(a_{s})}$ arrived at round t after a delay of $\begin{array}{r}{d_{s}\le \frac{1}{e^{2}\eta_{s}}- 1}\end{array}$   
3. Set $\tilde{L}_{t}^{(i)}=\tilde{L}_{t-1}^{(i)}$ for all i. Update the weights of arm $a_{s}$ for all $s \in S_{t}$ using   
$\tilde{L}_{t}^{(a_{s})}=\tilde{L}_{t}^{(a_{s})}+\eta_{s}\frac{l_{s}^{(a_{s})}}{p_{s}^{(a_{s})}+\gamma_{s}}.$ (44)   
4. Update the mixed action for $i=1,\ldots,K$ using   
$p_{t+1}^{(i)}=\frac{e^{-\tilde{L}_{t}^{(i)}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}e^{-\tilde{L}_{t}^{(j)}}}.$ (45)   
End

context.name: Lemma 8 (effect of delays, eq. 66)
context.statement:
Lemma 8. Let $\{\eta_{t}\}$ be a non-increasing step-size sequence. Let $\{d_{t}\}$ be a delay such that the cost from round t is received at round $t + d_{t}$ . Let $S_{t}$ be the set of feedback samples received and used at round t. Define the set $\mathcal{M}^{\ast}$ of all samples that are not received and used before round T. Then

$$
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\eta_{s}\left(\sum_{r=s}^{t-1}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{S}_{r}}\eta_{q}+\sum_{q\in\mathcal{S}_{t},q<s}\eta_{q}\right)\le 2\sum_{t\not\in\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}^{2}d_{t}.\tag{66}
$$

context.name: Lemma 9 (ratio bounds on the mixed action)
context.statement:
The following lemma generalizes Lemma 2 from Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2019) to a sequence of delays $\{d_{t}\}$ and a sequence of step-sizes $\{\eta_{t}\}$

Lemma 9. Let $\{\eta_{t}\}$ be a positive non-increasing step-size sequence such that $\eta_{t}\leq \frac{1}{2}e^{- 2}$ for all t. Let $\begin{array}{r}{\mathcal{D}= \Big \{t | d_{t}\geq \frac{1}{e^{2}\eta_{t}}- 1 \Big \}}\end{array}$ . Then for every s,t such that $s \in \mathcal{S}_{t}$ (so $s \notin \mathcal{D}$ ) Algorithm 3 maintains for all $i=1,...,K$ both $\begin{array}{r}{\frac{p_{s_{+}}^{(i)}}{p_{s_{-}}^{(i)}}\leq\frac{1}{1-e^{2}\eta_{s}}}\end{array}$ and $\frac{p_{s_{-}}^{(i)}}{p_{s}^{(i)}}\leq e^{2}$

context.name: Lemma 10 (softmax smoothness, eq. 107)
context.statement:
The next lemma shows standard smoothness properties of the softmax function, and we provide it here for completeness.

Lemma 10. Let $\begin{array}{r}{h_{i}\left(\pmb{x}\right)=\frac{e^{-x_{i}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}e^{-x_{j}}}}\end{array}$ and $h\left(\pmb{x}\right)=(h_{1}\left(\pmb{x}\right),...,h_{K}\left(\pmb{x}\right))$ . Then $\forall \mathbf{x}\in \mathbb{R}^{K}$ and $\forall \Delta \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{K}$

$$
\begin{array}{r}{\|h\left(\pmb{x}\right)-h\left(\pmb{x}+\Delta\right)\|_{1}\leq 2\left\langle h\left(\pmb{x}\right),\Delta\right\rangle .}\end{array}\tag{107}
$$

context.name: Lemma 11 (Neu 2015 concentration, eq. 111)
context.statement:
The next Lemma is taken from Neu (2015), and we provide a (very) slightly modified proof to verify that the same result holds even when the order of arrivals changes as a result of the delayed feedback.

Lemma 11. Let $\tilde{l}_{t}^{(i)}=\frac{l_{t}^{(i)}1_{\{a_{t}=i\}}}{p_{t}^{(i)}+\gamma_{t}}$ . If $\left\{\alpha_{t}^{(i)}\right\}$ is a non-negative sequence such that $\alpha_{t}^{(i)}\leq 2\gamma_{t}$ for all t and all i, then

$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t\notin{\mathcal{M}}^{*}}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\alpha_{t}^{(i)}\left(\tilde{l}_{t}^{(i)}-l_{t}^{(i)}\right)>\log\frac{1}{\delta}\right)\leq\delta .\tag{111}
$$

### Lemma 5
NOTE (Lemma 5, oblivious case) — The Lean adds a hypothesis (`a_fresh`) that the paper never states as an assumption of Lemma 5 or Algorithm 3, but uses inside the proof of the oblivious case of Lemma 5 (appendix Section 13.2, headed "Proof of Lemma 6" in the paper): each arm a_t is drawn with fresh randomness. nl_statement:
Lemma 5 (Weighted-Regret Bound for EXP3). Let $\{\eta_{t}\}$ be a non-increasing step-size sequence such that $\eta_{t}\leq\frac 12e^{-2}$ for all t. Let $\left\{l_{t}^{\left(i\right)}\right\}$ be a cost sequence such that $l_{t}^{(i)}\in [0,1]$ for every $t,i.$ Let $\{d_{t}\}$ be a delay sequence such that the cost from round t is received at round $t + d_{t}$ . Define the set $\mathcal{M}^{\ast}$ of all samples that are not received before round T or that were delayed by $\begin{array}{r}{d_{t}\geq \frac{1}{e^{2}\eta_{t}}- 1}\end{array}$ . Then using EXP3 (Algorithm 3) guarantees:

1. With an oblivious adversary and $\gamma_{t}= 0$ for all t:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(a_{t})}-\operatorname*{min}_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(i)}\right\}\leq\log K+\frac{e^{2}}{2}K\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}^{2}+4\sum_{t\notin\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}^{2}d_{t}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}.\tag{42}
$$

2. With an adaptive adversary and $\gamma_{t}= \eta_{t}$ for all t:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(a_{t})}-\operatorname*{min}_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(i)}\right\}\leq 2+2\log K+(1+\frac{e^{2}}{2})K\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}^{2}+4 e^{2}K\sum_{t\notin\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}^{2}d_{t}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}.\tag{43}
$$

context.name: Setup: problem formulation, adversaries, delays, missing samples (Section 2)
context.statement:
Consider a player that in each round t from 1 to $T$ picks an action $\pmb{a}_{t}\in \mathcal{K}$ from a set $\mathcal{K}$ . The cost at round t from playing $\pmb{a}_{t}$ is $l_{t}\left(\boldsymbol{a}_{t}\right)\in\left[0,1\right]$ . We consider two types of adversaries:

1. Oblivious Adversary: chooses the cost functions $l_{1},...,l_{T}$ before the game starts.

2. Adaptive Adversary: chooses the cost function $l_{t}$ after observing $\{a_{1}, \ldots a_{t - 1}\}$ , for each t.

With full information and no delays, the player gets to know the function $l_{t}$ immediately after playing $\pmb{a}_{t}$ . In the bandit delayed feedback scenario, the player only gets to know the value of ${l}_{t}\left(\pmb{a}_{t}\right)$ at the beginning of round $t + d_{t}$ . (i.e., after a delay of $d_{t}\geq 1$ rounds). The adversary (oblivious or adaptive) chooses the delay sequence $\{d_{t}\}$ before the game starts.

We assume that the cost feedback includes the timestamp of the action that incurred this cost. This is indeed the case in many applications, such as when robots take physical actions, a recommendation is made to a customer or a treatment is given to a patient. If the delays are bounded by d, Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2018) have shown that EXP3 can still be implemented even with no timestamps, with expected regret $O(\sqrt{dTK\log K})$ instead of $O\left({\sqrt{\left(d+K\right)T\log K}}\right)$ . For our unbounded delays case, it is not clear if FKM or EXP3 can be implemented without timestamps.

The set of costs (feedback samples) received and used at round t is denoted $\mathcal{S}_{t}$ , so $s \in \mathcal{S}_{t}$ means that the cost of $\pmb{a}_{s}$ from round s is received and used at round t. Since the game lasts for $T$ rounds, all costs for which $t + d_{t}> T$ are never received. Of course, the value of $d_{t}$ does not matter as long as $t + d_{t}> T$ , and these are just samples that the adversary chose to prevent the player from receiving. We name these costs the missing samples and denote their set by $\mathcal{M}$ .

While the rounds of the game are indexed by t, it will be useful to our analysis to index a finer time scale that counts the steps of the algorithm for every such t. We define $s_{-}, s_{+}$ as the steps a moment before and after the algorithm uses the feedback from round s, respectively. These steps are taking place in round t if $s \in S_{t}$

context.name: Setup: multi-armed bandit special case (Section 2)
context.statement:
We analyze two widely applied algorithms for the two central special cases of the scenario above:

2. Multi-Armed Bandit - $\mathcal{K}=\{1,...,K\},\ l_{t}:\{1,...,K\}\to [0,1].$ With no delays, the EXP3 algorithm (Auer et al., 2002) achieves an expected regret of $O \left({\sqrt{T K \log K}}\right)$ for this problem.

context.name: Setup: EXP3 with delays, mixed actions and the filtration F_t (eq. 41, Section 6)
context.statement:
Consider a player that at each round t picks one out of K arms. Let $a_{t}$ be the arm the player chooses at round t. The cost at round t of playing arm i is $l_{t}^{(i)}\in [0,1]$ , and let $l_{t}=\left(l_{t}^{(1)},...,l_{t}^{(K)}\right)$ be the cost vector. At round t, the EXP3 algorithm, detailed in Algorithm 3, chooses an arm at random using a distribution that depends on the history of the game. The variant when $\gamma_{t}\neq 0$ , as we use against an adaptive adversary, is known as EXP3-IX (see Neu (2015)). We denote the vector of probabilities of the player for choosing arms at round t by $\pmb{p}_{t}\in \Delta^{K}$ , where $\Delta^{K}$ denotes the K-simplex. This is also known as the mixed action of the player. We also define the following filtration

$$
\mathcal{F}_{t}=\sigma\left(\left\{a_{s}\vert s+d_{s}\le t\right\}\cup\left\{l_{s}\vert s\le t\right\}\right)\tag{41}
$$

which is generated from all the actions for which the feedback was received up to round t and all cost functions up to round t. Note that the mixed action $\pmb{p}_{t}$ is a $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ -measurable random variable since $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ includes everything that could affect the algorithm up to round t. With a slight abuse of notation, we use $\mathcal{F}_{s_{-}}$ to denote the filtration induced from all actions for which the feedback has been received and used up to step $s_{-}$ and all the cost functions up to round t.

context.name: Algorithm 3 (EXP3 with delays, eqs. 44-45)
context.statement:
Algorithm 3 EXP3 with delays   
Initialization: Let $\{\eta_{t}\}$ and $\{\gamma_{t}\}$ be non-negative non-increasing sequences such that $\eta_{1}\leq \frac{e^{- 2}}{2}$ and   
set $\tilde{L}_{1}^{(i)}=0$ and $\begin{array}{r}{p_{1}^{(i)}=\frac{1}{K}}\end{array}$ for $i=1,...,K.$   
For $t=1,...,T$ do   
1. Choose an arm $a_{t}$ at random according to the distribution $\pmb{p}_{t}$ .   
2. Collect in $S_{t}$ all the rounds s for which $l_{s}^{(a_{s})}$ arrived at round t after a delay of $\begin{array}{r}{d_{s}\le \frac{1}{e^{2}\eta_{s}}- 1}\end{array}$   
3. Set $\tilde{L}_{t}^{(i)}=\tilde{L}_{t-1}^{(i)}$ for all i. Update the weights of arm $a_{s}$ for all $s \in S_{t}$ using   
$\tilde{L}_{t}^{(a_{s})}=\tilde{L}_{t}^{(a_{s})}+\eta_{s}\frac{l_{s}^{(a_{s})}}{p_{s}^{(a_{s})}+\gamma_{s}}.$ (44)   
4. Update the mixed action for $i=1,\ldots,K$ using   
$p_{t+1}^{(i)}=\frac{e^{-\tilde{L}_{t}^{(i)}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}e^{-\tilde{L}_{t}^{(j)}}}.$ (45)   
End

context.name: Lemma 8 (effect of delays, eq. 66)
context.statement:
Lemma 8. Let $\{\eta_{t}\}$ be a non-increasing step-size sequence. Let $\{d_{t}\}$ be a delay such that the cost from round t is received at round $t + d_{t}$ . Let $S_{t}$ be the set of feedback samples received and used at round t. Define the set $\mathcal{M}^{\ast}$ of all samples that are not received and used before round T. Then

$$
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\eta_{s}\left(\sum_{r=s}^{t-1}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{S}_{r}}\eta_{q}+\sum_{q\in\mathcal{S}_{t},q<s}\eta_{q}\right)\le 2\sum_{t\not\in\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}^{2}d_{t}.\tag{66}
$$

context.name: Lemma 9 (ratio bounds on the mixed action)
context.statement:
The following lemma generalizes Lemma 2 from Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2019) to a sequence of delays $\{d_{t}\}$ and a sequence of step-sizes $\{\eta_{t}\}$

Lemma 9. Let $\{\eta_{t}\}$ be a positive non-increasing step-size sequence such that $\eta_{t}\leq \frac{1}{2}e^{- 2}$ for all t. Let $\begin{array}{r}{\mathcal{D}= \Big \{t | d_{t}\geq \frac{1}{e^{2}\eta_{t}}- 1 \Big \}}\end{array}$ . Then for every s,t such that $s \in \mathcal{S}_{t}$ (so $s \notin \mathcal{D}$ ) Algorithm 3 maintains for all $i=1,...,K$ both $\begin{array}{r}{\frac{p_{s_{+}}^{(i)}}{p_{s_{-}}^{(i)}}\leq\frac{1}{1-e^{2}\eta_{s}}}\end{array}$ and $\frac{p_{s_{-}}^{(i)}}{p_{s}^{(i)}}\leq e^{2}$

context.name: Lemma 10 (softmax smoothness, eq. 107)
context.statement:
The next lemma shows standard smoothness properties of the softmax function, and we provide it here for completeness.

Lemma 10. Let $\begin{array}{r}{h_{i}\left(\pmb{x}\right)=\frac{e^{-x_{i}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}e^{-x_{j}}}}\end{array}$ and $h\left(\pmb{x}\right)=(h_{1}\left(\pmb{x}\right),...,h_{K}\left(\pmb{x}\right))$ . Then $\forall \mathbf{x}\in \mathbb{R}^{K}$ and $\forall \Delta \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{K}$

$$
\begin{array}{r}{\|h\left(\pmb{x}\right)-h\left(\pmb{x}+\Delta\right)\|_{1}\leq 2\left\langle h\left(\pmb{x}\right),\Delta\right\rangle .}\end{array}\tag{107}
$$

context.name: Lemma 11 (Neu 2015 concentration, eq. 111)
context.statement:
The next Lemma is taken from Neu (2015), and we provide a (very) slightly modified proof to verify that the same result holds even when the order of arrivals changes as a result of the delayed feedback.

Lemma 11. Let $\tilde{l}_{t}^{(i)}=\frac{l_{t}^{(i)}1_{\{a_{t}=i\}}}{p_{t}^{(i)}+\gamma_{t}}$ . If $\left\{\alpha_{t}^{(i)}\right\}$ is a non-negative sequence such that $\alpha_{t}^{(i)}\leq 2\gamma_{t}$ for all t and all i, then

$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{t\notin{\mathcal{M}}^{*}}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\alpha_{t}^{(i)}\left(\tilde{l}_{t}^{(i)}-l_{t}^{(i)}\right)>\log\frac{1}{\delta}\right)\leq\delta .\tag{111}
$$

nl_notes:
### Lemma 5
NOTE (Lemma 5, adaptive case) — The Lean adds a hypothesis (`a_law_adaptive`) that the paper never states as an assumption of Lemma 5 or Algorithm 3, but uses inside the proof of Lemma 11 ("given 𝒢_t, a_t = i with probability p_t^(i)"), which the proof of the adaptive case of Lemma 5 applies (appendix Section 13.1, headed "Proof of Lemma 6" in the paper). Precisely, the conditional law of a_t given the arms a_1, …, a_{t-1} of the earlier rounds (the σ-algebra 𝒢_t of that proof) is p_t.

Theorem 6. Let $\left\{l_{t}^{\left(i\right)}\right\}$ be a cost sequence such that $l_{t}^{(i)}\in [0,1]$ for every $t,i$ Let $\{d_{t}\}$ be a delay sequence such that the cost from round t is received at round $t + d_{t}$ . Define the set $\mathcal{M}=$ $\{t|t+d_{t}>T,t\in [1,T]\}$ of all samples that are not received before round T. Let us choose the fixed step-size $\begin{array}{r}{\eta = \frac{e^{- 2}}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\log K}{K T + \sum_{t \notin \mathcal{M}}d_{t}}}}\end{array}$ . Then the expected regret of EXP3 (Algorithm 3 with $\gamma_{t}= 0$ for all t) against an oblivious adversary satisfies

$$
\mathbb{E}\left\{R\left(T\right)\right\}=\mathbb{E}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle l_{t},p_{t}\rangle-\operatorname*{min}_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{T}l_{t}^{\left(i\right)}\right\}=O\left(\sqrt{\log K\left(K T+\sum_{t\notin\mathcal{M}}d_{t}\right)}+\left|\mathcal{M}\right|\right).\tag{46}
$$

context.name: Setup: problem formulation, adversaries, delays, missing samples (Section 2)
context.statement:
Consider a player that in each round t from 1 to $T$ picks an action $\pmb{a}_{t}\in \mathcal{K}$ from a set $\mathcal{K}$ . The cost at round t from playing $\pmb{a}_{t}$ is $l_{t}\left(\boldsymbol{a}_{t}\right)\in\left[0,1\right]$ . We consider two types of adversaries:

1. Oblivious Adversary: chooses the cost functions $l_{1},...,l_{T}$ before the game starts.

2. Adaptive Adversary: chooses the cost function $l_{t}$ after observing $\{a_{1}, \ldots a_{t - 1}\}$ , for each t.

With full information and no delays, the player gets to know the function $l_{t}$ immediately after playing $\pmb{a}_{t}$ . In the bandit delayed feedback scenario, the player only gets to know the value of ${l}_{t}\left(\pmb{a}_{t}\right)$ at the beginning of round $t + d_{t}$ . (i.e., after a delay of $d_{t}\geq 1$ rounds). The adversary (oblivious or adaptive) chooses the delay sequence $\{d_{t}\}$ before the game starts.

We assume that the cost feedback includes the timestamp of the action that incurred this cost. This is indeed the case in many applications, such as when robots take physical actions, a recommendation is made to a customer or a treatment is given to a patient. If the delays are bounded by d, Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2018) have shown that EXP3 can still be implemented even with no timestamps, with expected regret $O(\sqrt{dTK\log K})$ instead of $O\left({\sqrt{\left(d+K\right)T\log K}}\right)$ . For our unbounded delays case, it is not clear if FKM or EXP3 can be implemented without timestamps.

The set of costs (feedback samples) received and used at round t is denoted $\mathcal{S}_{t}$ , so $s \in \mathcal{S}_{t}$ means that the cost of $\pmb{a}_{s}$ from round s is received and used at round t. Since the game lasts for $T$ rounds, all costs for which $t + d_{t}> T$ are never received. Of course, the value of $d_{t}$ does not matter as long as $t + d_{t}> T$ , and these are just samples that the adversary chose to prevent the player from receiving. We name these costs the missing samples and denote their set by $\mathcal{M}$ .

While the rounds of the game are indexed by t, it will be useful to our analysis to index a finer time scale that counts the steps of the algorithm for every such t. We define $s_{-}, s_{+}$ as the steps a moment before and after the algorithm uses the feedback from round s, respectively. These steps are taking place in round t if $s \in S_{t}$

context.name: Setup: multi-armed bandit special case (Section 2)
context.statement:
We analyze two widely applied algorithms for the two central special cases of the scenario above:

2. Multi-Armed Bandit - $\mathcal{K}=\{1,...,K\},\ l_{t}:\{1,...,K\}\to [0,1].$ With no delays, the EXP3 algorithm (Auer et al., 2002) achieves an expected regret of $O \left({\sqrt{T K \log K}}\right)$ for this problem.

context.name: Definition 1 (expected regret, eq. 1)
context.statement:
The player wants to have a learning algorithm that uses past observations to make good decisions over time. The performance of the player's algorithm is measured using the regret. The expected regret is the total expected cost over a horizon of $T$ rounds, compared to the total expected cost that results from playing the best fixed action in hindsight in all rounds:

Definition 1. Let $\begin{array}{r}{\pmb{a}^{*}=\underset{\pmb{a}\in\mathcal{K}}{\arg\operatorname*{min}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}l_{t}\left(\pmb{a}\right)}\end{array}$ . The expected regret is defined as

$$
\mathbb{E}\left\{R\left(T\right)\right\}\triangleq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left\{l_{t}\left(\pmb{a}_{t}\right)-l_{t}\left(\pmb{a}^{*}\right)\right\}\tag{1}
$$

where $\mathbb{E}$ is the expectation over the (possibly) random actions $\pmb{a}_{1},\ldots,\pmb{a}_{T}$ of the player.

context.name: Setup: EXP3 with delays, mixed actions and the filtration F_t (eq. 41, Section 6)
context.statement:
Consider a player that at each round t picks one out of K arms. Let $a_{t}$ be the arm the player chooses at round t. The cost at round t of playing arm i is $l_{t}^{(i)}\in [0,1]$ , and let $l_{t}=\left(l_{t}^{(1)},...,l_{t}^{(K)}\right)$ be the cost vector. At round t, the EXP3 algorithm, detailed in Algorithm 3, chooses an arm at random using a distribution that depends on the history of the game. The variant when $\gamma_{t}\neq 0$ , as we use against an adaptive adversary, is known as EXP3-IX (see Neu (2015)). We denote the vector of probabilities of the player for choosing arms at round t by $\pmb{p}_{t}\in \Delta^{K}$ , where $\Delta^{K}$ denotes the K-simplex. This is also known as the mixed action of the player. We also define the following filtration

$$
\mathcal{F}_{t}=\sigma\left(\left\{a_{s}\vert s+d_{s}\le t\right\}\cup\left\{l_{s}\vert s\le t\right\}\right)\tag{41}
$$

which is generated from all the actions for which the feedback was received up to round t and all cost functions up to round t. Note that the mixed action $\pmb{p}_{t}$ is a $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ -measurable random variable since $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ includes everything that could affect the algorithm up to round t. With a slight abuse of notation, we use $\mathcal{F}_{s_{-}}$ to denote the filtration induced from all actions for which the feedback has been received and used up to step $s_{-}$ and all the cost functions up to round t.

context.name: Algorithm 3 (EXP3 with delays, eqs. 44-45)
context.statement:
Algorithm 3 EXP3 with delays   
Initialization: Let $\{\eta_{t}\}$ and $\{\gamma_{t}\}$ be non-negative non-increasing sequences such that $\eta_{1}\leq \frac{e^{- 2}}{2}$ and   
set $\tilde{L}_{1}^{(i)}=0$ and $\begin{array}{r}{p_{1}^{(i)}=\frac{1}{K}}\end{array}$ for $i=1,...,K.$   
For $t=1,...,T$ do   
1. Choose an arm $a_{t}$ at random according to the distribution $\pmb{p}_{t}$ .   
2. Collect in $S_{t}$ all the rounds s for which $l_{s}^{(a_{s})}$ arrived at round t after a delay of $\begin{array}{r}{d_{s}\le \frac{1}{e^{2}\eta_{s}}- 1}\end{array}$   
3. Set $\tilde{L}_{t}^{(i)}=\tilde{L}_{t-1}^{(i)}$ for all i. Update the weights of arm $a_{s}$ for all $s \in S_{t}$ using   
$\tilde{L}_{t}^{(a_{s})}=\tilde{L}_{t}^{(a_{s})}+\eta_{s}\frac{l_{s}^{(a_{s})}}{p_{s}^{(a_{s})}+\gamma_{s}}.$ (44)   
4. Update the mixed action for $i=1,\ldots,K$ using   
$p_{t+1}^{(i)}=\frac{e^{-\tilde{L}_{t}^{(i)}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}e^{-\tilde{L}_{t}^{(j)}}}.$ (45)   
End

context.name: Lemma 5 (another result of the same paper)
context.statement:
Lemma 5 (Weighted-Regret Bound for EXP3). Let $\{\eta_{t}\}$ be a non-increasing step-size sequence such that $\eta_{t}\leq\frac 12e^{-2}$ for all t. Let $\left\{l_{t}^{\left(i\right)}\right\}$ be a cost sequence such that $l_{t}^{(i)}\in [0,1]$ for every $t,i.$ Let $\{d_{t}\}$ be a delay sequence such that the cost from round t is received at round $t + d_{t}$ . Define the set $\mathcal{M}^{\ast}$ of all samples that are not received before round T or that were delayed by $\begin{array}{r}{d_{t}\geq \frac{1}{e^{2}\eta_{t}}- 1}\end{array}$ . Then using EXP3 (Algorithm 3) guarantees:

1. With an oblivious adversary and $\gamma_{t}= 0$ for all t:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(a_{t})}-\operatorname*{min}_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(i)}\right\}\leq\log K+\frac{e^{2}}{2}K\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}^{2}+4\sum_{t\notin\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}^{2}d_{t}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}.\tag{42}
$$

2. With an adaptive adversary and $\gamma_{t}= \eta_{t}$ for all t:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(a_{t})}-\operatorname*{min}_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(i)}\right\}\leq 2+2\log K+(1+\frac{e^{2}}{2})K\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}^{2}+4 e^{2}K\sum_{t\notin\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}^{2}d_{t}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}.\tag{43}
$$

Lemma 6. EXP3 (Algorithm 3 with $\gamma_{t}= \eta_{t}$ for all t, against an adaptive adversary) with a non-increasing and positive step-size sequence $\{\eta_{t}\}$ such that $\eta_{t}\leq\frac 12e^{-2}$ for all t has no weighted-regret with respect to the sequence of delays $\{d_{t}\}$ and $\{\eta_{t}\}$ as the weight sequence, if the following two conditions hold:

1. $\textstyle \sum_{t = 1}^{\infty}\eta_{t}= \infty .$

2. $\operatorname*{lim}_{t\to\infty}\eta_{t}d_{t}<\infty$ and $\textstyle \sum_{t = 1}^{\infty}\eta_{t}^{2}d_{t}< \infty$

context.name: Setup: problem formulation, adversaries, delays, missing samples (Section 2)
context.statement:
Consider a player that in each round t from 1 to $T$ picks an action $\pmb{a}_{t}\in \mathcal{K}$ from a set $\mathcal{K}$ . The cost at round t from playing $\pmb{a}_{t}$ is $l_{t}\left(\boldsymbol{a}_{t}\right)\in\left[0,1\right]$ . We consider two types of adversaries:

1. Oblivious Adversary: chooses the cost functions $l_{1},...,l_{T}$ before the game starts.

2. Adaptive Adversary: chooses the cost function $l_{t}$ after observing $\{a_{1}, \ldots a_{t - 1}\}$ , for each t.

With full information and no delays, the player gets to know the function $l_{t}$ immediately after playing $\pmb{a}_{t}$ . In the bandit delayed feedback scenario, the player only gets to know the value of ${l}_{t}\left(\pmb{a}_{t}\right)$ at the beginning of round $t + d_{t}$ . (i.e., after a delay of $d_{t}\geq 1$ rounds). The adversary (oblivious or adaptive) chooses the delay sequence $\{d_{t}\}$ before the game starts.

We assume that the cost feedback includes the timestamp of the action that incurred this cost. This is indeed the case in many applications, such as when robots take physical actions, a recommendation is made to a customer or a treatment is given to a patient. If the delays are bounded by d, Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2018) have shown that EXP3 can still be implemented even with no timestamps, with expected regret $O(\sqrt{dTK\log K})$ instead of $O\left({\sqrt{\left(d+K\right)T\log K}}\right)$ . For our unbounded delays case, it is not clear if FKM or EXP3 can be implemented without timestamps.

The set of costs (feedback samples) received and used at round t is denoted $\mathcal{S}_{t}$ , so $s \in \mathcal{S}_{t}$ means that the cost of $\pmb{a}_{s}$ from round s is received and used at round t. Since the game lasts for $T$ rounds, all costs for which $t + d_{t}> T$ are never received. Of course, the value of $d_{t}$ does not matter as long as $t + d_{t}> T$ , and these are just samples that the adversary chose to prevent the player from receiving. We name these costs the missing samples and denote their set by $\mathcal{M}$ .

While the rounds of the game are indexed by t, it will be useful to our analysis to index a finer time scale that counts the steps of the algorithm for every such t. We define $s_{-}, s_{+}$ as the steps a moment before and after the algorithm uses the feedback from round s, respectively. These steps are taking place in round t if $s \in S_{t}$

context.name: Setup: multi-armed bandit special case (Section 2)
context.statement:
We analyze two widely applied algorithms for the two central special cases of the scenario above:

2. Multi-Armed Bandit - $\mathcal{K}=\{1,...,K\},\ l_{t}:\{1,...,K\}\to [0,1].$ With no delays, the EXP3 algorithm (Auer et al., 2002) achieves an expected regret of $O \left({\sqrt{T K \log K}}\right)$ for this problem.

context.name: Definition 2 (no weighted-regret, eq. 2) and remarks
context.statement:
Our key observation is that with delayed feedback, it is not the regret that matters for the game dynamics but rather what we call the weighted-regret. The weighted-regret weighs the costs in different rounds according to a given non-increasing sequence $\eta_{t}$ so it coincides with the regret when $\eta_{t}=\eta,\forall t$ . We define "no weighted-regret" to replace the traditional no-regret property:

Definition 2. Let $\{l_{t}:\mathcal{K}\to [0,1]\}_{t}$ be a sequence of cost functions, chosen by an adaptive adversary. Let $\pmb{a}^{*}=\arg\operatorname*{min}_{\pmb{a}\in\mathcal{K}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}\left(\pmb{a}\right)$ . Let $\{d_{t}\}$ be a delay sequence such that the cost from round t is received at round $t + d_{t}$ . We say that an algorithm that produces the random sequence of (single-agent) actions $\left\{\pmb{a}_{t}\right\}$ has no weighted-regret with respect to $\{d_{t}\}$ and the non-increasing weight

sequence $\{\eta_{t}\}$ if

$$
\operatorname*{lim}_{T\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left\{\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}\left(l_{t}\left(\pmb{a}_{t}\right)-l_{t}\left(\pmb{a}^{*}\right)\right)}{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}}\right\}=0\tag{2}
$$

where the expectation is with respect to the random $\left\{\pmb{a}_{t}\right\}$ generated by the algorithm.

Having no weighted-regret is only non-trivial when $\textstyle \sum_{t = 1}^{\infty}\eta_{t}\ = \infty$ When $\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\eta_{t}<\infty,$ the feedback from the last $\textstyle{\frac{T}{2}}$ rounds can be discarded without affecting (2). When $\textstyle \sum_{t = 1}^{\infty}\eta_{t}= \infty$ ,there is no round t after which we can discard all feedback and still maintain (2).

We define no weighted-regret with respect to an adaptive adversary since, in a non-cooperative game with cost functions $\{u_{n}\}$ , the "adversarial" cost function of player n is $l_{t}({\bf{a}}_{n})=u_{n}({\bf{a}}_{n},{\bf{a}}_{-n,t})$ so it is determined by the actions of the other players. In turn, the actions of the other players depend on the past actions of player n. Hence, the cost function of player n depends on her past actions, as with an adaptive adversary. In general, the equilibrium does not consist of absolute strategies such as "min-max" in zero-sum games. Hence, regret guarantees against an adaptive adversary allow proving convergence to the set of CCE for general non-cooperative games.

When taking the limit $T\to\infty,$ it is important to emphasize that we do not change the infinite sequence of delays $\{d_{t}\}$ , but only reveal more elements in this sequence. In other words, we are looking at the same game but over a longer time horizon. Therefore, while $\begin{array}{r}{d_{t}= \frac{T}{2}}\end{array}$ makes sense for a constant $T,$ it is misleading when taking $T \to \infty$ since it represents a delay that occurred at time t but changes with the limit, so the limit is no longer of the "same game".

context.name: Setup: EXP3 with delays, mixed actions and the filtration F_t (eq. 41, Section 6)
context.statement:
Consider a player that at each round t picks one out of K arms. Let $a_{t}$ be the arm the player chooses at round t. The cost at round t of playing arm i is $l_{t}^{(i)}\in [0,1]$ , and let $l_{t}=\left(l_{t}^{(1)},...,l_{t}^{(K)}\right)$ be the cost vector. At round t, the EXP3 algorithm, detailed in Algorithm 3, chooses an arm at random using a distribution that depends on the history of the game. The variant when $\gamma_{t}\neq 0$ , as we use against an adaptive adversary, is known as EXP3-IX (see Neu (2015)). We denote the vector of probabilities of the player for choosing arms at round t by $\pmb{p}_{t}\in \Delta^{K}$ , where $\Delta^{K}$ denotes the K-simplex. This is also known as the mixed action of the player. We also define the following filtration

$$
\mathcal{F}_{t}=\sigma\left(\left\{a_{s}\vert s+d_{s}\le t\right\}\cup\left\{l_{s}\vert s\le t\right\}\right)\tag{41}
$$

which is generated from all the actions for which the feedback was received up to round t and all cost functions up to round t. Note that the mixed action $\pmb{p}_{t}$ is a $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ -measurable random variable since $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ includes everything that could affect the algorithm up to round t. With a slight abuse of notation, we use $\mathcal{F}_{s_{-}}$ to denote the filtration induced from all actions for which the feedback has been received and used up to step $s_{-}$ and all the cost functions up to round t.

context.name: Algorithm 3 (EXP3 with delays, eqs. 44-45)
context.statement:
Algorithm 3 EXP3 with delays   
Initialization: Let $\{\eta_{t}\}$ and $\{\gamma_{t}\}$ be non-negative non-increasing sequences such that $\eta_{1}\leq \frac{e^{- 2}}{2}$ and   
set $\tilde{L}_{1}^{(i)}=0$ and $\begin{array}{r}{p_{1}^{(i)}=\frac{1}{K}}\end{array}$ for $i=1,...,K.$   
For $t=1,...,T$ do   
1. Choose an arm $a_{t}$ at random according to the distribution $\pmb{p}_{t}$ .   
2. Collect in $S_{t}$ all the rounds s for which $l_{s}^{(a_{s})}$ arrived at round t after a delay of $\begin{array}{r}{d_{s}\le \frac{1}{e^{2}\eta_{s}}- 1}\end{array}$   
3. Set $\tilde{L}_{t}^{(i)}=\tilde{L}_{t-1}^{(i)}$ for all i. Update the weights of arm $a_{s}$ for all $s \in S_{t}$ using   
$\tilde{L}_{t}^{(a_{s})}=\tilde{L}_{t}^{(a_{s})}+\eta_{s}\frac{l_{s}^{(a_{s})}}{p_{s}^{(a_{s})}+\gamma_{s}}.$ (44)   
4. Update the mixed action for $i=1,\ldots,K$ using   
$p_{t+1}^{(i)}=\frac{e^{-\tilde{L}_{t}^{(i)}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}e^{-\tilde{L}_{t}^{(j)}}}.$ (45)   
End

context.name: Section 6.2 introduction (conditions for no weighted-regret)
context.statement: In this subsection, we provide conditions for EXP3 to have no weighted-regret with respect to the delay sequence and its step-size sequence as the weight sequence of Section 3. As discussed in Section 3, $\textstyle \sum_{t = 1}^{\infty}\eta_{t}= \infty$ , is necessary for the no weighted-regret property to be non-trivial. All other conditions of Lemma 6 are as tight as the bound of Lemma 5.

context.name: Lemma 5 (another result of the same paper)
context.statement:
Lemma 5 (Weighted-Regret Bound for EXP3). Let $\{\eta_{t}\}$ be a non-increasing step-size sequence such that $\eta_{t}\leq\frac 12e^{-2}$ for all t. Let $\left\{l_{t}^{\left(i\right)}\right\}$ be a cost sequence such that $l_{t}^{(i)}\in [0,1]$ for every $t,i.$ Let $\{d_{t}\}$ be a delay sequence such that the cost from round t is received at round $t + d_{t}$ . Define the set $\mathcal{M}^{\ast}$ of all samples that are not received before round T or that were delayed by $\begin{array}{r}{d_{t}\geq \frac{1}{e^{2}\eta_{t}}- 1}\end{array}$ . Then using EXP3 (Algorithm 3) guarantees:

1. With an oblivious adversary and $\gamma_{t}= 0$ for all t:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(a_{t})}-\operatorname*{min}_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(i)}\right\}\leq\log K+\frac{e^{2}}{2}K\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}^{2}+4\sum_{t\notin\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}^{2}d_{t}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}.\tag{42}
$$

2. With an adaptive adversary and $\gamma_{t}= \eta_{t}$ for all t:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(a_{t})}-\operatorname*{min}_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}l_{t}^{(i)}\right\}\leq 2+2\log K+(1+\frac{e^{2}}{2})K\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}^{2}+4 e^{2}K\sum_{t\notin\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}^{2}d_{t}+\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}^{*}}\eta_{t}.\tag{43}
$$

nl_notes:
### Lemma 6
Lemma 6 concludes that EXP3 "has no weighted-regret", which Definition 2 / eq. (2) defines as the TWO-SIDED limit `lim_{T->inf} E{ sum eta_t (l_t(a_t) - l_t(a*)) / sum eta_t } = 0`.
The ratio lies in [-1,1], so `lim = 0` is equivalent to `limsup <= 0` AND `0 <= liminf`. 'The limit exists' adds nothing else. The formalization keeps exactly the proved half: `NoWeightedRegret := limsup (...) atTop <= 0`, NOT `Tendsto (...) atTop (nhds 0)`.
NOTE (Lemma 6) — As in the adaptive case of Lemma 5, which its proof applies, the Lean adds a hypothesis (`a_law_adaptive`): the conditional law of a_t given the arms a_1, …, a_{t-1} of the earlier rounds is p_t. The paper never states this as an assumption; it is used inside the proof of Lemma 11.
