Theorem 3 (Regret bound for dual-stabilized OMD) Assume we have $\eta_{t}\geq \eta_{t + 1}>$ 0 for each $t > 1$ . Define $\gamma_{t}=\eta_{t+1}/\eta_{t}\in(0,1]$ for all $t \geq 1$ . Let $\{f_{t}\}_{t \ge 1}$ be a sequence of convex functions with $f_{t}\colon \mathcal{X}\to \mathbb{R}$ for each $t \geq 1$ . Let $\{x_{t}\}_{t \ge 1}$ and $\{\hat{w}_{t}\}_{t \ge 2}$ be as in Algorithm 2. Then, for all $T > 0$ and $z \in \mathcal{X}$ ,

$$
\mathrm{Regret}(T,z)\ \leq\ \sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{D_{\Phi}\bigl({}_{x_{t+1}}^{x_{t}};w_{t+1}\bigr)}{\eta_{t}}+\frac{D_{\Phi}\bigl(z,x_{1}\bigr)}{\eta_{T+1}}.\tag{8}
$$

context.name: Setup: online convex optimization and regret (Section 3)
context.statement:
We consider the online convex optimization problem with unknown time horizon. For each time step $t\in\{1,2,\ldots\}$ the algorithm proposes a point $x_{t}$ from a closed convex set ${\mathcal{X}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and an adversary simultaneously picks a convex cost function $f_{t}$ which the algorithm has access to via a first-order oracle, that is, for any $x \in \mathcal{X}$ the algorithm can compute $f_{t}(x)$ and a subgradient $\hat{g}\in\partial f_{t}(x): =\{\hat{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\mid f_{t}(z)\geq f_{t}(x)+\langle\hat{g},z-x\rangle\forall z\in\mathcal{X}\}$ . We will assume1 that all cost functions $f_{t}$ in this text are subdifferentiable on $\mathcal{X}$ , that is, meaning that the subdifferential $\partial f_{t}(x)$ is non-empty for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$

The cost of the iteration at time t is defined as $f_{t}(x_{t})$ . In this setting the goal is to produce a sequence of proposals $\{x_{t}\}_{t \ge 1}$ that minimizes the regret against an unknown comparison point $z \in \mathcal{X}$ that has accrued up until time $T$:

$$
\mathrm{Regret}(T,z): =\ \sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(x_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(z).
$$

context.name: Standing assumptions on the mirror map Φ and hat notation (1) (Section 3)
context.statement:
Both dual averaging and online mirror descent are parameterized by a special convex function $\Phi,$ often referred as a regularizer or a mirror map (for D and X), which among other properties needs$^{2}$ to be of Legendre type (Rockafellar, 1970, Chapter 26). Formally, throughout the paper we assume that the function $\Phi\colon \bar{\mathcal{D}}\to \mathbb{R}$ is a closed convex function whose conjugate is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and such that $\bar{\mathcal{D}}$ satisfies $\mathcal{X}\subseteq \bar{\mathcal{D}}$ and $\mathrm{int}\,\bar{\mathcal{D}}\cap \mathrm{ri}\,\mathcal{X}\neq \varnothing$ (where $\mathrm{ri}\,\mathcal{X}$ denotes the relative interior of $\mathcal{X}$). Moreover, we also suppose that $\Phi$ is of Legendre type, which means that $\Phi$ is strictly convex on its domain$^{3}$ and essentially smooth, that is, for $\mathcal{D}: =\mathrm{int}\bar{\mathcal{D}}$ we have

$\mathcal{D}$ is nonempty,

$\Phi$ is differentiable on $\mathcal{D}$, and

$\lim_{x\to\partial\mathcal{D}}\|\nabla\Phi(x)\|= +\infty$ , where ∂D is the boundary of $\mathcal{D},\mathrm{i.e.,}\partial\mathcal{D}: =\mathrm{cl}\mathcal{D}\backslash\mathcal{D}$

The gradient of the mirror map $\nabla \Phi :{\mathcal{D}}\to \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and the gradient of its conjugate $\nabla \Phi^{*}: \mathbb{R}^{n}\to \mathcal{D}$ are mutually inverse bijections between the primal space $\mathcal{D}$ and the dual space $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . We will adopt the following notational convention. Any vector in the primal space will be written without a hat, such as $x \in \mathcal{D}$ . The same letter with a hat, namely $\hat{x}$, will denote the corresponding dual vector:

$$
{\hat{x}}: =\nabla\Phi(x)\qquad{\mathrm{and}}\qquad x: =\nabla\Phi^{*}({\hat{x}})\qquad{\mathrm{f o r~a l l~l e t t e r s~}}x .\tag{1}
$$

context.name: Essential smoothness and well-posedness of the Bregman projection (Section 3)
context.statement: Essential smoothness ensures not only that $\Phi$ is differentiable on the interior of its domain, but also that the slope of $\Phi$ increases arbitrarily fast near the boundary of its domain. The latter guarantees, at least intuitively, that the function is increasing near and in the direction of the boundary of its domain. This property is fundamental for mirror descent to be well-defined (although not essential for dual averaging) since it ensures that the Bregman projection onto $\mathcal{X}$ is attained by a point on $\mathcal{D}$ where Φ is differentiable (we give more details on this on Section 7), and uniqueness is a consequence of the strict convexity of Φ. Some mirror maps we shall look at are classical cases of the OCO literature such as the negative entropy $x \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}\mapsto \sum_{i = 1}^{n} x_{i}\ln x_{i}$ and the squared 2-norm ${\frac{1}{2}}\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ , and details on the reasons they are mirror maps can be found in the works of Shalev-Shwartz (2012); Bubeck (2011) and Bubeck (2015) (in particular, Bubeck, 2011, Section 5.2 discusses the properties of functions of Legendre type and why requiring the conjugate of the mirror map to be differentiable on the whole space is not necessary for mirror descent to be well-defined if one restricts the gradient steps in the dual space in some way).

context.name: Definition: Bregman divergence (2), difference notation (3) and Bregman projection
context.statement:
Given a mirror map $\Phi,$ the Bregman divergence with respect to $\Phi$ is defined as

$$
D_{\Phi}(x,y)\ : =\ \Phi(x)-\Phi(y)-\langle\nabla\Phi(y),x-y\rangle,\qquad\forall x\in\bar{\mathcal{D}},\forall y\in\mathcal{D}.\tag{2}
$$

Throughout this paper it will be convenient to use the notation

$$
D_{\Phi}({}_{b}^{a};c): =D_{\Phi}(a,c)-D_{\Phi}(b,c)=\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)-\langle\nabla\Phi(c),a-b\rangle .\tag{3}
$$

In the important special case where $\begin{array}{r}{\Phi(x)=\frac{1}{2}\|x\|_{2}^{2}}\end{array}$ , the Bregman divergence relates to the Euclidean distance, i.e., $\begin{array}{r}{D_{\Phi}(x,y)=\frac 12\|x-y\|_{2}^{2}}\end{array}$ When $\begin{array}{r}{\Phi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\log x_{i}}\end{array}$ , the Bregman divergence becomes the generalized Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. The projection operator induced by the Bregman divergence is $\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}$ given by $\{\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}\}(y): =\arg\min\{D_{\Phi}(x,y)\mid x\in\mathcal{X}\}$ for any $y \in \mathcal{X}\cap \mathcal{D}$

context.name: Algorithm 1: generic OMD / DA template
context.statement:
A general template for optimization in the mirror descent framework is shown in Algorithm 1. The two classical algorithms, online mirror descent and dual averaging, are incarnations of this, differing only in how the dual variable $\hat{y}_{t}$ is updated.

In this work, for a given initial point $x_{1}\in{\mathcal{X}}$ of the player, we are interested in the case when $\begin{array}{r}{\operatorname*{sup}_{z\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x_{1})}\end{array}$ is bounded, which still allows $\sup_{z,x\in{\mathcal{X}}}D_{\Phi}(z,x)$ to be unbounded. In fact, in the Euclidean setting $\begin{array}{r}{(\mathrm{i . e .,}\Phi=\frac{1}{2}\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}),\operatorname*{sup}_{z\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x_{1})}\end{array}$ is bounded if and only if the diameter of X given by $\sup_{x,y\in\mathcal{X}}\frac{1}{2}\Vert x-y\Vert_{2}^{2}$ is also bounded. However, for a general mirror map $\Phi$, assuming $\begin{array}{r}{\operatorname*{sup}_{z\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x_{1})}\end{array}$ is bounded is strictly weaker than assuming $\scriptstyle\operatorname*{sup}_{x,y\in{\mathcal{X}}}D_{\Phi}(x,y)$ is bounded. This is the case for the well-known experts' problem, where Φ is the negative entropy, $D_{\Phi}$ is the KL-divergence, X is the unit simplex $\Delta_{n}: =\{p\in [0,1]^{n}:\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=1\}$ , and $\begin{array}{r}{x_{1}: = \frac{1}{n}\vec{1},}\end{array}$ where $\vec{1}$ is the vector in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with entries all set to 1. In this case, we have $\sup_{z\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x_{1})\leq\ln n$ while $\begin{array}{r}{\operatorname*{sup}_{z,x\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x)= +\infty}\end{array}$ .

To conclude, throughout the paper we shall try to stick to the following naming convention: greek letters will denote scalars, lower-case roman letters will denote vectors, $\mathrm{e.g.},x,y$ ,and capital calligraphic letters shall denote sets, $\mathrm{e . g .}, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}$ . Any deviations from this convention (or the hat notation as in (1)) are intended to follow other conventions in the literature.

Algorithm 1 Pseudocode for both online mirror descent and dual averaging with adaptive   
learning rate given by $\eta_{t}$ on iteration t. These methods differ only in how the iterate $\hat{y}_{t + 1}$ is   
updated.   
Input: $x_{1}\in \mathcal{X}\cap \mathcal{D}, \eta : \mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{R}_{> 0}$   
for $t=1,2,\dots$ do   
Incur cost $f_{t}(x_{t})$ and receive $\hat{g}_{t}\in\partial f_{t}(x_{t})$   
$\hat{x}_{t}=\nabla\Phi(x_{t})$   
[OMD update] $\hat{y}_{t + 1}= \hat{x}_{t}- \eta_{t}\hat{g}_{t}$   
[DA update] $\begin{array}{r}{\hat{y}_{t + 1}= \hat{x}_{1}- \eta_{t}\sum_{i \leq t}\hat{g}_{i}}\end{array}$   
$\boldsymbol{y}_{t+1}=\nabla\Phi^{*}(\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}_{t+1})$   
$x_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(y_{t+1})$   
end for

context.name: Algorithm 2: dual-stabilized OMD, eqs. (5)-(7)
context.statement:
Algorithm 2 Dual-stabilized OMD (DS-OMD). The parameters $\gamma_{t}$ control the amount of   
stabilization.   
Input: $x_{1}\in\mathcal{X}\cap\mathcal{D},\eta:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}_{+},\ \gamma:\mathbb{N}\to(0,1]$   
for $t=1,2,\dots$ do   
Incur cost $f_{t}(x_{t})$ and receive $\hat{g}_{t}\in\partial f_{t}(x_{t})$   
$\hat{x}_{t}=\nabla\Phi(x_{t})$ map primal iterate to dual space   
$\hat{w}_{t + 1}= \hat{x}_{t}- \eta_{t}\hat{g}_{t}$ gradient step in dual space (5)   
$\hat{y}_{t+1}=\gamma_{t}\hat{w}_{t+1}+(1-\gamma_{t})\hat{x}_{1}$ stabilization in dual space (6)   
$\boldsymbol{y}_{t+1}=\nabla\Phi^{*}(\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}_{t+1})$ map dual iterate to primal space   
$x_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(y_{t+1})$ project onto feasible region (7)   
end for

context.name: Proposition 38 (generalized triangle inequality)
context.statement:
An immediate consequence is the "generalized triangle inequality for Bregman divergence", such as in Bubeck (2015, Eq. (4.1)) or in Beck and Teboulle (2003, Lemma 4.1).

Proposition 38 For all $a,b,d\in{\mathcal{D}}$

$$
D_{\Phi}(a,d)-D_{\Phi}(b,d)+D_{\Phi}(b,a)\ =\ \langle\hat{a}-\hat{d},a-b\rangle
$$

context.name: Proposition 39
context.statement:
Proposition 39 Let $a,b,c,u,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfy $\gamma\hat{a}+(1-\gamma)\hat{b}=\hat{c}$ for some $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}$ . Then

$$
\gamma D_{\Phi}({}_{v}^{u};a)\ : +\ :(1-\gamma)D_{\Phi}({}_{v}^{u};b)\ : =\ :D_{\Phi}({}_{v}^{u};c).
$$

context.name: Proposition 40 (Pythagorean theorem for Bregman divergence)
context.statement:
The following proposition is the "Pythagorean theorem for Bregman divergence". Recall that $\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(y)=\arg\operatorname*{min}_{u\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(u,y)$ . A proof may be found in Bubeck (2015, Lemma 4.1).

Proposition 40 Let $\mathcal{X}\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a convex set. Let $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\pi=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(p)$ . Then

$$
D_{\Phi}({}_{\pi}^{z};p)\geq D_{\Phi}({}_{\pi}^{z};\pi)=D_{\Phi}(z,\pi)\forall z\in\mathcal{X}.
$$

context.name: Lemma 34 (basic properties of the mirror map and Bregman divergence)
context.statement:
The following lemma collects basic facts regarding the a mirror map Φ (or simply a function of Legendre type) and the Bregman divergence it induces. See Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi (2006, Lemma 11.5 and Proposition 11.1).

Lemma 34 The mirror map $\Phi$ and the Bregman divergence it induces satisfy the following properties:

$D_{\Phi}(x,y)$ is convex in x.

$\nabla\Phi(\nabla\Phi^{*}(z))=z$ and $\nabla^{*}\Phi(\nabla\Phi(x))=x$ for all x and z.

$D_{\Phi}(x,y)=D_{\Phi^{*}}\bigl(\nabla\Phi(y),\nabla\Phi(x)\bigr)$ for all x and $y$

noncomputable def bregman (Φ : E → ℝ) (gΦ : E → E) (x y : E) : ℝ :=
  Φ x - Φ y - (@inner ℝ E _ (gΦ y) (x - y))

noncomputable def regret (f : ℕ → E → ℝ) (x : ℕ → E) (z : E) (T : ℕ) : ℝ :=

  sSup {v : ℝ | ∃ x : E, N.nrm x ≤ 1 ∧ v = (@inner ℝ E _ z x)}

context.name: Setup: online convex optimization and regret (Section 3)
context.statement:
We consider the online convex optimization problem with unknown time horizon. For each time step $t\in\{1,2,\ldots\}$ the algorithm proposes a point $x_{t}$ from a closed convex set ${\mathcal{X}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and an adversary simultaneously picks a convex cost function $f_{t}$ which the algorithm has access to via a first-order oracle, that is, for any $x \in \mathcal{X}$ the algorithm can compute $f_{t}(x)$ and a subgradient $\hat{g}\in\partial f_{t}(x): =\{\hat{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\mid f_{t}(z)\geq f_{t}(x)+\langle\hat{g},z-x\rangle\forall z\in\mathcal{X}\}$ . We will assume1 that all cost functions $f_{t}$ in this text are subdifferentiable on $\mathcal{X}$ , that is, meaning that the subdifferential $\partial f_{t}(x)$ is non-empty for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$

The cost of the iteration at time t is defined as $f_{t}(x_{t})$ . In this setting the goal is to produce a sequence of proposals $\{x_{t}\}_{t \ge 1}$ that minimizes the regret against an unknown comparison point $z \in \mathcal{X}$ that has accrued up until time $T$:

$$
\mathrm{Regret}(T,z): =\ \sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(x_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(z).
$$

context.name: Standing assumptions on the mirror map Φ and hat notation (1) (Section 3)
context.statement:
Both dual averaging and online mirror descent are parameterized by a special convex function $\Phi,$ often referred as a regularizer or a mirror map (for D and X), which among other properties needs$^{2}$ to be of Legendre type (Rockafellar, 1970, Chapter 26). Formally, throughout the paper we assume that the function $\Phi\colon \bar{\mathcal{D}}\to \mathbb{R}$ is a closed convex function whose conjugate is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and such that $\bar{\mathcal{D}}$ satisfies $\mathcal{X}\subseteq \bar{\mathcal{D}}$ and $\mathrm{int}\,\bar{\mathcal{D}}\cap \mathrm{ri}\,\mathcal{X}\neq \varnothing$ (where $\mathrm{ri}\,\mathcal{X}$ denotes the relative interior of $\mathcal{X}$). Moreover, we also suppose that $\Phi$ is of Legendre type, which means that $\Phi$ is strictly convex on its domain$^{3}$ and essentially smooth, that is, for $\mathcal{D}: =\mathrm{int}\bar{\mathcal{D}}$ we have

$\mathcal{D}$ is nonempty,

$\Phi$ is differentiable on $\mathcal{D}$, and

$\lim_{x\to\partial\mathcal{D}}\|\nabla\Phi(x)\|= +\infty$ , where ∂D is the boundary of $\mathcal{D},\mathrm{i.e.,}\partial\mathcal{D}: =\mathrm{cl}\mathcal{D}\backslash\mathcal{D}$

The gradient of the mirror map $\nabla \Phi :{\mathcal{D}}\to \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and the gradient of its conjugate $\nabla \Phi^{*}: \mathbb{R}^{n}\to \mathcal{D}$ are mutually inverse bijections between the primal space $\mathcal{D}$ and the dual space $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . We will adopt the following notational convention. Any vector in the primal space will be written without a hat, such as $x \in \mathcal{D}$ . The same letter with a hat, namely $\hat{x}$, will denote the corresponding dual vector:

$$
{\hat{x}}: =\nabla\Phi(x)\qquad{\mathrm{and}}\qquad x: =\nabla\Phi^{*}({\hat{x}})\qquad{\mathrm{f o r~a l l~l e t t e r s~}}x .\tag{1}
$$

context.name: Essential smoothness and well-posedness of the Bregman projection (Section 3)
context.statement: Essential smoothness ensures not only that $\Phi$ is differentiable on the interior of its domain, but also that the slope of $\Phi$ increases arbitrarily fast near the boundary of its domain. The latter guarantees, at least intuitively, that the function is increasing near and in the direction of the boundary of its domain. This property is fundamental for mirror descent to be well-defined (although not essential for dual averaging) since it ensures that the Bregman projection onto $\mathcal{X}$ is attained by a point on $\mathcal{D}$ where Φ is differentiable (we give more details on this on Section 7), and uniqueness is a consequence of the strict convexity of Φ. Some mirror maps we shall look at are classical cases of the OCO literature such as the negative entropy $x \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}\mapsto \sum_{i = 1}^{n} x_{i}\ln x_{i}$ and the squared 2-norm ${\frac{1}{2}}\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ , and details on the reasons they are mirror maps can be found in the works of Shalev-Shwartz (2012); Bubeck (2011) and Bubeck (2015) (in particular, Bubeck, 2011, Section 5.2 discusses the properties of functions of Legendre type and why requiring the conjugate of the mirror map to be differentiable on the whole space is not necessary for mirror descent to be well-defined if one restricts the gradient steps in the dual space in some way).

context.name: Definition: Bregman divergence (2), difference notation (3) and Bregman projection
context.statement:
Given a mirror map $\Phi,$ the Bregman divergence with respect to $\Phi$ is defined as

$$
D_{\Phi}(x,y)\ : =\ \Phi(x)-\Phi(y)-\langle\nabla\Phi(y),x-y\rangle,\qquad\forall x\in\bar{\mathcal{D}},\forall y\in\mathcal{D}.\tag{2}
$$

Throughout this paper it will be convenient to use the notation

$$
D_{\Phi}({}_{b}^{a};c): =D_{\Phi}(a,c)-D_{\Phi}(b,c)=\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)-\langle\nabla\Phi(c),a-b\rangle .\tag{3}
$$

In the important special case where $\begin{array}{r}{\Phi(x)=\frac{1}{2}\|x\|_{2}^{2}}\end{array}$ , the Bregman divergence relates to the Euclidean distance, i.e., $\begin{array}{r}{D_{\Phi}(x,y)=\frac 12\|x-y\|_{2}^{2}}\end{array}$ When $\begin{array}{r}{\Phi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\log x_{i}}\end{array}$ , the Bregman divergence becomes the generalized Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. The projection operator induced by the Bregman divergence is $\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}$ given by $\{\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}\}(y): =\arg\min\{D_{\Phi}(x,y)\mid x\in\mathcal{X}\}$ for any $y \in \mathcal{X}\cap \mathcal{D}$

context.name: Algorithm 1: generic OMD / DA template
context.statement:
A general template for optimization in the mirror descent framework is shown in Algorithm 1. The two classical algorithms, online mirror descent and dual averaging, are incarnations of this, differing only in how the dual variable $\hat{y}_{t}$ is updated.

In this work, for a given initial point $x_{1}\in{\mathcal{X}}$ of the player, we are interested in the case when $\begin{array}{r}{\operatorname*{sup}_{z\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x_{1})}\end{array}$ is bounded, which still allows $\sup_{z,x\in{\mathcal{X}}}D_{\Phi}(z,x)$ to be unbounded. In fact, in the Euclidean setting $\begin{array}{r}{(\mathrm{i . e .,}\Phi=\frac{1}{2}\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}),\operatorname*{sup}_{z\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x_{1})}\end{array}$ is bounded if and only if the diameter of X given by $\sup_{x,y\in\mathcal{X}}\frac{1}{2}\Vert x-y\Vert_{2}^{2}$ is also bounded. However, for a general mirror map $\Phi$, assuming $\begin{array}{r}{\operatorname*{sup}_{z\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x_{1})}\end{array}$ is bounded is strictly weaker than assuming $\scriptstyle\operatorname*{sup}_{x,y\in{\mathcal{X}}}D_{\Phi}(x,y)$ is bounded. This is the case for the well-known experts' problem, where Φ is the negative entropy, $D_{\Phi}$ is the KL-divergence, X is the unit simplex $\Delta_{n}: =\{p\in [0,1]^{n}:\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=1\}$ , and $\begin{array}{r}{x_{1}: = \frac{1}{n}\vec{1},}\end{array}$ where $\vec{1}$ is the vector in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with entries all set to 1. In this case, we have $\sup_{z\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x_{1})\leq\ln n$ while $\begin{array}{r}{\operatorname*{sup}_{z,x\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x)= +\infty}\end{array}$ .

To conclude, throughout the paper we shall try to stick to the following naming convention: greek letters will denote scalars, lower-case roman letters will denote vectors, $\mathrm{e.g.},x,y$ ,and capital calligraphic letters shall denote sets, $\mathrm{e . g .}, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}$ . Any deviations from this convention (or the hat notation as in (1)) are intended to follow other conventions in the literature.

Algorithm 1 Pseudocode for both online mirror descent and dual averaging with adaptive   
learning rate given by $\eta_{t}$ on iteration t. These methods differ only in how the iterate $\hat{y}_{t + 1}$ is   
updated.   
Input: $x_{1}\in \mathcal{X}\cap \mathcal{D}, \eta : \mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{R}_{> 0}$   
for $t=1,2,\dots$ do   
Incur cost $f_{t}(x_{t})$ and receive $\hat{g}_{t}\in\partial f_{t}(x_{t})$   
$\hat{x}_{t}=\nabla\Phi(x_{t})$   
[OMD update] $\hat{y}_{t + 1}= \hat{x}_{t}- \eta_{t}\hat{g}_{t}$   
[DA update] $\begin{array}{r}{\hat{y}_{t + 1}= \hat{x}_{1}- \eta_{t}\sum_{i \leq t}\hat{g}_{i}}\end{array}$   
$\boldsymbol{y}_{t+1}=\nabla\Phi^{*}(\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}_{t+1})$   
$x_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(y_{t+1})$   
end for

context.name: Algorithm 2: dual-stabilized OMD, eqs. (5)-(7)
context.statement:
Algorithm 2 Dual-stabilized OMD (DS-OMD). The parameters $\gamma_{t}$ control the amount of   
stabilization.   
Input: $x_{1}\in\mathcal{X}\cap\mathcal{D},\eta:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}_{+},\ \gamma:\mathbb{N}\to(0,1]$   
for $t=1,2,\dots$ do   
Incur cost $f_{t}(x_{t})$ and receive $\hat{g}_{t}\in\partial f_{t}(x_{t})$   
$\hat{x}_{t}=\nabla\Phi(x_{t})$ map primal iterate to dual space   
$\hat{w}_{t + 1}= \hat{x}_{t}- \eta_{t}\hat{g}_{t}$ gradient step in dual space (5)   
$\hat{y}_{t+1}=\gamma_{t}\hat{w}_{t+1}+(1-\gamma_{t})\hat{x}_{1}$ stabilization in dual space (6)   
$\boldsymbol{y}_{t+1}=\nabla\Phi^{*}(\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}_{t+1})$ map dual iterate to primal space   
$x_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(y_{t+1})$ project onto feasible region (7)   
end for

context.name: Proposition 38 (generalized triangle inequality)
context.statement:
An immediate consequence is the "generalized triangle inequality for Bregman divergence", such as in Bubeck (2015, Eq. (4.1)) or in Beck and Teboulle (2003, Lemma 4.1).

Proposition 38 For all $a,b,d\in{\mathcal{D}}$

$$
D_{\Phi}(a,d)-D_{\Phi}(b,d)+D_{\Phi}(b,a)\ =\ \langle\hat{a}-\hat{d},a-b\rangle
$$

context.name: Proposition 40 (Pythagorean theorem for Bregman divergence)
context.statement:
The following proposition is the "Pythagorean theorem for Bregman divergence". Recall that $\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(y)=\arg\operatorname*{min}_{u\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(u,y)$ . A proof may be found in Bubeck (2015, Lemma 4.1).

Proposition 40 Let $\mathcal{X}\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a convex set. Let $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\pi=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(p)$ . Then

$$
D_{\Phi}({}_{\pi}^{z};p)\geq D_{\Phi}({}_{\pi}^{z};\pi)=D_{\Phi}(z,\pi)\forall z\in\mathcal{X}.
$$

context.name: Algorithm 3: primal-stabilized OMD, eqs. (11)-(14)
context.statement:
Algorithm 3 Online mirror descent with primal stabilization.   
Input: $x_{1}\in \mathcal{X}\cap \mathcal{D}, \eta : \mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{R}, \gamma : \mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{R}.$   
for $t=1,2,\dots$ do   
Incur cost $f_{t}(x_{t})$ and receive $\hat{\boldsymbol g}_{t}\in\partial f_{t}(\boldsymbol x_{t})$   
$\hat{x}_{t}=\nabla\Phi(x_{t})$ map primal iterate to dual space   
$\hat{w}_{t + 1}= \hat{x}_{t}- \eta_{t}\hat{g}_{t}$ gradient step in dual space (11)   
$\boldsymbol{w}_{t+1}=\nabla\Phi^{*}(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_{t+1})$ map dual iterate to primal space (12)   
$y_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(w_{t+1})$ project onto feasible region (13)   
$x_{t+1}=\gamma_{t}y_{t+1}+(1-\gamma_{t})x_{1}$ stabilization in primal space (14)   
end for

context.name: Lemma 34 (basic properties of the mirror map and Bregman divergence)
context.statement:
The following lemma collects basic facts regarding the a mirror map Φ (or simply a function of Legendre type) and the Bregman divergence it induces. See Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi (2006, Lemma 11.5 and Proposition 11.1).

Lemma 34 The mirror map $\Phi$ and the Bregman divergence it induces satisfy the following properties:

$D_{\Phi}(x,y)$ is convex in x.

$\nabla\Phi(\nabla\Phi^{*}(z))=z$ and $\nabla^{*}\Phi(\nabla\Phi(x))=x$ for all x and z.

$D_{\Phi}(x,y)=D_{\Phi^{*}}\bigl(\nabla\Phi(y),\nabla\Phi(x)\bigr)$ for all x and $y$

$$
\mathrm{Regret}(T,z)~\le~\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{D_{\Phi}\bigl({{}_{x_{t+1}}^{x_{t}};\nabla\Phi^{*}(\hat{x}_{t}-\eta_{t}\hat{g}_{t})\bigr)}}{\eta_{t}}+\frac{D_{\Phi}\bigl(z,x_{1}\bigr)}{\eta_{T+1}}~\forall T>0 .\tag{20}

context.name: Setup: online convex optimization and regret (Section 3)
context.statement:
We consider the online convex optimization problem with unknown time horizon. For each time step $t\in\{1,2,\ldots\}$ the algorithm proposes a point $x_{t}$ from a closed convex set ${\mathcal{X}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and an adversary simultaneously picks a convex cost function $f_{t}$ which the algorithm has access to via a first-order oracle, that is, for any $x \in \mathcal{X}$ the algorithm can compute $f_{t}(x)$ and a subgradient $\hat{g}\in\partial f_{t}(x): =\{\hat{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\mid f_{t}(z)\geq f_{t}(x)+\langle\hat{g},z-x\rangle\forall z\in\mathcal{X}\}$ . We will assume1 that all cost functions $f_{t}$ in this text are subdifferentiable on $\mathcal{X}$ , that is, meaning that the subdifferential $\partial f_{t}(x)$ is non-empty for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$

The cost of the iteration at time t is defined as $f_{t}(x_{t})$ . In this setting the goal is to produce a sequence of proposals $\{x_{t}\}_{t \ge 1}$ that minimizes the regret against an unknown comparison point $z \in \mathcal{X}$ that has accrued up until time $T$:

$$
\mathrm{Regret}(T,z): =\ \sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(x_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(z).
$$

context.name: Standing assumptions on the mirror map Φ and hat notation (1) (Section 3)
context.statement:
Both dual averaging and online mirror descent are parameterized by a special convex function $\Phi,$ often referred as a regularizer or a mirror map (for D and X), which among other properties needs$^{2}$ to be of Legendre type (Rockafellar, 1970, Chapter 26). Formally, throughout the paper we assume that the function $\Phi\colon \bar{\mathcal{D}}\to \mathbb{R}$ is a closed convex function whose conjugate is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and such that $\bar{\mathcal{D}}$ satisfies $\mathcal{X}\subseteq \bar{\mathcal{D}}$ and $\mathrm{int}\,\bar{\mathcal{D}}\cap \mathrm{ri}\,\mathcal{X}\neq \varnothing$ (where $\mathrm{ri}\,\mathcal{X}$ denotes the relative interior of $\mathcal{X}$). Moreover, we also suppose that $\Phi$ is of Legendre type, which means that $\Phi$ is strictly convex on its domain$^{3}$ and essentially smooth, that is, for $\mathcal{D}: =\mathrm{int}\bar{\mathcal{D}}$ we have

$\mathcal{D}$ is nonempty,

$\Phi$ is differentiable on $\mathcal{D}$, and

$\lim_{x\to\partial\mathcal{D}}\|\nabla\Phi(x)\|= +\infty$ , where ∂D is the boundary of $\mathcal{D},\mathrm{i.e.,}\partial\mathcal{D}: =\mathrm{cl}\mathcal{D}\backslash\mathcal{D}$

The gradient of the mirror map $\nabla \Phi :{\mathcal{D}}\to \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and the gradient of its conjugate $\nabla \Phi^{*}: \mathbb{R}^{n}\to \mathcal{D}$ are mutually inverse bijections between the primal space $\mathcal{D}$ and the dual space $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . We will adopt the following notational convention. Any vector in the primal space will be written without a hat, such as $x \in \mathcal{D}$ . The same letter with a hat, namely $\hat{x}$, will denote the corresponding dual vector:

$$
{\hat{x}}: =\nabla\Phi(x)\qquad{\mathrm{and}}\qquad x: =\nabla\Phi^{*}({\hat{x}})\qquad{\mathrm{f o r~a l l~l e t t e r s~}}x .\tag{1}
$$

context.name: Essential smoothness and well-posedness of the Bregman projection (Section 3)
context.statement: Essential smoothness ensures not only that $\Phi$ is differentiable on the interior of its domain, but also that the slope of $\Phi$ increases arbitrarily fast near the boundary of its domain. The latter guarantees, at least intuitively, that the function is increasing near and in the direction of the boundary of its domain. This property is fundamental for mirror descent to be well-defined (although not essential for dual averaging) since it ensures that the Bregman projection onto $\mathcal{X}$ is attained by a point on $\mathcal{D}$ where Φ is differentiable (we give more details on this on Section 7), and uniqueness is a consequence of the strict convexity of Φ. Some mirror maps we shall look at are classical cases of the OCO literature such as the negative entropy $x \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}\mapsto \sum_{i = 1}^{n} x_{i}\ln x_{i}$ and the squared 2-norm ${\frac{1}{2}}\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ , and details on the reasons they are mirror maps can be found in the works of Shalev-Shwartz (2012); Bubeck (2011) and Bubeck (2015) (in particular, Bubeck, 2011, Section 5.2 discusses the properties of functions of Legendre type and why requiring the conjugate of the mirror map to be differentiable on the whole space is not necessary for mirror descent to be well-defined if one restricts the gradient steps in the dual space in some way).

context.name: Definition: Bregman divergence (2), difference notation (3) and Bregman projection
context.statement:
Given a mirror map $\Phi,$ the Bregman divergence with respect to $\Phi$ is defined as

$$
D_{\Phi}(x,y)\ : =\ \Phi(x)-\Phi(y)-\langle\nabla\Phi(y),x-y\rangle,\qquad\forall x\in\bar{\mathcal{D}},\forall y\in\mathcal{D}.\tag{2}
$$

Throughout this paper it will be convenient to use the notation

$$
D_{\Phi}({}_{b}^{a};c): =D_{\Phi}(a,c)-D_{\Phi}(b,c)=\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)-\langle\nabla\Phi(c),a-b\rangle .\tag{3}
$$

In the important special case where $\begin{array}{r}{\Phi(x)=\frac{1}{2}\|x\|_{2}^{2}}\end{array}$ , the Bregman divergence relates to the Euclidean distance, i.e., $\begin{array}{r}{D_{\Phi}(x,y)=\frac 12\|x-y\|_{2}^{2}}\end{array}$ When $\begin{array}{r}{\Phi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\log x_{i}}\end{array}$ , the Bregman divergence becomes the generalized Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. The projection operator induced by the Bregman divergence is $\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}$ given by $\{\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}\}(y): =\arg\min\{D_{\Phi}(x,y)\mid x\in\mathcal{X}\}$ for any $y \in \mathcal{X}\cap \mathcal{D}$

context.name: Algorithm 1: generic OMD / DA template
context.statement:
A general template for optimization in the mirror descent framework is shown in Algorithm 1. The two classical algorithms, online mirror descent and dual averaging, are incarnations of this, differing only in how the dual variable $\hat{y}_{t}$ is updated.

In this work, for a given initial point $x_{1}\in{\mathcal{X}}$ of the player, we are interested in the case when $\begin{array}{r}{\operatorname*{sup}_{z\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x_{1})}\end{array}$ is bounded, which still allows $\sup_{z,x\in{\mathcal{X}}}D_{\Phi}(z,x)$ to be unbounded. In fact, in the Euclidean setting $\begin{array}{r}{(\mathrm{i . e .,}\Phi=\frac{1}{2}\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}),\operatorname*{sup}_{z\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x_{1})}\end{array}$ is bounded if and only if the diameter of X given by $\sup_{x,y\in\mathcal{X}}\frac{1}{2}\Vert x-y\Vert_{2}^{2}$ is also bounded. However, for a general mirror map $\Phi$, assuming $\begin{array}{r}{\operatorname*{sup}_{z\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x_{1})}\end{array}$ is bounded is strictly weaker than assuming $\scriptstyle\operatorname*{sup}_{x,y\in{\mathcal{X}}}D_{\Phi}(x,y)$ is bounded. This is the case for the well-known experts' problem, where Φ is the negative entropy, $D_{\Phi}$ is the KL-divergence, X is the unit simplex $\Delta_{n}: =\{p\in [0,1]^{n}:\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=1\}$ , and $\begin{array}{r}{x_{1}: = \frac{1}{n}\vec{1},}\end{array}$ where $\vec{1}$ is the vector in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with entries all set to 1. In this case, we have $\sup_{z\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x_{1})\leq\ln n$ while $\begin{array}{r}{\operatorname*{sup}_{z,x\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(z,x)= +\infty}\end{array}$ .

To conclude, throughout the paper we shall try to stick to the following naming convention: greek letters will denote scalars, lower-case roman letters will denote vectors, $\mathrm{e.g.},x,y$ ,and capital calligraphic letters shall denote sets, $\mathrm{e . g .}, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}$ . Any deviations from this convention (or the hat notation as in (1)) are intended to follow other conventions in the literature.

Algorithm 1 Pseudocode for both online mirror descent and dual averaging with adaptive   
learning rate given by $\eta_{t}$ on iteration t. These methods differ only in how the iterate $\hat{y}_{t + 1}$ is   
updated.   
Input: $x_{1}\in \mathcal{X}\cap \mathcal{D}, \eta : \mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{R}_{> 0}$   
for $t=1,2,\dots$ do   
Incur cost $f_{t}(x_{t})$ and receive $\hat{g}_{t}\in\partial f_{t}(x_{t})$   
$\hat{x}_{t}=\nabla\Phi(x_{t})$   
[OMD update] $\hat{y}_{t + 1}= \hat{x}_{t}- \eta_{t}\hat{g}_{t}$   
[DA update] $\begin{array}{r}{\hat{y}_{t + 1}= \hat{x}_{1}- \eta_{t}\sum_{i \leq t}\hat{g}_{i}}\end{array}$   
$\boldsymbol{y}_{t+1}=\nabla\Phi^{*}(\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}_{t+1})$   
$x_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(y_{t+1})$   
end for

context.name: Algorithm 2: dual-stabilized OMD, eqs. (5)-(7)
context.statement:
Algorithm 2 Dual-stabilized OMD (DS-OMD). The parameters $\gamma_{t}$ control the amount of   
stabilization.   
Input: $x_{1}\in\mathcal{X}\cap\mathcal{D},\eta:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}_{+},\ \gamma:\mathbb{N}\to(0,1]$   
for $t=1,2,\dots$ do   
Incur cost $f_{t}(x_{t})$ and receive $\hat{g}_{t}\in\partial f_{t}(x_{t})$   
$\hat{x}_{t}=\nabla\Phi(x_{t})$ map primal iterate to dual space   
$\hat{w}_{t + 1}= \hat{x}_{t}- \eta_{t}\hat{g}_{t}$ gradient step in dual space (5)   
$\hat{y}_{t+1}=\gamma_{t}\hat{w}_{t+1}+(1-\gamma_{t})\hat{x}_{1}$ stabilization in dual space (6)   
$\boldsymbol{y}_{t+1}=\nabla\Phi^{*}(\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}_{t+1})$ map dual iterate to primal space   
$x_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(y_{t+1})$ project onto feasible region (7)   
end for

context.name: Proposition 39
context.statement:
Proposition 39 Let $a,b,c,u,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfy $\gamma\hat{a}+(1-\gamma)\hat{b}=\hat{c}$ for some $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}$ . Then

$$
\gamma D_{\Phi}({}_{v}^{u};a)\ : +\ :(1-\gamma)D_{\Phi}({}_{v}^{u};b)\ : =\ :D_{\Phi}({}_{v}^{u};c).
$$

context.name: Proposition 40 (Pythagorean theorem for Bregman divergence)
context.statement:
The following proposition is the "Pythagorean theorem for Bregman divergence". Recall that $\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(y)=\arg\operatorname*{min}_{u\in\mathcal{X}}D_{\Phi}(u,y)$ . A proof may be found in Bubeck (2015, Lemma 4.1).

Proposition 40 Let $\mathcal{X}\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a convex set. Let $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\pi=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(p)$ . Then

$$
D_{\Phi}({}_{\pi}^{z};p)\geq D_{\Phi}({}_{\pi}^{z};\pi)=D_{\Phi}(z,\pi)\forall z\in\mathcal{X}.
$$

context.name: Setup: lazy gradient step (18), stabilization (19) and Claim 7 (Section 5.3)
context.statement:
In this section, we show that Nesterov's dual averaging algorithm can be obtained from a small modification to dual-stabilized online mirror descent. Furthermore, our proof of Theorem 3 can be adapted to analyze DA.

The main difference between DS-OMD and dual averaging is in the gradient step, as we now explain. In iteration t of DS-OMD, the gradient step in (5) is taken from $\hat{x}_{t}$ ,the dual counterpart of the iterate $x_{t}\colon$

$$
\mathrm{D S - O M D \ g r a d i e n t \ s t e p}: \quad \hat{w}_{t + 1}= \hat{x}_{t}- \eta_{t}\hat{g}_{t}.
$$

Suppose that the algorithm is modified so that the gradient step is taken from $\hat{y}_{t}$ , the dual point from iteration t before projection onto the feasible region. (Here $\hat{y}_{1}$ is defined to be $\hat{x}_{1}$.) The resulting gradient step is:

$$
\mathrm{L a z y ~ g r a d i e n t ~ s t e p}\colon \hat{w}_{t + 1}= \hat{y}_{t}- \eta_{t}\hat{g}_{t}.\tag{18}
$$

As before, we set

$$
\hat{y}_{t+1}~=~\gamma_{t}\hat{w}_{t+1}+(1-\gamma_{t})\hat{x}_{1}\tag{19}
$$

where $\gamma_{t}= \eta_{t + 1}/ \eta_{t}$ . Then a simple inductive proof yields the following claim.

Claim 7 $\hat{w}_{t}= \hat{x}_{1}- \eta_{t - 1}\sum_{i < t}\hat{g}_{i}$ and $\hat{y}_{t}= \hat{x}_{1}- \eta_{t}\sum_{i < t}\hat{g}_{i}$ for all $t > 1$.

Thus, the algorithm with the lazy gradient step can be written as in Algorithm 4. This is equivalent to Algorithm 1 with the DA update, except that $\eta_{t}$ in Algorithm 1 corresponds to $\eta_{t + 1}$ in Algorithm 4. In the next theorem we analyze DA with similar techniques to the ones used in Theorems 3 and 5.

context.name: Algorithm 4: dual averaging with re-indexed learning rate
context.statement:
Algorithm 4 Dual averaging with learning rate re-indexed as $\eta_{2}, \eta_{3}, \ldots$   
Input: $x_{1}\in\mathcal{X}\cap\mathcal{D},~\eta:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}_{+},~\gamma:\mathbb{N}\to(0,1]$   
$\hat{y}_{1}=\nabla\Phi(x_{1})$   
for $t=1,2,\dots$ do   
Incur cost $f_{t}(x_{t})$ and receive $\hat{g}_{t}\in\partial f_{t}(x_{t})$   
$\begin{array}{r}{\hat{y}_{t + 1}= \hat{x}_{1}- \eta_{t + 1}\sum_{i \leq t}\hat{g}_{i}}\end{array}$ dual averaging update   
$\boldsymbol{y}_{t+1}=\nabla\Phi^{*}(\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}_{t+1})$ map dual iterate to primal space   
$x_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(y_{t+1})$ project onto feasible region   
end for

context.name: Proposition 36 (linearity of D_Φ(^a_b; p) in p̂)
context.statement:
Recall that in (3) we defined the notation

$$
D_{\Phi}({}_{b}^{a};c): =D_{\Phi}(a,c)-D_{\Phi}(b,c)=\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)-\langle\nabla\Phi(c),a-b\rangle .
$$

This has several useful properties, which we now discuss.

Proposition 36 $D_{\Phi}({}_{b}^{a}; p)$ is linear in $\hat{p}$. In particular,

$$
D_{\Phi}\big({}_{b}^{a};\nabla\Phi^{*}(\widehat{p}-\widehat{q})\big)\ =\ D_{\Phi}\big({}_{b}^{a};p\big)+\big\langle\widehat{q},a-b\big\rangle\qquad\forall\widehat{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.
$$

context.name: Proposition 37
context.statement:
Proposition 37 For all $a,b,c,d\in\mathcal{D}$

$$
D_{\Phi}\big({}_{b}^{a};d\big)-D_{\Phi}\big({}_{b}^{a};c\big)=\langle\hat{c}-\hat{d},a-b\rangle=D_{\Phi}\big({}_{b}^{a};d\big)+D_{\Phi}\big({}_{a}^{b};c\big).
$$

context.name: Proposition 41
context.statement:
A generalization of the previous proposition can be obtained by using linearity.

Proposition 41 Let $\mathcal{X}\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a convex set. Let $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\pi=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}^{\Phi}(p)$ . Then

$$
D_{\Phi}\big({}_{\pi}^{v};\nabla\Phi^{*}({\widehat{p}}-{\widehat{q}})\big)\ \geq\ D_{\Phi}\big({}_{\pi}^{v};\nabla\Phi^{*}({\widehat{\pi}}-{\widehat{q}})\big)\qquad\forall v\in\mathcal{X},{\widehat{q}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.
$$

context.name: Lemma 34 (basic properties of the mirror map and Bregman divergence)
context.statement:
The following lemma collects basic facts regarding the a mirror map Φ (or simply a function of Legendre type) and the Bregman divergence it induces. See Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi (2006, Lemma 11.5 and Proposition 11.1).

Lemma 34 The mirror map $\Phi$ and the Bregman divergence it induces satisfy the following properties:

$D_{\Phi}(x,y)$ is convex in x.

$\nabla\Phi(\nabla\Phi^{*}(z))=z$ and $\nabla^{*}\Phi(\nabla\Phi(x))=x$ for all x and z.

$D_{\Phi}(x,y)=D_{\Phi^{*}}\bigl(\nabla\Phi(y),\nabla\Phi(x)\bigr)$ for all x and $y$

Lemma 6 For an MDP with rewards $r^{k}(s,a)$ and transition probability $\tilde{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a)$ such that $\|\tilde{P}(\cdot|s,a)-P(\cdot|s,a)\|_{1}\leq\epsilon_{s,a},$ the Bellman error $B_{\pi_{e}}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)$ for state-action pair s, a is upper bounded as

$$
\begin{array}{r}{B_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)\leq\left\|\tilde{P}(\cdot|s,a)-P(\cdot|s,a)\right\|_{1}\|h_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(\cdot)\|_{\infty},\quad|B_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)|\leq\tilde{D}\operatorname*{min}\left\{\epsilon_{s,a},2\right\},}\end{array}\tag{28}
$$

where $\tilde{D}\geq 0$ is an upper bound on the diameter of the MDP with transition probability $\tilde{P}$ and on the span of the bias, $h_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s)-h_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s^{\prime})\leq\tilde{D}$ for all $s,s^{\prime}$

context.name: Setup: MDP, rewards, policy and average reward (Section 3)
context.statement:
We consider an infinite horizon discounted Markov decision process (MDP) $\mathcal{M}$ defined by the tuple $\left(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r^{1},r^{2},\cdot\cdot\cdot,r^{K},\rho_{0}\right)$ . $\mathcal{S}$ denotes a finite set of state space of size S, and $\mathcal{A}$ denotes a finite set of A actions. $P:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to [0,1]^{S}$ denotes the probability transition distribution. K denotes the number of objectives and $[K]=\{1,2,\cdots,K\}$ is the set of K objectives. Let $r^{k}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to [0,1]$ be the bounded reward function for objective $k \in [ K ]$. Lastly, $\rho_{0}:\mathcal{S}\to [0,1]$ is the distribution of initial state. We motivate our choice of bounds on rewards from the fact that many problems in practice require explicit reward shaping. Hence, the controller or the learner is aware of the bounds on the rewards. We consider the bounds to be [0, 1] for our case which is easy to satisfy by reward shaping.

We use a stochastic policy $\pi:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to [0,1]$ which returns the probability of selecting action $a \in{\mathcal{A}}$ for any given state $s \in{\mathcal{S}}$. Following policy π on the MDP, the agent observes a sequence of random variables $\{S_{t}, A_{t}\}_{t}$ where $S_{t}$ denotes the state of the agent at time t and $A_{t}$ denotes the action taken by the agent at time t. The expected discounted long term reward and expected per step reward of the objective k are given by $J_{\pi}^{P,k}$ and $\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}$ , respectively, when the joint policy π is followed. Formally, for discount factor $\gamma\in(0,1)$ , $J_{\pi}^{P,k}$ and $\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}$ are defined as

$$
J_{\pi}^{P,k}=\mathbb{E}_{S_{0},A_{0},S_{1},A_{1},\cdots}[\operatorname*{lim}_{\tau\to\infty}\sum_{t=0}^{\tau}\gamma^{t}r^{k}(S_{t},A_{t})]\tag{1}
$$

$$
S_{0}\sim\rho_{0}(S_{0}),\ A_{t}\sim\pi(A_{t}|S_{t}),\ S_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot|S_{t},A_{t})
$$

$$
\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}=\mathbb{E}_{S_{0},A_{0},S_{1},A_{1},\cdots}[\operatorname*{lim}_{\tau\to\infty}\frac{1}{\tau}\sum_{t=0}^{\tau}r^{k}(S_{t},A_{t})]\tag{2}
$$

$$
=\operatorname*{lim}_{\gamma\to 1}(1-\gamma)J_{\pi}^{P,k}\tag{3}
$$

context.name: Bias Bellman equation, eq. (4)
context.statement:
Equation (3) follows from the Laurent series expansion of $J_{\pi}^{k}$ (Puterman, 1994). For brevity, in the rest of the paper $\mathbb{E}_{S_{t}, A_{t}, S_{t + 1}; t \geq 0}[ \cdot ]$ will be denoted as $\mathbb{E}_{\rho,\pi,P}[\cdot]$ , where $S_{0}\sim \rho_{0}, \ A_{t}\sim$ $\pi(\cdot|S_{t}),\ S_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot|S_{t},A_{t})$ . The expected per step reward satisfies the following Bellman equation

$$
h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)+\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi}\left[r^{k}(s,a)\right]+\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi}\left[\sum_{s^{\prime}}P(s^{\prime}|s,a)h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s^{\prime})\right]\tag{4}
$$

where $h_{\pi}^{k}(s)$ is the bias of policy π for state s.

context.name: Discounted value and Q-functions, eqs. (5)-(6)
context.statement:
We also define the discounted value function $V_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s)$ and Q-value functions $Q_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s,a)$ as follows:

$$
V_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{A_{0},S_{1},A_{1},\cdots}[\operatorname*{lim}_{\tau\to\infty}\sum_{t=0}^{\tau}\gamma^{t}r^{k}(S_{t},A_{t})|S_{0}=s]\tag{5}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l}{{Q_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}_{S_{1},A_{1},\cdots}[\displaystyle\operatorname*{lim}_{\tau\to\infty}\sum_{t=0}^{\tau}\gamma^{t}r^{k}(S_{t},A_{t})\vert S_{0}=s,A_{0}=a]}}\\ {{\mathrm{~}=r^{k}(s,a)+\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi}[\displaystyle\sum_{s^{\prime}}P(s^{\prime}\vert s,a)V_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s^{\prime})]}}\end{array}\tag{6}
$$

context.name: Bias vs. discounted value, eq. (7)
context.statement:
Further, the bias $h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)$ and the value function $V_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}$ are related as

$$
h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s_{1})-h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s_{2})=\operatorname*{lim}_{\gamma\to 1}(V_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s_{1})-V_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s_{2})),{\mathrm{~w h e r e~}}s_{1},s_{2}\in{\mathcal{S}}.\tag{7}
$$

For notation simplicity, we may drop the superscript P when discussing about variables for the true MDP.

context.name: Induced Markov chain and Definition 1 (Diameter), eq. (8)
context.statement:
Note that each policy induces a Markov Chain on the states $\mathcal{S}$ with transition probabilities $\begin{array}{r}{P_{\pi,s}(s^{\prime})=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a|s)P(s^{\prime}|s,a)}\end{array}$ . After defining a policy, we can now define the diameter of the MDP $\mathcal{M}$ as:

Definition 1 (Diameter) Consider the Markov Chain induced by the policy π on the MDP $\mathcal{M}$. Let $T(s^{\prime}|\mathcal{M},\pi,s)$ be a random variable that denotes the first time step when this Markov Chain enters state s' starting from state s. Then, the diameter of the MDP $\mathcal{M}$ is defined as:

$$
D(\mathcal{M})=\operatorname*{max}_{\pi}\operatorname*{max}_{s^{\prime}\neq s}\mathbb{E}\left[T(s^{\prime}|\mathcal{M},\pi,s)\right]\tag{8}
$$

context.name: Assumption 1 (ergodic MDP), eq. (9)
context.statement:
Further, starting from an arbitrary initial state distribution, the state distribution may take a while to converge to the steady state distribution. For any policy π, let $P_{\pi,s}^{t}=(P_{\pi,s})^{t}$ be the t-step probability distribution of the states when policy π is applied to MDP with transition probabilities P starting from state s.

We are now ready to state our first assumption on the MDP. We assume that the Markov Decision Process is ergodic. This implies that: 1. for any policy all states, $s \in{\mathcal{S}}$ communicate with each other; 2. for any policy, the process converges to the steady state distribution exponentially fast. Formally, we have

Assumption 1 The Markov Decision Process, $\mathcal{M}$, is ergodic. Then, we have,

1. The diameter, D, of $\mathcal{M}$ is finite.

2. For any policy π, for some $C > 0$ and $0 \leq \rho < 1$ , we have

$$
\|P_{\pi,s}^{t}-d_{\pi}\|_{TV}\leq C\rho^{t}\tag{9}
$$

where $d_{\pi}$ is the steady state distribution induced by policy π on the MDP.

context.name: Bellman error, eq. (26)
context.statement:
To compute the regret incurred by the optimal policy $\pi_{e}$ for the sampled MDP on the true MDP ${\mathcal{M}},$ we use Bellman error. For some policy $\pi,$ we define Bellman error $B_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)$ for the infinite horizon MDPs as the difference between the cumulative expected rewards obtained for deviating from the system model with transition $\tilde{P}$ for one step by taking action a in state s and then following policy π. We have:

$$
\begin{array}{r l}&{B_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)=\left(Q_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)-r(s,a)-\gamma\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}P(s^{\prime}|s,a)V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)\right)}\\ &{B_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)=\underset{\gamma\to 1}{\operatorname*{lim}}B_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)}\end{array}\tag{26}
$$

context.name: Lemma 11 (another result of the same paper)
context.statement:
Lemma 11 (Bounded Span of MDP) For an MDP $\mathcal{M}$ with rewards $r^{k}(s,a)$ and transition probabilities P, for any stationary policy π with average reward $\lambda_{\pi}^{k}$ , the difference of bias of any two states $s,$ and $s^{\prime},$ is upper bounded by the diameter of the MDP D as:

$$
h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)-h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s^{\prime})\leq D~\forall~s,s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}.\tag{102}
$$

nl_notes:
### Lemma 6
NOTE (Lemma 6) — In the Lean, `bellmanError` is defined directly as the closed form Σ_{s'} (P̃ − P)(s'|s,a)·h(s') of the paper's eq. (134), so the γ → 1 limit of eq. (26) does not have to be derived. (The paper's eq. (6) omits the discount γ; its proof uses the γ-discounted Q_γ.) The goal is the first inequality of eq. (28), B ≤ ‖P̃ − P‖₁·‖h‖∞, together with |B| ≤ D̃·min{ε, 2}; the middle link ‖P̃ − P‖₁·‖h‖∞ ≤ D̃·min{ε, 2} is not part of it, because `h` is any solution of `hBellman` and need not be normalised (h + const is also a solution).

The statement also adds a hypothesis the paper does not state: the bias-span bound h(s) − h(s′) ≤ D̃ for all s, s′ (`hspan`), with D̃ ≥ 0 any upper bound on the diameter of P̃. The paper's proof uses this bound directly (it takes it from its Lemma 11), so the statement assumes it rather than requiring it to be derived.

import Mathlib

open scoped BigOperators
open MeasureTheory

namespace ResearchLevel

variable {S : Type*} {A : Type*}

noncomputable def bellmanError (Pt P : S → A → S → ℝ) (h : S → ℝ)
    [Fintype S] (s : S) (a : A) : ℝ :=
  ∑ s' : S, (Pt s a s' - P s a s') * h s'

noncomputable def transL1 (Pt P : S → A → S → ℝ)
    [Fintype S] (s : S) (a : A) : ℝ :=
  ∑ s' : S, |Pt s a s' - P s a s'|

noncomputable def biasSupNorm [Fintype S] [Nonempty S] (h : S → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  Finset.univ.sup' Finset.univ_nonempty (fun s' => |h s'|)

noncomputable def hitTime {S Ω : Type*} (X : ℕ → Ω → S) (s' : S) (ω : Ω) : ℕ :=
  sInf {t : ℕ | 1 ≤ t ∧ X t ω = s'}

def IsDiameterBoundOfChain {S Ω : Type*} [Fintype S] [MeasurableSpace Ω]
    (μ : Measure Ω) (X : S → ℕ → Ω → S) (D : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ s s' : S, s ≠ s' →
    (∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, ∃ t : ℕ, 1 ≤ t ∧ X s t ω = s') ∧
    Integrable (fun ω => (hitTime (X s) s' ω : ℝ)) μ ∧
    ∫ ω, (hitTime (X s) s' ω : ℝ) ∂μ ≤ D

def IsDiameterUpperBound (Ω : Type*) {S A : Type*} [Fintype S] [MeasurableSpace S]
    [Fintype A] [MeasurableSpace Ω] (P : S → A → S → ℝ) (D : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (μ₂ : Measure Ω), IsProbabilityMeasure μ₂ →
  ∀ π₂ : S → A → ℝ, (∀ s, (∀ a, 0 ≤ π₂ s a) ∧ ∑ a, π₂ s a = 1) →
  ∀ (X₂ : S → ℕ → Ω → S) (F₂ : ℕ → MeasurableSpace Ω),
    (∀ s₀ t, Measurable (X₂ s₀ t)) →
    (∀ s₀ : S, μ₂ {ω | X₂ s₀ 1 ω = s₀} = 1) →
    Monotone F₂ → (∀ t, F₂ t ≤ (inferInstance : MeasurableSpace Ω)) →
    (∀ s₀ : S, ∀ t t' : ℕ, t ≤ t' → Measurable[F₂ t'] (X₂ s₀ t)) →
    (∀ s₀ : S, ∀ t : ℕ, 1 ≤ t → ∀ H : Set Ω, MeasurableSet[F₂ t] H →
        ∀ x y : S, μ₂ (H ∩ {ω | X₂ s₀ t ω = x}) ≠ 0 →
        μ₂ (H ∩ {ω | X₂ s₀ t ω = x} ∩ {ω | X₂ s₀ (t + 1) ω = y})
          = ENNReal.ofReal (∑ a : A, π₂ x a * P x a y)
              * μ₂ (H ∩ {ω | X₂ s₀ t ω = x})) →
    IsDiameterBoundOfChain μ₂ X₂ D

def IsDiameterBound (Ω : Type*) {S A : Type*} [Fintype S] [MeasurableSpace S]
    [Fintype A] [MeasurableSpace Ω] (P : S → A → S → ℝ) (D : ℝ) : Prop :=
  IsDiameterUpperBound Ω P D ∧ ∀ D' : ℝ, IsDiameterUpperBound Ω P D' → D ≤ D'

  (∑ t' ∈ Finset.Icc 1 t, if Sp t' ω = s ∧ Ap t' ω = a ∧ Sp (t' + 1) ω = s'

nl_statement:
Lemma 11 (Bounded Span of MDP) For an MDP $\mathcal{M}$ with rewards $r^{k}(s,a)$ and transition probabilities P, for any stationary policy π with average reward $\lambda_{\pi}^{k}$ , the difference of bias of any two states $s,$ and $s^{\prime},$ is upper bounded by the diameter of the MDP D as:

$$
h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)-h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s^{\prime})\leq D~\forall~s,s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}.\tag{102}
$$

context.name: Setup: MDP, rewards, policy and average reward (Section 3)
context.statement:
We consider an infinite horizon discounted Markov decision process (MDP) $\mathcal{M}$ defined by the tuple $\left(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r^{1},r^{2},\cdot\cdot\cdot,r^{K},\rho_{0}\right)$ . $\mathcal{S}$ denotes a finite set of state space of size S, and $\mathcal{A}$ denotes a finite set of A actions. $P:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to [0,1]^{S}$ denotes the probability transition distribution. K denotes the number of objectives and $[K]=\{1,2,\cdots,K\}$ is the set of K objectives. Let $r^{k}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to [0,1]$ be the bounded reward function for objective $k \in [ K ]$. Lastly, $\rho_{0}:\mathcal{S}\to [0,1]$ is the distribution of initial state. We motivate our choice of bounds on rewards from the fact that many problems in practice require explicit reward shaping. Hence, the controller or the learner is aware of the bounds on the rewards. We consider the bounds to be [0, 1] for our case which is easy to satisfy by reward shaping.

We use a stochastic policy $\pi:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to [0,1]$ which returns the probability of selecting action $a \in{\mathcal{A}}$ for any given state $s \in{\mathcal{S}}$. Following policy π on the MDP, the agent observes a sequence of random variables $\{S_{t}, A_{t}\}_{t}$ where $S_{t}$ denotes the state of the agent at time t and $A_{t}$ denotes the action taken by the agent at time t. The expected discounted long term reward and expected per step reward of the objective k are given by $J_{\pi}^{P,k}$ and $\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}$ , respectively, when the joint policy π is followed. Formally, for discount factor $\gamma\in(0,1)$ , $J_{\pi}^{P,k}$ and $\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}$ are defined as

$$
J_{\pi}^{P,k}=\mathbb{E}_{S_{0},A_{0},S_{1},A_{1},\cdots}[\operatorname*{lim}_{\tau\to\infty}\sum_{t=0}^{\tau}\gamma^{t}r^{k}(S_{t},A_{t})]\tag{1}
$$

$$
S_{0}\sim\rho_{0}(S_{0}),\ A_{t}\sim\pi(A_{t}|S_{t}),\ S_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot|S_{t},A_{t})
$$

$$
\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}=\mathbb{E}_{S_{0},A_{0},S_{1},A_{1},\cdots}[\operatorname*{lim}_{\tau\to\infty}\frac{1}{\tau}\sum_{t=0}^{\tau}r^{k}(S_{t},A_{t})]\tag{2}
$$

$$
=\operatorname*{lim}_{\gamma\to 1}(1-\gamma)J_{\pi}^{P,k}\tag{3}
$$

context.name: Bias Bellman equation, eq. (4)
context.statement:
Equation (3) follows from the Laurent series expansion of $J_{\pi}^{k}$ (Puterman, 1994). For brevity, in the rest of the paper $\mathbb{E}_{S_{t}, A_{t}, S_{t + 1}; t \geq 0}[ \cdot ]$ will be denoted as $\mathbb{E}_{\rho,\pi,P}[\cdot]$ , where $S_{0}\sim \rho_{0}, \ A_{t}\sim$ $\pi(\cdot|S_{t}),\ S_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot|S_{t},A_{t})$ . The expected per step reward satisfies the following Bellman equation

$$
h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)+\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi}\left[r^{k}(s,a)\right]+\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi}\left[\sum_{s^{\prime}}P(s^{\prime}|s,a)h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s^{\prime})\right]\tag{4}
$$

where $h_{\pi}^{k}(s)$ is the bias of policy π for state s.

context.name: Induced Markov chain and Definition 1 (Diameter), eq. (8)
context.statement:
Note that each policy induces a Markov Chain on the states $\mathcal{S}$ with transition probabilities $\begin{array}{r}{P_{\pi,s}(s^{\prime})=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a|s)P(s^{\prime}|s,a)}\end{array}$ . After defining a policy, we can now define the diameter of the MDP $\mathcal{M}$ as:

Definition 1 (Diameter) Consider the Markov Chain induced by the policy π on the MDP $\mathcal{M}$. Let $T(s^{\prime}|\mathcal{M},\pi,s)$ be a random variable that denotes the first time step when this Markov Chain enters state s' starting from state s. Then, the diameter of the MDP $\mathcal{M}$ is defined as:

$$
D(\mathcal{M})=\operatorname*{max}_{\pi}\operatorname*{max}_{s^{\prime}\neq s}\mathbb{E}\left[T(s^{\prime}|\mathcal{M},\pi,s)\right]\tag{8}
$$

context.name: Assumption 1 (ergodic MDP), eq. (9)
context.statement:
Further, starting from an arbitrary initial state distribution, the state distribution may take a while to converge to the steady state distribution. For any policy π, let $P_{\pi,s}^{t}=(P_{\pi,s})^{t}$ be the t-step probability distribution of the states when policy π is applied to MDP with transition probabilities P starting from state s.

We are now ready to state our first assumption on the MDP. We assume that the Markov Decision Process is ergodic. This implies that: 1. for any policy all states, $s \in{\mathcal{S}}$ communicate with each other; 2. for any policy, the process converges to the steady state distribution exponentially fast. Formally, we have

Assumption 1 The Markov Decision Process, $\mathcal{M}$, is ergodic. Then, we have,

1. The diameter, D, of $\mathcal{M}$ is finite.

2. For any policy π, for some $C > 0$ and $0 \leq \rho < 1$ , we have

$$
\|P_{\pi,s}^{t}-d_{\pi}\|_{TV}\leq C\rho^{t}\tag{9}
$$

where $d_{\pi}$ is the steady state distribution induced by policy π on the MDP.

noncomputable def bellmanError (Pt P : S → A → S → ℝ) (h : S → ℝ)
    [Fintype S] (s : S) (a : A) : ℝ :=
  ∑ s' : S, (Pt s a s' - P s a s') * h s'

noncomputable def transL1 (Pt P : S → A → S → ℝ)
    [Fintype S] (s : S) (a : A) : ℝ :=
  ∑ s' : S, |Pt s a s' - P s a s'|

noncomputable def biasSupNorm [Fintype S] [Nonempty S] (h : S → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  Finset.univ.sup' Finset.univ_nonempty (fun s' => |h s'|)

noncomputable def hitTime {S Ω : Type*} (X : ℕ → Ω → S) (s' : S) (ω : Ω) : ℕ :=
  sInf {t : ℕ | 1 ≤ t ∧ X t ω = s'}

def IsDiameterBoundOfChain {S Ω : Type*} [Fintype S] [MeasurableSpace Ω]
    (μ : Measure Ω) (X : S → ℕ → Ω → S) (D : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ s s' : S, s ≠ s' →
    (∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, ∃ t : ℕ, 1 ≤ t ∧ X s t ω = s') ∧
    Integrable (fun ω => (hitTime (X s) s' ω : ℝ)) μ ∧
    ∫ ω, (hitTime (X s) s' ω : ℝ) ∂μ ≤ D

def IsDiameterUpperBound (Ω : Type*) {S A : Type*} [Fintype S] [MeasurableSpace S]
    [Fintype A] [MeasurableSpace Ω] (P : S → A → S → ℝ) (D : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (μ₂ : Measure Ω), IsProbabilityMeasure μ₂ →
  ∀ π₂ : S → A → ℝ, (∀ s, (∀ a, 0 ≤ π₂ s a) ∧ ∑ a, π₂ s a = 1) →
  ∀ (X₂ : S → ℕ → Ω → S) (F₂ : ℕ → MeasurableSpace Ω),
    (∀ s₀ t, Measurable (X₂ s₀ t)) →
    (∀ s₀ : S, μ₂ {ω | X₂ s₀ 1 ω = s₀} = 1) →
    Monotone F₂ → (∀ t, F₂ t ≤ (inferInstance : MeasurableSpace Ω)) →
    (∀ s₀ : S, ∀ t t' : ℕ, t ≤ t' → Measurable[F₂ t'] (X₂ s₀ t)) →
    (∀ s₀ : S, ∀ t : ℕ, 1 ≤ t → ∀ H : Set Ω, MeasurableSet[F₂ t] H →
        ∀ x y : S, μ₂ (H ∩ {ω | X₂ s₀ t ω = x}) ≠ 0 →
        μ₂ (H ∩ {ω | X₂ s₀ t ω = x} ∩ {ω | X₂ s₀ (t + 1) ω = y})
          = ENNReal.ofReal (∑ a : A, π₂ x a * P x a y)
              * μ₂ (H ∩ {ω | X₂ s₀ t ω = x})) →
    IsDiameterBoundOfChain μ₂ X₂ D

def IsDiameterBound (Ω : Type*) {S A : Type*} [Fintype S] [MeasurableSpace S]
    [Fintype A] [MeasurableSpace Ω] (P : S → A → S → ℝ) (D : ℝ) : Prop :=
  IsDiameterUpperBound Ω P D ∧ ∀ D' : ℝ, IsDiameterUpperBound Ω P D' → D ≤ D'

context.name: Setup: MDP, rewards, policy and average reward (Section 3)
context.statement:
We consider an infinite horizon discounted Markov decision process (MDP) $\mathcal{M}$ defined by the tuple $\left(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r^{1},r^{2},\cdot\cdot\cdot,r^{K},\rho_{0}\right)$ . $\mathcal{S}$ denotes a finite set of state space of size S, and $\mathcal{A}$ denotes a finite set of A actions. $P:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to [0,1]^{S}$ denotes the probability transition distribution. K denotes the number of objectives and $[K]=\{1,2,\cdots,K\}$ is the set of K objectives. Let $r^{k}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to [0,1]$ be the bounded reward function for objective $k \in [ K ]$. Lastly, $\rho_{0}:\mathcal{S}\to [0,1]$ is the distribution of initial state. We motivate our choice of bounds on rewards from the fact that many problems in practice require explicit reward shaping. Hence, the controller or the learner is aware of the bounds on the rewards. We consider the bounds to be [0, 1] for our case which is easy to satisfy by reward shaping.

We use a stochastic policy $\pi:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to [0,1]$ which returns the probability of selecting action $a \in{\mathcal{A}}$ for any given state $s \in{\mathcal{S}}$. Following policy π on the MDP, the agent observes a sequence of random variables $\{S_{t}, A_{t}\}_{t}$ where $S_{t}$ denotes the state of the agent at time t and $A_{t}$ denotes the action taken by the agent at time t. The expected discounted long term reward and expected per step reward of the objective k are given by $J_{\pi}^{P,k}$ and $\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}$ , respectively, when the joint policy π is followed. Formally, for discount factor $\gamma\in(0,1)$ , $J_{\pi}^{P,k}$ and $\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}$ are defined as

$$
J_{\pi}^{P,k}=\mathbb{E}_{S_{0},A_{0},S_{1},A_{1},\cdots}[\operatorname*{lim}_{\tau\to\infty}\sum_{t=0}^{\tau}\gamma^{t}r^{k}(S_{t},A_{t})]\tag{1}
$$

$$
S_{0}\sim\rho_{0}(S_{0}),\ A_{t}\sim\pi(A_{t}|S_{t}),\ S_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot|S_{t},A_{t})
$$

$$
\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}=\mathbb{E}_{S_{0},A_{0},S_{1},A_{1},\cdots}[\operatorname*{lim}_{\tau\to\infty}\frac{1}{\tau}\sum_{t=0}^{\tau}r^{k}(S_{t},A_{t})]\tag{2}
$$

$$
=\operatorname*{lim}_{\gamma\to 1}(1-\gamma)J_{\pi}^{P,k}\tag{3}
$$

context.name: Good event E_t, eq. (29), and empirical estimates
context.statement:
A major part of the regret analysis is how well the learned model estimates the true system model. For that, bound the deviation of the estimates of the estimated transition probabilities of the Markov Decision Processes $\mathcal{M}$. For that we use $\ell_{1}$ deviation bounds from (Weissman et al., 2003). Consider, the following event,

$$
\mathcal{E}_{t}=\left\{\|\bar{P}_{t}(\cdot|s,a)-P(\cdot|s,a)\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{\frac{14S\log(2AT)}{\operatorname*{max}\{1,n_{t}(s,a)\}}}\forall(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\right\}\tag{29}
$$

where $\begin{array}{r}{n_{t}(s,a)=\sum_{t^{\prime}=1}^{t}\mathbf{1}_{\{S_{t^{\prime}}=s,a_{t^{\prime}}=a\}}}\end{array}$ and $\begin{array}{r}{\bar{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a)=\left(\sum_{t^{\prime}=1}^{t}\mathbf{1}_{\{S_{t^{\prime}}=s,a_{t^{\prime}}=a,S_{t^{\prime}+1}=s^{\prime}\}}\right)/n_{t}(s,a)}\end{array}$ of the empirical estimate of the transition probabilities.

context.name: Algorithm 1 (Model-Based Joint Decision Making) and its description (Section 5.1)
context.statement:
Algorithm 1 Model-Based Joint Decision Making Algorithm   
1: procedure Model Based Online($\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},[K],f,r$)   
2: Initialize $N(s,a,s^{\prime})=1\forall(s,a,s^{\prime})\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{S}$   
3: Initialize $\nu_{0}(s,a)=0~\forall~(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}$   
4: Initialize $\textstyle\pi_{1}(a|s)={\frac{1}{|{\mathcal{A}}|}}\forall(a,s)\in{\mathcal{A}}\times{\mathcal{S}}$   
5: Initialize $e = 1$   
6: for time steps $t=1,2,\cdots$ do   
7: Observe current state $S_{t}$   
8: Sample action to play $A_{t}\sim\pi_{e}(\cdot|S_{t})$   
9: Play $A_{t},$ obtain reward $r_{t}\in [0,1]^{K}$ and observe next state $S_{t + 1}$   
10: Update $N(S_{t},A_{t},S_{t+1})\gets N(S_{t},A_{t},S_{t+1})+1,\nu_{e}(S_{t},A_{t})\gets\nu_{e}(S_{t},A_{t})+1$   
11: if $\begin{array}{r}{\nu_{e}(S_{t},A_{t})\ge\operatorname*{max}\{1,\sum_{e^{\prime}<e}\nu_{e^{\prime}}(S_{t},A_{t})\}}\end{array}$ then   
12: Update epoch counter $e \gets e + 1$   
13: Initialize $\nu_{e}(s,a)=0~\forall~(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}$   
14: $P_{e}(s^{\prime}|s,a)\sim Dir(N(s,a,\cdot))\ \forall\ (s,a)$   
15: Solve steady state distribution $d(s,a)$ as the solution of the optimization   
problem in Equations (20-23)   
16: Obtain optimal policy $\pi_{e}$ as   
$\pi_{e}(a|s)={\frac{d(s,a)}{\sum_{a\in{\mathcal{A}}}d(s,a)}}$   
17: end if   
18: end for   
19: end procedure

Algorithm 1 describes the overall procedure that estimates the transition probabilities and the reward functions. The algorithm takes as input the state space $\mathcal{S}$, action space ${\mathcal{A}},$ set of agents [K], the reward structure $r$, and the objective function $f .$ It initializes the next state visit count for each state-action pair $N(s,a,s^{\prime})$ by one for Dirichlet sampling. For initial exploration, the policy uses a uniform distribution over all the actions. The algorithm proceeds in epochs e with $t_{e}$ denoting the time step t at which epoch e starts. Also, $\nu_{e}(s,a)$ stores the number of times a state-action pair is visited in epoch e. We assume that the controller is optimizing for infinite horizon and thus there is no stopping condition for epoch loop in Line 6. For each time index $t \in [ t_{e}, t_{e + 1})$ in epoch $e,$ the controller observes the state, samples and plays the action according to $\pi_{e}(\cdot|s)$ , and observes the rewards for each agent and next state. It then updates the state visit count for the observed state and played action pair. We break the current epoch e if the total number of visitations of any state action pair in current epoch exceeds total visitations in previous epoch. This epoch breaking strategy ensures that each state-action triggers epoch switches exponentially slower. This increasing epoch duration bounds the policy switching cost (Jaksch et al., 2010). After breaking the epoch, we sample transition probabilities from the updated posterior and find a new optimal policy for the sampled MDP by solving the optimization framework described in Equation(20).

import Mathlib

open scoped BigOperators
open MeasureTheory

namespace ResearchLevel

variable {S : Type*} {A : Type*}

noncomputable def bellmanError (Pt P : S → A → S → ℝ) (h : S → ℝ)
    [Fintype S] (s : S) (a : A) : ℝ :=
  ∑ s' : S, (Pt s a s' - P s a s') * h s'

noncomputable def transL1 (Pt P : S → A → S → ℝ)
    [Fintype S] (s : S) (a : A) : ℝ :=
  ∑ s' : S, |Pt s a s' - P s a s'|

noncomputable def biasSupNorm [Fintype S] [Nonempty S] (h : S → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  Finset.univ.sup' Finset.univ_nonempty (fun s' => |h s'|)

noncomputable def hitTime {S Ω : Type*} (X : ℕ → Ω → S) (s' : S) (ω : Ω) : ℕ :=
  sInf {t : ℕ | 1 ≤ t ∧ X t ω = s'}

def IsDiameterBoundOfChain {S Ω : Type*} [Fintype S] [MeasurableSpace Ω]
    (μ : Measure Ω) (X : S → ℕ → Ω → S) (D : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ s s' : S, s ≠ s' →
    (∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, ∃ t : ℕ, 1 ≤ t ∧ X s t ω = s') ∧
    Integrable (fun ω => (hitTime (X s) s' ω : ℝ)) μ ∧
    ∫ ω, (hitTime (X s) s' ω : ℝ) ∂μ ≤ D

def IsDiameterUpperBound (Ω : Type*) {S A : Type*} [Fintype S] [MeasurableSpace S]
    [Fintype A] [MeasurableSpace Ω] (P : S → A → S → ℝ) (D : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (μ₂ : Measure Ω), IsProbabilityMeasure μ₂ →
  ∀ π₂ : S → A → ℝ, (∀ s, (∀ a, 0 ≤ π₂ s a) ∧ ∑ a, π₂ s a = 1) →
  ∀ (X₂ : S → ℕ → Ω → S) (F₂ : ℕ → MeasurableSpace Ω),
    (∀ s₀ t, Measurable (X₂ s₀ t)) →
    (∀ s₀ : S, μ₂ {ω | X₂ s₀ 1 ω = s₀} = 1) →
    Monotone F₂ → (∀ t, F₂ t ≤ (inferInstance : MeasurableSpace Ω)) →
    (∀ s₀ : S, ∀ t t' : ℕ, t ≤ t' → Measurable[F₂ t'] (X₂ s₀ t)) →
    (∀ s₀ : S, ∀ t : ℕ, 1 ≤ t → ∀ H : Set Ω, MeasurableSet[F₂ t] H →
        ∀ x y : S, μ₂ (H ∩ {ω | X₂ s₀ t ω = x}) ≠ 0 →
        μ₂ (H ∩ {ω | X₂ s₀ t ω = x} ∩ {ω | X₂ s₀ (t + 1) ω = y})
          = ENNReal.ofReal (∑ a : A, π₂ x a * P x a y)
              * μ₂ (H ∩ {ω | X₂ s₀ t ω = x})) →
    IsDiameterBoundOfChain μ₂ X₂ D

def IsDiameterBound (Ω : Type*) {S A : Type*} [Fintype S] [MeasurableSpace S]
    [Fintype A] [MeasurableSpace Ω] (P : S → A → S → ℝ) (D : ℝ) : Prop :=
  IsDiameterUpperBound Ω P D ∧ ∀ D' : ℝ, IsDiameterUpperBound Ω P D' → D ≤ D'


theorem lemma6 {Ω : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Ω] [Fintype S] [Nonempty S] [DecidableEq S] [MeasurableSpace S] [MeasurableSingletonClass S] [Fintype A]
    (Pt P : S → A → S → ℝ) (h : S → ℝ) (s : S) (a : A) (Dt ε : ℝ)
    (hD : 0 ≤ Dt)
    (hP_nonneg : ∀ s', 0 ≤ P s a s') (hP_sum : ∑ s', P s a s' = 1)
    (hPt_nonneg : ∀ s', 0 ≤ Pt s a s') (hPt_sum : ∑ s', Pt s a s' = 1)
    (hP_prob : ∀ x b, (∀ y, 0 ≤ P x b y) ∧ ∑ y, P x b y = 1)
    (hPt_prob : ∀ x b, (∀ y, 0 ≤ Pt x b y) ∧ ∑ y, Pt x b y = 1)
    (hε : transL1 Pt P s a ≤ ε)
    (hspan : ∀ x y : S, h x - h y ≤ Dt)
    (hDiam : IsDiameterUpperBound Ω Pt Dt)
    (π : S → A → ℝ) (hπ_prob : ∀ x, (∀ a', 0 ≤ π x a') ∧ ∑ a', π x a' = 1)
    (r : S → A → ℝ) (hr_bound : ∀ x b, r x b ∈ Set.Icc (0:ℝ) 1)
    (Pπ : S → S → ℝ) (hPπ_def : ∀ x y, Pπ x y = ∑ a' : A, π x a' * Pt x a' y)
    (hPπ_prob : ∀ x, (∀ y, 0 ≤ Pπ x y) ∧ ∑ y, Pπ x y = 1)
    (rπ : S → ℝ) (hrπ_def : ∀ x, rπ x = ∑ a' : A, π x a' * r x a')
    (lam : ℝ)
    (hBellman : ∀ x, h x = rπ x - lam + ∑ y, Pπ x y * h y)
    (hErgodic : ∀ π₂ : S → A → ℝ, (∀ x, (∀ a, 0 ≤ π₂ x a) ∧ ∑ a, π₂ x a = 1) →
        ∃ (d : S → ℝ) (C ρ : ℝ), 0 ≤ C ∧ 0 ≤ ρ ∧ ρ < 1 ∧
          ∀ t : ℕ, ∀ x : S,
            ∑ y, |((Matrix.of fun u v => ∑ a, π₂ u a * P u a v) ^ t) x y - d y|
              ≤ C * ρ ^ t)
    (hCommunicate : ∀ π₂ : S → A → ℝ, (∀ x, (∀ a, 0 ≤ π₂ x a) ∧ ∑ a, π₂ x a = 1) →
        ∀ x y : S, ∃ t : ℕ,
          0 < ((Matrix.of fun u v => ∑ a, π₂ u a * P u a v) ^ t) x y) :
    bellmanError Pt P h s a ≤ transL1 Pt P s a * biasSupNorm h
      ∧ |bellmanError Pt P h s a| ≤ Dt * min ε 2 := by
  sorry

noncomputable def visitCount {S A Ω : Type*} [DecidableEq S] [DecidableEq A]
    (Sp : ℕ → Ω → S) (Ap : ℕ → Ω → A) (t : ℕ) (s : S) (a : A) (ω : Ω) : ℕ :=
  ∑ t' ∈ Finset.Icc 1 t, if Sp t' ω = s ∧ Ap t' ω = a then 1 else 0

noncomputable def empTrans {S A Ω : Type*} [DecidableEq S] [DecidableEq A]
    (Sp : ℕ → Ω → S) (Ap : ℕ → Ω → A) (t : ℕ) (s : S) (a : A) (s' : S) (ω : Ω) : ℝ :=
  (∑ t' ∈ Finset.Icc 1 t, if Sp t' ω = s ∧ Ap t' ω = a ∧ Sp (t' + 1) ω = s'
      then (1 : ℝ) else 0) / (visitCount Sp Ap t s a ω : ℝ)

def goodEvent {S A Ω : Type*} [Fintype S] [Fintype A] [DecidableEq S] [DecidableEq A]

  ∀ s : S, ∀ a : A,

          / max 1 (visitCount Sp Ap t s a ω : ℝ))

context.name: Setup: robust risk Eq. (1) and DRERM (Section 1)
context.statement:
Concretely, let $\mathcal{X}$ be the instance space, while $\mathcal{Y}=\{+1,-1\}$ denotes the label space. We formalize the distributional shift that we would like to protect against as an uncertainty set $\mathcal{U}(P)$ containing distributions with certain constraints, such as moment condition (Delage and Ye, 2010), Wasserstein distance (Gao, 2020) and f-divergence (Duchi and Namkoong, 2021). For a distribution P over $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}=\{(x,y):x\in\mathcal{X},y\in\mathcal{Y}\}$ , we observe m i.i.d. samples $S \sim P^{m}$ , and distributionally robust learning attempts to learn a predictor $h : \mathcal{X}\to \mathcal{Y}$ having small distributionally robust risk,

$$
R_{\mathcal{U}}(h;P): =\operatorname*{sup}_{Q\in\mathcal{U}(P)}\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim Q}[\mathbb{1}[h(x)\neq y]].\tag{1}
$$

The common approach to distributionally robust learning involves selecting a hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}\subseteq \mathcal{Y}^{\mathcal{X}}$ and learning a predictor $\hat{h}: \mathcal{X}\to \mathcal{Y}$ from $\mathcal{H}$ through Distributionally Robust Empirical Risk Minimization:

$$
\begin{array}{r}{\hat{h}\in\mathrm{DRERM}_{\mathcal{H}}(S): =\underset{h\in\mathcal{H}}{\mathrm{argmin}}\hat{R}_{\mathcal{U}}(h;S),}\end{array}
$$

where $\begin{array}{r}{\hat{R}_{\mathcal{U}}(h;S): =\operatorname*{sup}_{Q\in\mathcal{U}(P_{m})}\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim Q}[\mathbb{1}\left[h(x)\neq y\right]]}\end{array}$ and $P_{m}$ denotes the empirical distribution over samples S.

context.name: Uncertainty set and chi^2-divergence D_2 (Section 1)
context.statement:
Namely, we consider the distributional shift as follows:

$$
\mathcal{U}(P)=\{Q\ll P:D_{2}(Q\|P)\leq\rho\},
$$

where $\begin{array}{r}{D_{2}(Q\|P): =\frac{1}{2}\int\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}-1\right)^{2}dP}\end{array}$ and $Q \ll P$ indicates that distribution Q is absolutely continuous with respect to $P .$ The $\chi^{2}$-divergence is a commonly explored concept in the distributionally robust optimization (DRO) literature (Duchi and Namkoong, 2019). Moreover, it is also a crucial concept in a variety of fields such as information theory, statistics, learning, signal processing, and various branches of mathematics (Park et al., 2011; Saraswat, 2014; Nishiyama and Sason, 2020). The $\chi^{2}$-divergence plays a fundamental role in problems related to source and channel coding, combinatorics, large deviation theory, goodness-of-fit, and independence tests in statistics, as demonstrated by Csiszár et al. (2004). Additionally, it is widely recognized for its computational feasibility and statistical properties, as noted in Tsybakov (2009).

context.name: Problem setup (Section 2)
context.statement: Given a hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}\subseteq \mathcal{Y}^{\mathcal{X}}$ , our goal is to design a learning rule $\mathcal{A}:(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{*}\mapsto\mathcal{Y}^{\mathcal{X}}$ such that for any distribution P over $\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}$ , the rule $\mathcal{A}$ will find a predictor that can compete with the best predictor $h^{\ast}\in \mathcal{H}$ in terms of the distributionally robust risk using a number of samples that is independent of the distribution P. In this paper, we use $(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{*}$ to denote the set of all sequences in the space $\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}$ . The following definitions formalize the notion of distributionally robust PAC learning under the realizable case and agnostic settings.

context.name: Definition 1 (Agnostic Distributionally Robust PAC Learnability)
context.statement:
Definition 1 (Agnostic Distributionally Robust PAC Learnability) For any $\varepsilon,\delta\in$ (0, 1), the sample complexity of agnostic distributionally robust $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-PAC learning of $\mathcal{H}$ with respect to the distributional shift $\mathcal{U}$, denoted by $\mathcal{M}_{AG}(\varepsilon,\delta;\mathcal{H},\mathcal{U})$ , is defined as the smallest $m \in \mathbb{N}\cup \{0 \}$ for which there exists a learning rule $\mathcal{A}:(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{*}\mapsto\mathcal{Y}^{\mathcal{X}}$ such that, for every data distribution P over $\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}$ , with probability of at least $1 - \delta$ over $S \sim P^{m}$ ,

$$
R_{\mathcal{U}}(\mathcal{A}(S);P)\leq\operatorname*{inf}_{h\in\mathcal{H}}R_{\mathcal{U}}(h;P)+\varepsilon .
$$

If no such m exists, define $\mathcal{M}_{AG}(\varepsilon,\delta;\mathcal{H},\mathcal{U})=\infty$ . We say that $\mathcal{H}$ is distributionally robustly PAC-learnable in the agnostic setting with respect to the distributional shift $\mathcal{U}$ if $\forall\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1)$ , $\mathcal{M}_{AG}(\varepsilon,\delta;\mathcal{H},\mathcal{U})$ scales polynomially with $1 / \varepsilon$ and $1 / \delta$

context.name: Definition 3 (VC dimension)
context.statement: Definition 3 (VC dimension) We say that a sequence $\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\}\subseteq{\mathcal{X}}$ is shattered by $\mathcal{H}$ if $\forall y_{1},\ldots,y_{k}\in\mathcal{Y},\exists h\in\mathcal{H}$ such that $\forall i\in [k],h(x_{i})=y_{i}$ . The VC dimension of $\mathcal{H}$ (denoted as $vc(\mathcal{H}))$ is then defined as the largest integer k for which there exists $\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\}\subseteq{\mathcal{X}}$ that is shattered by $\mathcal{H}$. If no such k exists, then $vc(\mathcal{H})$ is said to be infinite.

context.name: Loss class L_H
context.statement:
Denote the loss class of $\mathcal{H}$ by $\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{H}}$ , where

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{H}}=\Big\{(x,y)\mapsto\mathbb{1}[h(x)\neq y]:h\in\mathcal{H}\Big\}.
$$

context.name: Notation R_2(h;P) (Section 3)
context.statement:
We use $R_{2}(h;P)$ to denote the distributionally robust risk under distributional shift

$$
\begin{array}{r}{\mathcal{U}(P)=\left\{Q\ll P:D_{2}(Q\|P)\leq\rho\right\}.}\end{array}
$$

context.name: Proposition 4 (Duality Formulation), Eq. (2) (Shapiro 2017)
context.statement:
We recall the following duality formulation (Shapiro, 2017, Section 3.2) for distributionally robust risk, which is essential in our derivation.

Proposition 4 (Duality Formulation) For any probability P on $\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}$ , any $\rho > 0$ , and $c_{2}(\rho): =\sqrt{1+2\rho},$ for all $h \in \mathcal H$ , we have

$$
R_{2}(h;P)=\operatorname*{inf}_{\eta\in\mathbb{R}}\Big\{c_{2}(\rho)\mathbb{E}_{P}\Big [(\mathbb{1}[h(x)\neq y]-\eta)_{+}^{2}\Big]^{1/2}+\eta\Big\},\tag{2}
$$

where $a_{+}: =\operatorname*{max}\left(a,0\right)$

context.name: g_2 and Lemma 5 (compact range for eta), Remark 6
context.statement:
To bring the above proposition into effect, we need the following lemma. In the interests of simplicity, for any fixed $h \in \mathcal H$ , let

$$
\begin{array}{r}{g_{2}(\eta,P): =c_{2}(\rho)\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[(\mathbb{1}\left[h(x)\neq y\right]-\eta)_{+}^{2}\right]^{1/2}+\eta .}\end{array}
$$

Lemma 5 For any distribution $P$ ,

$$
\operatorname*{inf}_{\eta\in\mathbb{R}}g_{2}(\eta,P)=\operatorname*{inf}_{\eta}\left\{g_{2}(\eta,P):\eta\in\left[-\frac{1}{c_{2}(\rho)-1},1\right]\right\}.
$$

Remark 6 The above lemma restricts the domain of η to a compact set, which is crucial to our uniform convergence result.

context.name: Remark 8 (dependence on 1/(c_2(rho)-1))
context.statement: Remark 8 The dependence on $\frac{1}{c_{2}(\rho)-1}$ is due to the lower bound for η in Lemma 5. While more advanced techniques could potentially yield a better dependence on $\rho,$ it is worth noting that the upper bound shows that the finite VC dimension is sufficient for distributionally robust PAC learnability for finite non-zero values of ρ.

context.name: Notation phi_{eta,h} (Appendix A.1)
context.statement: We use $\varphi_{\eta,h}(x,y)$ to denote $\mathbb{1}[h(x)\neq y]-\eta$ and $c_{2}$ as the shorthand of $c_{2}(\rho)$ when there is no ambiguity.

context.name: Definition 16 (Rademacher Complexity)
context.statement:
Moreover, we introduce the definition of Rademacher Complexity and Growth Function in order to bound the excess risk in terms of VC dimension.

Definition 16 (Rademacher Complexity) We define the empirical Rademacher Complexity of a hypothesis class $\mathcal{F}$ for a given sample $z_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i}),i=1,\dots,m$ as follows :

$$
\hat{\mathcal{R}}_{m}(\mathcal{F}): =\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\operatorname*{sup}_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sigma_{i}f(z_{i})\right],
$$

where $\sigma=(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{m}) $ is a vector of i.i.d. Rademacher variables. The Rademacher Complexity is defined as the expectation of this quantity:

$$
\mathcal{R}_{m}(\mathcal{F}): =\mathbb{E}_{(z_{1},\ldots,z_{m})\sim P^{m}}\left[\hat{\mathcal{R}}_{m}(\mathcal{F})\right].
$$

context.name: Lemma 20 (Hoeffding's Inequality; Shalev-Shwartz & Ben-David Lemma 4.5)
context.statement:
The following Hoeffding's lemma can be found in (Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, 2014, Lemma 4.5).

Lemma 20 (Hoeffding's Inequality) Let $\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{m}$ be a sequence of i.i.d. random variables, and assume that for all $i,\mathbb{E}[\theta_{i}]=\mu$ and $\mathbb{P}[ a \leq \theta_{i}\leq b ] = 1$ . Then, for any $\varepsilon > 0$ ,

$$
\mathbb{P}\left[\left|\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\theta_{i}-\mu\right| >\varepsilon\right]\leq 2\exp{(-2m\varepsilon^{2}/(b-a)^{2})}.
$$

context.name: Lemma 21 (Talagrand's Lemma; Mohri et al. Lemma 4.2)
context.statement:
We next recall an important lemma that is useful for bounding the Rademacher complexity and can be found in (Mohri et al., 2012, Lemma 4.2).

Lemma 21 (Talagrand's Lemma) Let ψ be a ρ-Lipschitz function. For any function class $\mathcal{H}$, we have:

$$
\mathcal{R}_{m}(\psi\circ\mathcal{H})\leq\rho\mathcal{R}_{m}(\mathcal{H}).
$$

context.name: Lemma 22 (Shalev-Shwartz & Ben-David Lemma A.1)
context.statement:
The following lemma is fundamental and can be found in (Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, 2014, Lemma A.1).

Lemma 22 Let $a > 1$ and $b > 0$ Then: $x\geq 4a\log(2a)+2b\implies x\geq a\log(x)+b.$
