context.name: Classification-calibration and Fisher consistency (Section 2)
context.statement:
Lin (2004) proposed Fisher consistency as a necessary condition on a loss function. It is defined to be that any global minimizer $\check{f}$ (if it exists) of $\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}f(\mathbf{X}))]$ , generally referred to as a population minimizer, has the same sign function as the Bayes rule almost surely. Later, Bartlett et al. (2006) defined classification-calibration. A loss function L is called classification-calibrated if any global minimizer $\bar{f}$ (if it exists) of $\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}f(\mathbf{X}))\mid\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}]$ has the same sign as the Bayes rule almost surely. For example, the hinge loss is classification-calibrated, which can be directly shown by Theorem 2 of Bartlett et al. (2006).

An unspoken assumption in those two definitions is the existence of a global minimizer. When $\bar{f}$ exists (which can be easily checked) and $|\mathrm{E}[L({\bf Y}\bar{f}({\bf X}))]| <\infty .$ then a population minimizer $\check{f}$ exists. We further see that loss function L is classification-calibrated if and only if it is Fisher consistent. The 'if' statement follows from the fact that any $\bar{f}$ is also a population minimizer and the definition of Fisher consistency. The 'only if' statement comes from the fact that $\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}{\bar{f}}(\mathbf{X}))\mid\mathbf{X}]=\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}{\check{f}}(\mathbf{X}))\mid\mathbf{X}]$ almost surely and that for any $\delta_{\mathbf{X}}$ such that $\operatorname{sgn}(\delta_{\mathbf{X}})\neq\operatorname{sgn}(p(\mathbf{X})-1/2),\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}{\bar{f}}(\mathbf{X}))\mid\mathbf{X}]<\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}\delta_{\mathbf{X}})\mid\mathbf{X}]$ almost surely by the definition of classification-calibration.

For a non-negative loss function L, $\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}\bar{f}(\mathbf{X}))]$ is always finite. However, the LHS loss does not guarantee the finiteness of $\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}\bar{f}(\mathbf{X}))]$ (see Theorem 4 for further information), thereby not ensuring the existence of a global minimizer that Fisher consistency implicitly assumes. Instead, we verify that the LHS loss is classification-calibrated. The LHS loss is the first negatively divergent loss function proven to satisfy the classification-calibration property.

context.name: Remark 1 (why p(x) in (0,1))
context.statement: Remark 1 In general, a global minimizer of $\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}f(\mathbf{X}))\mid\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}]$ is allowed to take values $\pm \infty$ because what matters is only the sign of the minimizer $(Lin,~2004)$ If we allow the minimum objective to take values $\pm \infty$ , Theorem 1 can be extended to include $p(\mathbf{x})$ equals to 0 and 1. It is because if $p(\mathbf{x})=0$, then $\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}\alpha)\mid\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}]=L(-\alpha)\to-\infty$ as $\alpha \to - \infty$. If $p ({\bf x}) = 1$ , then $\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}f(\mathbf{X}))\mid\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}]=L(\alpha)\to-\infty$ as $\alpha \to \infty$.

context.name: Remark 2 (uniqueness of the linear LHS solution)
context.statement:
Remark 2 (Uniqueness) The minimizer $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is uniquely determined because the LHS loss is convex and the $\ell_{2}$ regularizer is strictly convex. However, $\hat{\beta}_{0}$ may not. Here is an illustrative example. Let the data be

$$
\begin{array}{r l r l r l}{y_{1}= -1,}&{{}y_{2}= -1,}&{}&{{}y_{3}=1,}&{}&{{}y_{4}=1,}\\ {x_{1}=1,}&{{}x_{2}= -1,}&{}&{{}x_{3}=1,}&{}&{{}x_{4}= -1.}\end{array}
$$

Then both $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ are global minimizers. Non-uniqueness of the intercept term can also occur in the linear SVM.

context.name: Existence approach for the linear LHS classifier (Section 3.1)
context.statement:
When L is a non-negative continuous loss function, there exists a global minimizer to the regularized ERM problem. Proving existence is considered well-understood. The sublevel set of the objective function L of the regularized ERM problem, $\{\beta:{\mathcal{L}}(\beta)\leq c\}$ , is compact for any $c \in \mathbb{R}$ , and the global minimizer of the continuous objective function on a compact set must exist by the extreme value theorem.

In contrast, it is not trivial to show the existence of a global minimizer of the linear LHS classifier. The loss term in the regularized ERM can diverge to negative infinity even though the LHS loss is convex and training data have finite samples. To show the existence, we find a specific compact set D of $\beta,$ so that the objective function of the linear LHS classifier can have a global minimizer on D. Then, we show that the objective value at the global minimizer on D is always smaller than any objective value on $D^{c}$

The 'only if' statement comes from the fact that $\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}{\bar{f}}(\mathbf{X}))\mid\mathbf{X}]=\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}{\check{f}}(\mathbf{X}))\mid\mathbf{X}]$ almost surely and that for any $\delta_{\mathbf{X}}$ such that $\operatorname{sgn}(\delta_{\mathbf{X}})\neq\operatorname{sgn}(p(\mathbf{X})-1/2),\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}{\bar{f}}(\mathbf{X}))\mid\mathbf{X}]<\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}\delta_{\mathbf{X}})\mid\mathbf{X}]$ almost surely by the definition of classification-calibration.

For a non-negative loss function L, $\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}\bar{f}(\mathbf{X}))]$ is always finite. However, the LHS loss does not guarantee the finiteness of $\operatorname{E}[L(\mathbf{Y}\bar{f}(\mathbf{X}))]$ (see Theorem 4 for further information), thereby not ensuring the existence of a global minimizer that Fisher consistency implicitly assumes. Instead, we verify that the LHS loss is classification-calibrated. The LHS loss is the first negatively divergent loss function proven to satisfy the classification-calibration property.

We define a negatively divergent loss functions $L_{r}$ as follows: with $r\in(1,\infty)$,

$$

$$

Figure 3 illustrates (15) for various r values. Note the LHS loss is (15) with r diverging to ∞.

context.name: Setup: finite-sum problem (1) (Section 1)
context.statement:
Large numbers of applications in machine learning (Le Thi et al., 2022), computer vision (Xu et al., 2021) and numerical optimization (Fehrman et al., 2020) are often implemented to be a finite-sum structure of the form

$$
\operatorname*{min}_{w\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(w)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}(w),\tag{1}
$$

where n denotes the total number of the instances, w defines the parameter to learn and $f_{i}(\cdot):\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ represents a loss function corresponding to the i-th instance with d dimensions. In this work, we are mainly interested in each $f_{i}(w)$ and $f(w)$ that are L-smooth but may be non-convex. More concretely and vividly, the cases Problem (1) referred into logistic regression, eigenvector computation, multi-kernel learning, neural networks, to name a few.

context.name: Notation (Section 1.2)
context.statement: Throughout this work, we take $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ to define the set of d-dimensional real number vectors. For vectors, the mark w · v is used to denote their inner product. Additionally, we use [n] to define the set $\{1,2,\ldots,\mathtt{n}\}$ . The symbol $\| \cdot \|$ and $\| \cdot \|_{p}$ are chosen to represent the Euclidean norm and p-norm on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ respectively. Moreover, Denote by $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{w})$ the gradient of the loss function $f(w)$ . We adopt $\mathbb{E}[ \cdot ]$ to represent the expectation with respect to the underlying probability space. We use $(w)_{i}$ to represent the i-th element of vector $\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{R}^{d}$

context.name: SVRG update (3) and Powerball update (4); definition of σ_γ (Section 3)
context.statement:
Since this work will delve into the theoretical and numerical characteristics of SVRGE in PSO algorithms, we offer some discussions about the updating scheme of the original SVRG algorithm, originally developed in (Johnson and Zhang, 2013). Comparing with the conventional SGD algorithm that worked with the update scheme:

$$
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\eta_{k}\nabla f_{i}(w_{k}),\tag{2}
$$

for solving Problem (1), the update scheme of SVRG usually took the form:

$$
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\eta_{k}\big(\nabla f_{i}\big(w_{k}\big)-\nabla f_{i}\big(\tilde{w}\big)+\nabla f\big(\tilde{w}\big)\big),\tag{3}
$$

where $\tilde{w}$ was a snapshot point and $\eta_{k}> 0$ was the learning rate. In general, there were two loops in the SVRG-like approach, where the iterative rule (3) located in the inner loop. The outer loop was used to store the historical information, then transferred it into the inner loop.

The iterative scheme (3), utilizing historical information $(\mathrm{i}.\mathrm{e}.,\nabla f_{i}(\tilde{w})$ and $\nabla f(\tilde{w}))$ , made the stochastic optimization algorithms enjoy a lower variance than classical SGD, and resulted in a faster convergence rate and a better generalization in practice.

In contrast, when dealing with Problem (1), the classical iterative scheme of the PSO algorithm was:

$$
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\eta_{k}\sigma_{\gamma}(\nabla f_{i}(w_{k})),\tag{4}
$$

where the power coefficient $\gamma\in [0,1),\sigma_{\gamma}(\nabla f_{i}(w_{k}))=\mathrm{sign}(\nabla f_{i}(w_{k}))|\nabla f_{i}(w_{k})|^{\gamma}$ Here $\mathrm{sign}(x)$ backed to the sign of $x$, or 0 if $x = 0$. Also, it was noted that the operations sign(w) and $\sigma_{\gamma}(w)$ was applied to each element if the parameter $y \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ was a vector. For example, $\sigma_{\gamma}(y)=(\sigma_{\gamma}((y)_{1}),\sigma_{\gamma}((y)_{2}),\dots,\sigma_{\gamma}((y)_{d}))$

context.name: Algorithm 1: PB-SVRGE
context.statement:
Naturally, it was asked whether SVRGE created a positive effect on PSO algorithms? In order to respond to this question, we first proposed the PB-SVRGE algorithm (Algorithm 1) and analyzed its theoretical and empirical properties in the upcoming sections.

Algorithm 1 PB-SVRGE   
Input: $\widetilde{w}^{0}= w_{K}^{0}= w^{0}$ , epoch length $K,$ outer loop size ${\mathfrak{S}}= T / K$ , mini-batch size $b$, learning rate   
$\{\eta_{j}\}_{j = 0}^{K - 1}$ , power coefficient $\gamma .$   
for $s=0,\ldots,{\mathfrak{S}}-1$ do   
$w_{0}^{s + 1}= w_{K}^{s}$   
$g^{s+1}=\nabla f(\tilde{w}^{s})$   
for $k=0,\ldots,K-1$ do   
Randomly choose $S \subseteq [ n ]$ with $|S| =b,$ compute a new stochastic estimate $\nabla f(w_{k}^{s})$   
$\nu_{k}^{s+1}=\nabla f_{S}(w_{k}^{s+1})-\nabla f_{S}(\tilde{w}^{s})+g^{s+1}$   
$w_{k+1}^{s+1}=w_{k}^{s+1}-\eta_{k}\sigma(\nu_{k}^{s+1})$   
end for   
Set $\widetilde{w}^{s + 1}= w_{K}^{s + 1}$   
end for

context.name: Setup: finite-sum problem (1) (Section 1)
context.statement:
Large numbers of applications in machine learning (Le Thi et al., 2022), computer vision (Xu et al., 2021) and numerical optimization (Fehrman et al., 2020) are often implemented to be a finite-sum structure of the form

$$
\operatorname*{min}_{w\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(w)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}(w),\tag{1}
$$

where n denotes the total number of the instances, w defines the parameter to learn and $f_{i}(\cdot):\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ represents a loss function corresponding to the i-th instance with d dimensions. In this work, we are mainly interested in each $f_{i}(w)$ and $f(w)$ that are L-smooth but may be non-convex. More concretely and vividly, the cases Problem (1) referred into logistic regression, eigenvector computation, multi-kernel learning, neural networks, to name a few.

context.name: Notation (Section 1.2)
context.statement: Throughout this work, we take $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ to define the set of d-dimensional real number vectors. For vectors, the mark w · v is used to denote their inner product. Additionally, we use [n] to define the set $\{1,2,\ldots,\mathtt{n}\}$ . The symbol $\| \cdot \|$ and $\| \cdot \|_{p}$ are chosen to represent the Euclidean norm and p-norm on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ respectively. Moreover, Denote by $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{w})$ the gradient of the loss function $f(w)$ . We adopt $\mathbb{E}[ \cdot ]$ to represent the expectation with respect to the underlying probability space. We use $(w)_{i}$ to represent the i-th element of vector $\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{R}^{d}$

context.name: SVRG update (3) and Powerball update (4); definition of σ_γ (Section 3)
context.statement:
Since this work will delve into the theoretical and numerical characteristics of SVRGE in PSO algorithms, we offer some discussions about the updating scheme of the original SVRG algorithm, originally developed in (Johnson and Zhang, 2013). Comparing with the conventional SGD algorithm that worked with the update scheme:

$$
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\eta_{k}\nabla f_{i}(w_{k}),\tag{2}
$$

for solving Problem (1), the update scheme of SVRG usually took the form:

$$
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\eta_{k}\big(\nabla f_{i}\big(w_{k}\big)-\nabla f_{i}\big(\tilde{w}\big)+\nabla f\big(\tilde{w}\big)\big),\tag{3}
$$

where $\tilde{w}$ was a snapshot point and $\eta_{k}> 0$ was the learning rate. In general, there were two loops in the SVRG-like approach, where the iterative rule (3) located in the inner loop. The outer loop was used to store the historical information, then transferred it into the inner loop.

The iterative scheme (3), utilizing historical information $(\mathrm{i}.\mathrm{e}.,\nabla f_{i}(\tilde{w})$ and $\nabla f(\tilde{w}))$ , made the stochastic optimization algorithms enjoy a lower variance than classical SGD, and resulted in a faster convergence rate and a better generalization in practice.

In contrast, when dealing with Problem (1), the classical iterative scheme of the PSO algorithm was:

$$
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\eta_{k}\sigma_{\gamma}(\nabla f_{i}(w_{k})),\tag{4}
$$

where the power coefficient $\gamma\in [0,1),\sigma_{\gamma}(\nabla f_{i}(w_{k}))=\mathrm{sign}(\nabla f_{i}(w_{k}))|\nabla f_{i}(w_{k})|^{\gamma}$ Here $\mathrm{sign}(x)$ backed to the sign of $x$, or 0 if $x = 0$. Also, it was noted that the operations sign(w) and $\sigma_{\gamma}(w)$ was applied to each element if the parameter $y \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ was a vector. For example, $\sigma_{\gamma}(y)=(\sigma_{\gamma}((y)_{1}),\sigma_{\gamma}((y)_{2}),\dots,\sigma_{\gamma}((y)_{d}))$

context.name: Algorithm 1: PB-SVRGE
context.statement:
Naturally, it was asked whether SVRGE created a positive effect on PSO algorithms? In order to respond to this question, we first proposed the PB-SVRGE algorithm (Algorithm 1) and analyzed its theoretical and empirical properties in the upcoming sections.

Algorithm 1 PB-SVRGE   
Input: $\widetilde{w}^{0}= w_{K}^{0}= w^{0}$ , epoch length $K,$ outer loop size ${\mathfrak{S}}= T / K$ , mini-batch size $b$, learning rate   
$\{\eta_{j}\}_{j = 0}^{K - 1}$ , power coefficient $\gamma .$   
for $s=0,\ldots,{\mathfrak{S}}-1$ do   
$w_{0}^{s + 1}= w_{K}^{s}$   
$g^{s+1}=\nabla f(\tilde{w}^{s})$   
for $k=0,\ldots,K-1$ do   
Randomly choose $S \subseteq [ n ]$ with $|S| =b,$ compute a new stochastic estimate $\nabla f(w_{k}^{s})$   
$\nu_{k}^{s+1}=\nabla f_{S}(w_{k}^{s+1})-\nabla f_{S}(\tilde{w}^{s})+g^{s+1}$   
$w_{k+1}^{s+1}=w_{k}^{s+1}-\eta_{k}\sigma(\nu_{k}^{s+1})$   
end for   
Set $\widetilde{w}^{s + 1}= w_{K}^{s + 1}$   
end for

Assumption 1 (L-smoothness) and inequality (6)
context.statement:
This work considers the theoretical properties of PB-SVRGE on non-convex optimization problems.   
To proceed the analysis, we make the following standard smoothness assumptions.

Assumption 1. Each cost function $f_{i}(w)$ in Problem (1) is differential and has a L-Lipschitz gradient, that is,

$$
\forall w,\nu\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\quad\|\nabla f_{i}(w)-\nabla f_{i}(\nu)\|\le L\|w-\nu\|.\tag{5}
$$

The conclusion in Assumption 1 indicates that the average function $f(w)$ , presented in Problem (1), has a L-Lipschitz gradient as well.

Clearly, from the smooth property of the cost function, we have the following result:

$$
f(w)\leq f(\nu)+\nabla f(\nu)^{T}(w-\nu)+\frac{L}{2}\parallel w-\nu\parallel^{2}.\tag{6}
$$

context.name: Setup: finite-sum problem (1) (Section 1)
context.statement:
Large numbers of applications in machine learning (Le Thi et al., 2022), computer vision (Xu et al., 2021) and numerical optimization (Fehrman et al., 2020) are often implemented to be a finite-sum structure of the form

$$
\operatorname*{min}_{w\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(w)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}(w),\tag{1}
$$

where n denotes the total number of the instances, w defines the parameter to learn and $f_{i}(\cdot):\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}$ represents a loss function corresponding to the i-th instance with d dimensions. In this work, we are mainly interested in each $f_{i}(w)$ and $f(w)$ that are L-smooth but may be non-convex. More concretely and vividly, the cases Problem (1) referred into logistic regression, eigenvector computation, multi-kernel learning, neural networks, to name a few.

context.name: Notation (Section 1.2)
context.statement: Throughout this work, we take $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ to define the set of d-dimensional real number vectors. For vectors, the mark w · v is used to denote their inner product. Additionally, we use [n] to define the set $\{1,2,\ldots,\mathtt{n}\}$ . The symbol $\| \cdot \|$ and $\| \cdot \|_{p}$ are chosen to represent the Euclidean norm and p-norm on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ respectively. Moreover, Denote by $\nabla f(\boldsymbol{w})$ the gradient of the loss function $f(w)$ . We adopt $\mathbb{E}[ \cdot ]$ to represent the expectation with respect to the underlying probability space. We use $(w)_{i}$ to represent the i-th element of vector $\boldsymbol{w}\in \mathbb{R}^{d}$

context.name: SVRG update (3) and Powerball update (4); definition of σ_γ (Section 3)
context.statement:
Since this work will delve into the theoretical and numerical characteristics of SVRGE in PSO algorithms, we offer some discussions about the updating scheme of the original SVRG algorithm, originally developed in (Johnson and Zhang, 2013). Comparing with the conventional SGD algorithm that worked with the update scheme:

$$
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\eta_{k}\nabla f_{i}(w_{k}),\tag{2}
$$

for solving Problem (1), the update scheme of SVRG usually took the form:

$$
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\eta_{k}\big(\nabla f_{i}\big(w_{k}\big)-\nabla f_{i}\big(\tilde{w}\big)+\nabla f\big(\tilde{w}\big)\big),\tag{3}
$$

where $\tilde{w}$ was a snapshot point and $\eta_{k}> 0$ was the learning rate. In general, there were two loops in the SVRG-like approach, where the iterative rule (3) located in the inner loop. The outer loop was used to store the historical information, then transferred it into the inner loop.

The iterative scheme (3), utilizing historical information $(\mathrm{i}.\mathrm{e}.,\nabla f_{i}(\tilde{w})$ and $\nabla f(\tilde{w}))$ , made the stochastic optimization algorithms enjoy a lower variance than classical SGD, and resulted in a faster convergence rate and a better generalization in practice.

In contrast, when dealing with Problem (1), the classical iterative scheme of the PSO algorithm was:

$$
w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\eta_{k}\sigma_{\gamma}(\nabla f_{i}(w_{k})),\tag{4}
$$

where the power coefficient $\gamma\in [0,1),\sigma_{\gamma}(\nabla f_{i}(w_{k}))=\mathrm{sign}(\nabla f_{i}(w_{k}))|\nabla f_{i}(w_{k})|^{\gamma}$ Here $\mathrm{sign}(x)$ backed to the sign of $x$, or 0 if $x = 0$. Also, it was noted that the operations sign(w) and $\sigma_{\gamma}(w)$ was applied to each element if the parameter $y \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ was a vector. For example, $\sigma_{\gamma}(y)=(\sigma_{\gamma}((y)_{1}),\sigma_{\gamma}((y)_{2}),\dots,\sigma_{\gamma}((y)_{d}))$

context.name: Algorithm 1: PB-SVRGE
context.statement:
Naturally, it was asked whether SVRGE created a positive effect on PSO algorithms? In order to respond to this question, we first proposed the PB-SVRGE algorithm (Algorithm 1) and analyzed its theoretical and empirical properties in the upcoming sections.

Algorithm 1 PB-SVRGE   
Input: $\widetilde{w}^{0}= w_{K}^{0}= w^{0}$ , epoch length $K,$ outer loop size ${\mathfrak{S}}= T / K$ , mini-batch size $b$, learning rate   
$\{\eta_{j}\}_{j = 0}^{K - 1}$ , power coefficient $\gamma .$   
for $s=0,\ldots,{\mathfrak{S}}-1$ do   
$w_{0}^{s + 1}= w_{K}^{s}$   
$g^{s+1}=\nabla f(\tilde{w}^{s})$   
for $k=0,\ldots,K-1$ do   
Randomly choose $S \subseteq [ n ]$ with $|S| =b,$ compute a new stochastic estimate $\nabla f(w_{k}^{s})$   
$\nu_{k}^{s+1}=\nabla f_{S}(w_{k}^{s+1})-\nabla f_{S}(\tilde{w}^{s})+g^{s+1}$   
$w_{k+1}^{s+1}=w_{k}^{s+1}-\eta_{k}\sigma(\nu_{k}^{s+1})$   
end for   
Set $\widetilde{w}^{s + 1}= w_{K}^{s + 1}$   
end for

Assumption 1 (L-smoothness) and inequality (6)
context.statement:
This work considers the theoretical properties of PB-SVRGE on non-convex optimization problems.   
To proceed the analysis, we make the following standard smoothness assumptions.

Assumption 1. Each cost function $f_{i}(w)$ in Problem (1) is differential and has a L-Lipschitz gradient, that is,

$$
\forall w,\nu\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\quad\|\nabla f_{i}(w)-\nabla f_{i}(\nu)\|\le L\|w-\nu\|.\tag{5}
$$

The conclusion in Assumption 1 indicates that the average function $f(w)$ , presented in Problem (1), has a L-Lipschitz gradient as well.

Clearly, from the smooth property of the cost function, we have the following result:

$$
f(w)\leq f(\nu)+\nabla f(\nu)^{T}(w-\nu)+\frac{L}{2}\parallel w-\nu\parallel^{2}.\tag{6}
$$

context.name: RSBB learning rate (25) (Section 4)
context.statement:
We here briefly discussed the RSBB method. In RSBB, it also employed the similar updating rule to SGD in (2), i.e., $w_{k+1}=w_{k}-\eta_{k}\nabla f_{i}\big(w_{k}\big)$ , but the learning rate

$$
\eta_{k}= \frac{\zeta}{b_{H}}\cdot \frac{\| s_{k}\|^{2}}{s_{k}\cdot y_{k}+ \tau \| s_{k}\|^{2}},\tag{25}
$$

where $s_{k}= w_{k}- w_{k - 1}$ and $y_{k}=\nabla f_{S_{H}}(w_{k})-\nabla f_{S_{H}}(w_{k-1})$ for $k \geq 1$ . Note that, here, $S_{H}\subseteq [ n ]$ with $b_{H}$ samples $(\mathrm{i}.\mathrm{e}.,|S_{H}| =b_{H})$ and $\begin{array}{r}{\nabla f_{S_{H}}(w_{k})=\frac{1}{b_{H}}\sum_{i\in S_{H}}\nabla f_{i}(w_{k})}\end{array}$ . In addition, $\zeta$ and $\tau$ were two positive parameters. Specifically, $\zeta$ was employed to control the convergence speed. The term $\tau \| s_{k}\|^{2}$ was used to avoid the denominator of the original BB step size being zero. For the BB-type technique, it enjoyed a high-order information, resorting employing a simple but a low computational cost way to approximate the Hessian matrix unlike Newton or quasi-Newton type methods.

Theorem 8 Let $\mathcal{L}:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{A}\longrightarrow[0,1]$ be a loss function, and let $\phi:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{A}\longrightarrow[0,1]$ be a cost function that dominates it. Take $F$ to be a class of functions from $\mathcal{X}$ into $\mathcal{A}$, and suppose the pairs $(X_{i},Y_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ are drawn independently from the probability measure $P$. Then for every integer $n$ and every $0 < \delta < 1$, the following holds with probability no less than $1 - \delta$ over samples of size $n$: for all $f$ in $F$,

$$
\mathbf{E}\mathcal{L}(Y,f(X))\leq\hat{\mathbf{E}}_{n}\phi(Y,f(X))+R_{n}(\tilde{\phi}\circ F)+\sqrt{\frac{8\ln(2/\delta)}{n}},
$$

with $\tilde{\phi}\circ F=\{(x,y)\mapsto\phi(y,f(x))-\phi(y,0):f\in F\}$

context.name: Setup: decision-theoretic learning setting (Section 1)
context.statement: The following section presents a bound of this type that holds in a broader, decision-theoretic framework. In that framework there are an input space $\mathcal{X}$, an action space $\mathcal{A}$ and an output space $\mathcal{Y}$. The $n$ training examples $(X_{1},Y_{1}),\dots,(X_{n},Y_{n})$ are drawn independently from a probability measure $P$ on $\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}$. A loss function $\mathcal{L}:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{A}\longrightarrow[0,1]$ is given, where $\mathcal{L}(y,a)$ measures the cost incurred by choosing action $a \in{\mathcal{A}}$ when the outcome turns out to be $y \in \mathcal{Y}$. Learning seeks a function $f$ from $\mathcal{X}$ to ${\mathcal{A}}$ whose expected loss $\mathbf{E}{\mathcal{L}}(Y,f(X))$ is as small as possible.

context.name: Definition 2 (maximum discrepancy, Rademacher and Gaussian complexities)
context.statement:
Definition 2 Suppose $\mu$ is a probability distribution on a set $\mathcal{X}$, and $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ are independent samples drawn from $\mu$. Let $F$ be a class of functions from $\mathcal{X}$ to $\mathbb{R}$. The maximum discrepancy of $F$ is the random variable

$$
\hat{D}_{n}(F)=\operatorname*{sup}_{f\in F}\left(\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n/2}f(X_{i})-\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=n/2+1}^{n}f(X_{i})\right).
$$

Its expectation, the expected maximum discrepancy of $F$, is written $D_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}\hat{D}_{n}(F)$

Next, let

$$
{\hat{R}}_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}[\operatorname*{sup}_{f\in F}|{\frac{2}{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}f(X_{i})| |X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]\ ,
$$

with $\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{n}$ independent random variables, each uniform on $\{\pm 1 \}$. The Rademacher complexity of $F$ is then $R_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}\hat{R}_{n}(F)$. In the same way, let

$$
\hat{G}_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}[\operatorname*{sup}_{f\in F}|{\frac{2}{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}g_{i}f(X_{i})| |X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]\ ,
$$

with $g_{1},\ldots,g_{n}$ independent Gaussian $N(0,1)$ random variables. The Gaussian complexity of $F$ is $G_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}\hat{G}_{n}(F)$

context.name: Notation: empirical average hat E_n h
context.statement:
Given a training sample $(X_{1},Y_{1}),\dots,(X_{n},Y_{n})$ and a function $h : \mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}$, we use the notation

$$
\hat{\mathbf{E}}_{n}h(X,Y)=(1/n)\sum_{i=1}^{n}h(X_{i},Y_{i}).
$$

context.name: Notation: dominating cost function, phi o F, function-class operations (Section 2)
context.statement: First, some notation. For an independent sample $(X_{i},Y_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ with the distribution of $(X,Y)$, $P_{n}$ is the empirical measure supported on the sample, and $\mu_{n}$ is the empirical measure supported on $(X_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$. A function $\phi : \mathcal{Y}\times \mathcal{A}\to \mathbb{R}$ is said to dominate a loss function $\mathcal{L}$ when $\phi(y,a)\geq{\mathcal{L}}(y,a)$ holds for every $y \in \mathcal{Y}$ and every $a \in{\mathcal{A}}$. Given a class of functions $F$: conv $F$ denotes the set of convex combinations of members of $F$; $- F = \{- f : f \in F \}$; absconv $F$ denotes the set of convex combinations of members of $F \cup{- F}$; and $c F = \{c f : f \in F \}$. When $\phi$ is defined on the range of the functions in $F$, we put $\phi \circ F = \{\phi \circ f | f \in F \}$. The characteristic function of a set $A$ is written ${\bf 1}_{A}$ or $\mathbf{1}(A)$. Lastly, $C$ and $c$ denote constants whose values may differ from one line to the next, or even inside a single line.

context.name: Theorem 9 (McDiarmid's Inequality)
context.statement:
The argument relies on McDiarmid's inequality (McDiarmid, 1989).

Theorem 9 (McDiarmid's Inequality) Suppose $X_{1},...,X_{n}$ are independent random variables with values in a set $A$, and $f : A^{n}\to \mathbb{R}$ is such that

$$
\operatorname*{sup}_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},x_{i}^{\prime}\in A}\left|f(x_{1},...,x_{n})-f(x_{1},...,x_{i-1},x_{i}^{\prime},x_{i+1},... x_{n})\right|\leq c_{i}
$$

holds for each $1 \leq i \leq n$. Then every $t > 0$ satisfies

$$
P\left\{f(X_{1},...,X_{n})-{\bf E}f(X_{1},...,X_{n})\geq t\right\}\leq e^{-2t^{2}/\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}^{2}}.
$$

### Theorem 8
NOTE (Theorem 8) — The Lean assumes the index set of the function class is countable (`[Countable ι]`); the paper states no such condition. Without it the theorem is not provable in ZFC: under CH, a class indexed by a well-order of [0,1] of type ω₁ satisfies every other hypothesis while the empirical and expected quantities separate maximally at the supremum of the sample points. This is the usual countability / permissibility convention for suprema over a function class.

def paperEmpRad {ι : Type v} {𝒮 : Type w} (n : ℕ) (f : ι → 𝒮 → ℝ) (S : Fin n → 𝒮) : ℝ :=

    (n : ℕ) (f : ι → 𝒮 → ℝ) (μ : Measure Ω) (X : Ω → 𝒮) : ℝ :=

context.name: Setup: decision-theoretic learning setting (Section 1)
context.statement: The following section presents a bound of this type that holds in a broader, decision-theoretic framework. In that framework there are an input space $\mathcal{X}$, an action space $\mathcal{A}$ and an output space $\mathcal{Y}$. The $n$ training examples $(X_{1},Y_{1}),\dots,(X_{n},Y_{n})$ are drawn independently from a probability measure $P$ on $\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}$. A loss function $\mathcal{L}:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{A}\longrightarrow[0,1]$ is given, where $\mathcal{L}(y,a)$ measures the cost incurred by choosing action $a \in{\mathcal{A}}$ when the outcome turns out to be $y \in \mathcal{Y}$. Learning seeks a function $f$ from $\mathcal{X}$ to ${\mathcal{A}}$ whose expected loss $\mathbf{E}{\mathcal{L}}(Y,f(X))$ is as small as possible.

context.name: Notation: empirical frequency hat P_n (Theorem 1)
context.statement:
here VCdim(F) stands for the Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension of $F$,

$$
{\hat{P}}_{n}(S)={\frac{1}{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}_{S}(X_{i},Y_{i}),
$$

and ${\bf 1}_{S}$ denotes the indicator function of $S$.

context.name: Definition 2 (maximum discrepancy, Rademacher and Gaussian complexities)
context.statement:
Definition 2 Suppose $\mu$ is a probability distribution on a set $\mathcal{X}$, and $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ are independent samples drawn from $\mu$. Let $F$ be a class of functions from $\mathcal{X}$ to $\mathbb{R}$. The maximum discrepancy of $F$ is the random variable

$$
\hat{D}_{n}(F)=\operatorname*{sup}_{f\in F}\left(\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n/2}f(X_{i})-\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=n/2+1}^{n}f(X_{i})\right).
$$

Its expectation, the expected maximum discrepancy of $F$, is written $D_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}\hat{D}_{n}(F)$

Next, let

$$
{\hat{R}}_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}[\operatorname*{sup}_{f\in F}|{\frac{2}{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}f(X_{i})| |X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]\ ,
$$

with $\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{n}$ independent random variables, each uniform on $\{\pm 1 \}$. The Rademacher complexity of $F$ is then $R_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}\hat{R}_{n}(F)$. In the same way, let

$$
\hat{G}_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}[\operatorname*{sup}_{f\in F}|{\frac{2}{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}g_{i}f(X_{i})| |X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]\ ,
$$

with $g_{1},\ldots,g_{n}$ independent Gaussian $N(0,1)$ random variables. The Gaussian complexity of $F$ is $G_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}\hat{G}_{n}(F)$

context.statement: Part (b) is proved by a small sharpening of the proof of a more general statement, Theorem 8 below; the argument is given in Appendix B.

Given a training sample $(X_{1},Y_{1}),\dots,(X_{n},Y_{n})$ and a function $h : \mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}$, we use the notation

$$
\hat{\mathbf{E}}_{n}h(X,Y)=(1/n)\sum_{i=1}^{n}h(X_{i},Y_{i}).

context.name: Notation: dominating cost function, phi o F, function-class operations (Section 2)
context.statement: First, some notation. For an independent sample $(X_{i},Y_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ with the distribution of $(X,Y)$, $P_{n}$ is the empirical measure supported on the sample, and $\mu_{n}$ is the empirical measure supported on $(X_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$. A function $\phi : \mathcal{Y}\times \mathcal{A}\to \mathbb{R}$ is said to dominate a loss function $\mathcal{L}$ when $\phi(y,a)\geq{\mathcal{L}}(y,a)$ holds for every $y \in \mathcal{Y}$ and every $a \in{\mathcal{A}}$. Given a class of functions $F$: conv $F$ denotes the set of convex combinations of members of $F$; $- F = \{- f : f \in F \}$; absconv $F$ denotes the set of convex combinations of members of $F \cup{- F}$; and $c F = \{c f : f \in F \}$. When $\phi$ is defined on the range of the functions in $F$, we put $\phi \circ F = \{\phi \circ f | f \in F \}$. The characteristic function of a set $A$ is written ${\bf 1}_{A}$ or $\mathbf{1}(A)$. Lastly, $C$ and $c$ denote constants whose values may differ from one line to the next, or even inside a single line.

context.name: Theorem 9 (McDiarmid's Inequality)
context.statement:
The argument relies on McDiarmid's inequality (McDiarmid, 1989).

Theorem 9 (McDiarmid's Inequality) Suppose $X_{1},...,X_{n}$ are independent random variables with values in a set $A$, and $f : A^{n}\to \mathbb{R}$ is such that

$$
\operatorname*{sup}_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},x_{i}^{\prime}\in A}\left|f(x_{1},...,x_{n})-f(x_{1},...,x_{i-1},x_{i}^{\prime},x_{i+1},... x_{n})\right|\leq c_{i}
$$

holds for each $1 \leq i \leq n$. Then every $t > 0$ satisfies

$$
P\left\{f(X_{1},...,X_{n})-{\bf E}f(X_{1},...,X_{n})\geq t\right\}\leq e^{-2t^{2}/\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}^{2}}.
$$

$$

context.statement:
Theorem 8 Let $\mathcal{L}:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{A}\longrightarrow[0,1]$ be a loss function, and let $\phi:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{A}\longrightarrow[0,1]$ be a cost function that dominates it. Take $F$ to be a class of functions from $\mathcal{X}$ into $\mathcal{A}$, and suppose the pairs $(X_{i},Y_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ are drawn independently from the probability measure $P$. ### Theorem 5(b)
NOTE (Theorem 5(b)) — The Lean assumes the index set of the function class is countable (`[Countable ι]`); the paper states no such condition. Without it the theorem is not provable in ZFC: under CH, take a well-order of [0,1] of type ω₁ and F_t(x) = 1 if x precedes or equals t, else −1; every other hypothesis holds, yet at t = the supremum of the sample points the empirical risk is 0 and the expected risk is 1. This is the usual countability / permissibility convention for suprema over a function class.

context.name: Definition 2 (maximum discrepancy, Rademacher and Gaussian complexities)
context.statement:
Definition 2 Suppose $\mu$ is a probability distribution on a set $\mathcal{X}$, and $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ are independent samples drawn from $\mu$. Let $F$ be a class of functions from $\mathcal{X}$ to $\mathbb{R}$. The maximum discrepancy of $F$ is the random variable

$$
\hat{D}_{n}(F)=\operatorname*{sup}_{f\in F}\left(\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n/2}f(X_{i})-\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=n/2+1}^{n}f(X_{i})\right).
$$

Its expectation, the expected maximum discrepancy of $F$, is written $D_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}\hat{D}_{n}(F)$

Next, let

$$
{\hat{R}}_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}[\operatorname*{sup}_{f\in F}|{\frac{2}{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}f(X_{i})| |X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]\ ,
$$

with $\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{n}$ independent random variables, each uniform on $\{\pm 1 \}$. The Rademacher complexity of $F$ is then $R_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}\hat{R}_{n}(F)$. In the same way, let

$$
\hat{G}_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}[\operatorname*{sup}_{f\in F}|{\frac{2}{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}g_{i}f(X_{i})| |X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]\ ,
$$

with $g_{1},\ldots,g_{n}$ independent Gaussian $N(0,1)$ random variables. The Gaussian complexity of $F$ is $G_{n}(F)=\mathbf{E}\hat{G}_{n}(F)$

context.name: Notation: dominating cost function, phi o F, function-class operations (Section 2)
context.statement: First, some notation. For an independent sample $(X_{i},Y_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ with the distribution of $(X,Y)$, $P_{n}$ is the empirical measure supported on the sample, and $\mu_{n}$ is the empirical measure supported on $(X_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$. A function $\phi : \mathcal{Y}\times \mathcal{A}\to \mathbb{R}$ is said to dominate a loss function $\mathcal{L}$ when $\phi(y,a)\geq{\mathcal{L}}(y,a)$ holds for every $y \in \mathcal{Y}$ and every $a \in{\mathcal{A}}$. Given a class of functions $F$: conv $F$ denotes the set of convex combinations of members of $F$; $- F = \{- f : f \in F \}$; absconv $F$ denotes the set of convex combinations of members of $F \cup{- F}$; and $c F = \{c f : f \in F \}$. When $\phi$ is defined on the range of the functions in $F$, we put $\phi \circ F = \{\phi \circ f | f \in F \}$. The characteristic function of a set $A$ is written ${\bf 1}_{A}$ or $\mathbf{1}(A)$. Lastly, $C$ and $c$ denote constants whose values may differ from one line to the next, or even inside a single line.

context.name: Theorem 9 (McDiarmid's Inequality)
context.statement:
The argument relies on McDiarmid's inequality (McDiarmid, 1989).

Theorem 9 (McDiarmid's Inequality) Suppose $X_{1},...,X_{n}$ are independent random variables with values in a set $A$, and $f : A^{n}\to \mathbb{R}$ is such that

$$
\operatorname*{sup}_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},x_{i}^{\prime}\in A}\left|f(x_{1},...,x_{n})-f(x_{1},...,x_{i-1},x_{i}^{\prime},x_{i+1},... x_{n})\right|\leq c_{i}
$$

holds for each $1 \leq i \leq n$. Then every $t > 0$ satisfies

$$
P\left\{f(X_{1},...,X_{n})-{\bf E}f(X_{1},...,X_{n})\geq t\right\}\leq e^{-2t^{2}/\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}^{2}}.
$$

Theorem 1. Suppose that the regularizer ψ $: \mathcal{X}\mapsto \mathbb{R}$ is 1-strongly convex with respect to the norm $\| \cdot \|$ , and let $\| \cdot \|_{*}$ be the dual norm of $\| \cdot \|$ . The dynamic regret of OpTIMISTIC OMD whose update rule is specified in (6) is bounded as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{r}{\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t})\leq\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}\|\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-M_{t}\|_{*}^{2}+\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1}{\eta_{t}}\Big(\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{u}_{t},\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t})-\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{u}_{t},\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1})\Big)}\\ {-\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1}{\eta_{t}}\Big(\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1},\mathbf{x}_{t})+\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\Big),}\end{array}\tag{7}
$$

which holds for any comparator sequence $\mathbf{u}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X}$

context.name: Setup: online convex optimization protocol (Introduction)
context.statement: At iteration t, the player chooses a decision vector $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ from a convex set $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d}$ . Subsequently, the adversary discloses a convex function $f_{t}: \mathcal{X}\mapsto \mathbb{R}$ ,and the player incurs a loss denoted by $f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})$

context.name: Setup: problem setup and feedback models (Section 3.1)
context.statement:
Online Convex Optimization (OCO) can be modeled as an iterated game between the player and the environments. At iteration $t \in [ T ]$ , the player first chooses the decision $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ from a convex feasible set $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d}$ , then the environments reveal the loss function $f_{t}: \mathcal{X}\mapsto \mathbb{R}$ and the player suffers the loss $f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})$ and observes a certain information about the function $f_{t}(\cdot).$ 2 According to the revealed information, the online learning problems are typically classified into full-information online learning and partial-information online learning (or sometimes called bandit online learning). In this paper, we focus on the full-information one, which can be further categorized into the following two setups:

(i) multi-gradient feedback: the player can access the entire gradient function $\nabla f_{t}(\cdot)$ and thus can evaluate the gradient multiple times at each round;

(ii) one-gradient feedback: the player can observe the gradient information $\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})$ after submitting the decision $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ at each round.

In Section 4.2, we develop the Sword algorithm, which achieves the gradient-variation dynamic regret under the multi-gradient feedback model. In Section 4.3, we present an improved algorithm called Sword++ that can achieve the same dynamic regret guarantee (up to constants) under the more challenging one-gradient feedback model.

To handle non-stationary environments, we focus on the dynamic regret measure, which compares the online algorithm to a sequence of time-varying comparators $\mathbf{u}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X}$ as defined in (2). An upper bound of dynamic regret should be a function of comparators, and typically the bound depends on some regularities that measure the fluctuation of the comparator sequence, such as the path length $\begin{array}{r}{P_{T}= \sum_{t = 2}^{T}\lVert \mathbf{u}_{t}- \mathbf{u}_{t - 1}\rVert_{2}}\end{array}$ Throughout the paper, we focus on the Euclidean norm for simplicity, and it is straightforward to extend our results to general primal-dual norms.

In addition to the regret measure, we further consider the gradient query complexity. Note that algorithms designed for the multi-gradient feedback model may query the gradients for multiple times at each round. However, most algorithms designed for the static regret minimization only require one gradient per iteration, namely, using $\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})$ for the next update only. Therefore, it is more desirable to achieve the favorable regret guarantees under the one-gradient feedback model. In other words, our aim is to develop first-order methods for dynamic regret minimization that require only one gradient query per iteration.

context.name: Dynamic regret, eq. (2)
context.statement:
To address this limitation, dynamic regret is proposed to compete with changing comparators $\mathbf{u}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X}$

$$
\mathrm{D-Regret}_{T}(\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t}),\tag{2}
$$

context.name: Optimistic OMD: update rule (6), Bregman divergence, strong convexity (Section 3.2)
context.statement:
We employ the algorithmic framework of Optimistic Online Mirror Descent (OpTIMISTIC OMD) (Chiang et al., 2012; Rakhlin and Sridharan, 2013) as a general building block for designing algorithms for non-stationary online learning. Optimistic OMD is an algorithmic realization of optimistic online learning. Compared to the standard online learning setup, the player receives an additional element at each round: an optimistic vector $M_{t}\in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ This vector acts as a predictive hint or an optimistic estimate of the upcoming gradient, thereby called "optimistic vector" or simply "optimism". Optimistic OMD starts from the initial point $\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\in \mathcal{X}$ and performs the following two-step updates at each round:

$$
\begin{array}{r l}&{\mathbf{x}_{t}=\underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}{\arg\operatorname*{min}}~\big\{\eta_{t}\langle M_{t},\mathbf{x}\rangle+\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{x},\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\big\},}\\ &{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1}=\underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}{\arg\operatorname*{min}}~\big\{\eta_{t}\langle\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}),\mathbf{x}\rangle+\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{x},\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\big\},}\end{array}\tag{6}
$$

which firstly updates by the optimistic vector $M_{t}$ and then updates by the received gradient $\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})$ . In above, $\eta_{t}> 0$ is a (potentially) time-varying step size, and $\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes the Bregman divergence associated with the regularizer $\psi$ defined as $\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\psi(\mathbf{x})-\psi(\mathbf{y})-$ $\langle\nabla\psi(\mathbf{y}),\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\rangle$ . We may assume the regularizer to be σ-strongly convex with respect to the norm $\begin{array}{r}{\|\cdot\|,\operatorname{i.e.,}\psi(\mathbf{y})\geq\psi(\mathbf{x})+\langle\nabla\psi(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\rangle+\frac{\sigma}{2}\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\|^{2}}\end{array}$ holds for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\in{\mathcal{X}}$ . We have the following general result regarding dynamic regret of optimistic OMD.

context.name: Lemma 5 (stability lemma, Chiang et al. 2012, Proposition 7)
context.statement: Lemma 5 (stability lemma (Chiang et al., 2012, Proposition 7)). Consider the following two updates: $\begin{array}{r}{(i)\mathbf{x}_{*}=\arg\operatorname*{min}_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\langle\mathbf{a},\mathbf{x}\rangle+\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c})}\end{array}$ , and $(i i)\mathbf{x}_{*}^{\prime}=\arg\operatorname*{min}_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\langle\mathbf{a}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}\rangle+\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c})$ When the regularizer $\psi : \mathcal{X}\mapsto \mathbb{R}$ is a 1-strongly convex function with respect to the norm $\| \cdot \|$ , we have $\| \mathbf{x}_{*}- \mathbf{x}_{*}^{\prime}\| \leq \| \mathbf{a}- \mathbf{a}^{\prime}\|_{*}$

context.name: Remark: Theorem 1 does not need smoothness
context.statement: We have the following remarks regarding the assumptions. The general dynamic regret analysis of Optimistic OMD (Theorem 1) does not require the smoothness assumption. Nevertheless, this assumption is crucial for achieving problem-dependent dynamic regret bounds.

context.name: Lemma 4 (another result of the same paper)
context.statement:
Lemma 4 (Bregman proximal inequality (Chen and Teboulle, 1993, Lemma 3.2)). Let X be a convex set in a Banach space. Let $f : \mathcal{X}\mapsto \mathbb{R}$ be a closed proper convex function on X. Given a convex regularizer $\psi : \mathcal{X}\mapsto \mathbb{R}$ , we denote its induced Bregman divergence by $\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\cdot,\cdot)$ . Then, any update of the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_{k}=\underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}{\arg\operatorname*{min}}\{f(\mathbf{x})+\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_{k-1})\}
$$

satisfies the following inequality for any $\mathbf{u}\in \mathcal{X}$

$$
\begin{array}{r}{f ({\mathbf x}_{k}) - f ({\mathbf u}) \le \mathcal{D}_{\psi}({\mathbf u},{\mathbf x}_{k - 1}) - \mathcal{D}_{\psi}({\mathbf u},{\mathbf x}_{k}) - \mathcal{D}_{\psi}({\mathbf x}_{k},{\mathbf x}_{k - 1}) .}\end{array}\tag{60}
$$

Lemma 4 (Bregman proximal inequality (Chen and Teboulle, 1993, Lemma 3.2)). Let X be a convex set in a Banach space. Let $f : \mathcal{X}\mapsto \mathbb{R}$ be a closed proper convex function on X. Given a convex regularizer $\psi : \mathcal{X}\mapsto \mathbb{R}$ , we denote its induced Bregman divergence by $\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\cdot,\cdot)$ . Then, any update of the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_{k}=\underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}{\arg\operatorname*{min}}\{f(\mathbf{x})+\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}_{k-1})\}
$$

satisfies the following inequality for any $\mathbf{u}\in \mathcal{X}$

$$
\begin{array}{r}{f ({\mathbf x}_{k}) - f ({\mathbf u}) \le \mathcal{D}_{\psi}({\mathbf u},{\mathbf x}_{k - 1}) - \mathcal{D}_{\psi}({\mathbf u},{\mathbf x}_{k}) - \mathcal{D}_{\psi}({\mathbf x}_{k},{\mathbf x}_{k - 1}) .}\end{array}\tag{60}
$$

context.name: Optimistic OMD: update rule (6), Bregman divergence, strong convexity (Section 3.2)
context.statement:
We employ the algorithmic framework of Optimistic Online Mirror Descent (OpTIMISTIC OMD) (Chiang et al., 2012; Rakhlin and Sridharan, 2013) as a general building block for designing algorithms for non-stationary online learning. Optimistic OMD is an algorithmic realization of optimistic online learning. Compared to the standard online learning setup, the player receives an additional element at each round: an optimistic vector $M_{t}\in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ This vector acts as a predictive hint or an optimistic estimate of the upcoming gradient, thereby called "optimistic vector" or simply "optimism". Optimistic OMD starts from the initial point $\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\in \mathcal{X}$ and performs the following two-step updates at each round:

$$
\begin{array}{r l}&{\mathbf{x}_{t}=\underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}{\arg\operatorname*{min}}~\big\{\eta_{t}\langle M_{t},\mathbf{x}\rangle+\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{x},\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\big\},}\\ &{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1}=\underset{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}{\arg\operatorname*{min}}~\big\{\eta_{t}\langle\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}),\mathbf{x}\rangle+\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{x},\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\big\},}\end{array}\tag{6}
$$

which firstly updates by the optimistic vector $M_{t}$ and then updates by the received gradient $\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})$ . In above, $\eta_{t}> 0$ is a (potentially) time-varying step size, and $\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes the Bregman divergence associated with the regularizer $\psi$ defined as $\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\psi(\mathbf{x})-\psi(\mathbf{y})-$ $\langle\nabla\psi(\mathbf{y}),\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\rangle$ . We may assume the regularizer to be σ-strongly convex with respect to the norm $\begin{array}{r}{\|\cdot\|,\operatorname{i.e.,}\psi(\mathbf{y})\geq\psi(\mathbf{x})+\langle\nabla\psi(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\rangle+\frac{\sigma}{2}\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\|^{2}}\end{array}$ holds for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\in{\mathcal{X}}$ . We have the following general result regarding dynamic regret of optimistic OMD.

context.name: Setup: online convex optimization protocol (Introduction)
context.statement: At iteration t, the player chooses a decision vector $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ from a convex set $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d}$ . Subsequently, the adversary discloses a convex function $f_{t}: \mathcal{X}\mapsto \mathbb{R}$ ,and the player incurs a loss denoted by $f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})$

context.name: Setup: problem setup and feedback models (Section 3.1)
context.statement:
Online Convex Optimization (OCO) can be modeled as an iterated game between the player and the environments. At iteration $t \in [ T ]$ , the player first chooses the decision $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ from a convex feasible set $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d}$ , then the environments reveal the loss function $f_{t}: \mathcal{X}\mapsto \mathbb{R}$ and the player suffers the loss $f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})$ and observes a certain information about the function $f_{t}(\cdot).$ 2 According to the revealed information, the online learning problems are typically classified into full-information online learning and partial-information online learning (or sometimes called bandit online learning). In this paper, we focus on the full-information one, which can be further categorized into the following two setups:

(i) multi-gradient feedback: the player can access the entire gradient function $\nabla f_{t}(\cdot)$ and thus can evaluate the gradient multiple times at each round;

(ii) one-gradient feedback: the player can observe the gradient information $\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})$ after submitting the decision $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ at each round.

In Section 4.2, we develop the Sword algorithm, which achieves the gradient-variation dynamic regret under the multi-gradient feedback model. In Section 4.3, we present an improved algorithm called Sword++ that can achieve the same dynamic regret guarantee (up to constants) under the more challenging one-gradient feedback model.

To handle non-stationary environments, we focus on the dynamic regret measure, which compares the online algorithm to a sequence of time-varying comparators $\mathbf{u}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X}$ as defined in (2). An upper bound of dynamic regret should be a function of comparators, and typically the bound depends on some regularities that measure the fluctuation of the comparator sequence, such as the path length $\begin{array}{r}{P_{T}= \sum_{t = 2}^{T}\lVert \mathbf{u}_{t}- \mathbf{u}_{t - 1}\rVert_{2}}\end{array}$ Throughout the paper, we focus on the Euclidean norm for simplicity, and it is straightforward to extend our results to general primal-dual norms.

In addition to the regret measure, we further consider the gradient query complexity. Note that algorithms designed for the multi-gradient feedback model may query the gradients for multiple times at each round. However, most algorithms designed for the static regret minimization only require one gradient per iteration, namely, using $\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})$ for the next update only. Therefore, it is more desirable to achieve the favorable regret guarantees under the one-gradient feedback model. In other words, our aim is to develop first-order methods for dynamic regret minimization that require only one gradient query per iteration.

$$

context.statement: Assumption 1. The norm of the gradients of online functions over the domain $\mathcal{X}$ is bounded by G, i.e., $\|\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x})\|_{2}\leq G$ , for all $\mathbf{x}\in \mathcal{X}$ and $t \in [ T ]$ .

context.name: Assumption 2 (domain contains origin, diameter D)
context.statement: Assumption 2. The domain $\mathcal{X}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d}$ contains the origin $\mathbf{0}$, and the diameter of the domain $\mathcal{X}$ is at most D, i.e., $\| \mathbf{x}- \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\|_{2}\leq D$ for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in \mathcal{X}$

context.name: Assumption 3 (L-smoothness)
context.statement: Assumption 3. All the online functions are L-smooth, i.e., $\|\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x})-\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\|_{2}\leq L\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\|_{2}$ for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $t \in [ T ]$

context.name: Remark: Theorem 1 does not need smoothness
context.statement: We have the following remarks regarding the assumptions. The general dynamic regret analysis of Optimistic OMD (Theorem 1) does not require the smoothness assumption. Nevertheless, this assumption is crucial for achieving problem-dependent dynamic regret bounds.

context.name: OEGD update (8) and its reduction to Optimistic OMD (Section 4.1)
context.statement:
In the study of static regret, Chiang et al. (2012) propose the online extra-gradient descent (OEGD) algorithm and prove that the algorithm enjoys gradient-variation static regret. Specifically, OEGD starts from $\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\in \mathcal{X}$ and then updates by

$$
\begin{array}{r}{\mathbf{x}_{t}=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}\left[\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t}-\eta\nabla f_{t-1}(\mathbf{x}_{t-1})\right],\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}\left[\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t}-\eta\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\right],}\end{array}\tag{8}
$$

where we define $f_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{0})=\mathbf{0}$ and $\Pi_{\mathcal{X}}[ \cdot ]$ the Euclidean projection onto the nearest point in $\mathcal{X}.$ We consider a fixed step size $\eta > 0$ for simplicity. For convex and smooth functions, Chiang et al. (2012) prove that OEGD enjoys an $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{1+V_{T}})$ gradient-variation static regret.

Actually, OEGD can be viewed as a specialization of Optimistic OMD (6) presented in Section 3.2, by choosing the regularizer $\begin{array}{r}{\psi(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}}\end{array}$ and the optimistic vector $M_{t}=$ $\nabla f_{t-1}\big(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\big)$ as well as a fixed step size $\eta > 0$ Therefore, Theorem 1 directly implies the following dynamic regret upper bound for OEGD, with proof in Appendix A.

context.name: Path length P_T, eq. (4)
context.statement:
$$
P_{T}= \sum_{t = 2}^{T}\lVert \mathbf{u}_{t}- \mathbf{u}_{t - 1}\rVert_{2}\tag{4}
$$

is the path length of comparators $\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{T}$ and thus reflects the non-stationarity of environments.

context.name: Gradient variation V_T, eq. (5)
context.statement:
Specifically, we focus on the following two problem-dependent quantities: the gradient variation of online functions $V_{T}$ , and the cumulative loss of the comparator sequence $F_{T}$ , defined as

$$
V_{T}=\sum_{t=2}^{T}\operatorname*{sup}_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal X}\|\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf x)-\nabla f_{t-1}(\mathbf x)\|_{2}^{2},~\mathrm{and}~F_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\mathbf u_{t}).\tag{5}
$$

context.name: Theorem 1 (another result of the same paper)
context.statement:
Theorem 1. Suppose that the regularizer ψ $: \mathcal{X}\mapsto \mathbb{R}$ is 1-strongly convex with respect to the norm $\| \cdot \|$ , and let $\| \cdot \|_{*}$ be the dual norm of $\| \cdot \|$ . The dynamic regret of OpTIMISTIC OMD whose update rule is specified in (6) is bounded as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{r}{\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{t})\leq\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}\|\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-M_{t}\|_{*}^{2}+\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1}{\eta_{t}}\Big(\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{u}_{t},\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t})-\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{u}_{t},\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1})\Big)}\\ {-\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1}{\eta_{t}}\Big(\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1},\mathbf{x}_{t})+\mathcal{D}_{\psi}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\Big),}\end{array}\tag{7}
$$

which holds for any comparator sequence $\mathbf{u}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{u}_{T}\in\mathcal{X}$

context.name: Setup: data points, preferences, classifiers (Section 2)
context.statement: Basic Setup. We consider binary classification, where each data point is characterized by a tuple $(x,y,r)$ . Like classic classification setups, $\mathbf{\boldsymbol{x}}\in \mathcal{X}$ is the feature vector and $y \in$ $\{+1,-1\}$ is its label. The only difference of our setup from classic classification problems is the additional $r \in R \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ , which is the data point's (positive or negative) preference/reward of being labeled as +1. The data point's reward for label −1 is, without loss of generality, normalized to be 0. A classifier is a mapping $h:\mathcal{X}\to\{+1,-1\}$ . Our model is essentially the same as that of (Hardt et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2019), except that the r in our model can be any real value from set R whereas the aforementioned works assume $r = 1$ for all data points. Notably, we also allow r to be negative, which means some data points prefer to be classified as label $-1$. This generalization is natural and very useful because it allows much richer agent preferences. For instance, it casts the adversarial/robust classification problem as a special case of our model as well (see discussions later). Intuitively, the set R captures the richness of agents' preferences. As we will prove, how rich it is will affect both the statistical learnability and computational tractability of the learning problem.

context.name: Setup: strategic manipulation and cost functions (Section 2)
context.statement:
The Strategic Manipulation of Test Data. We consider strategic behaviors during the test phase and assume that the training data is unaltered/uncontaminated. An illustration of the setup can be found in Figure 1. A generic test data point is denoted as $(x,y,r)$ . The test data point is strategic and may shift its feature to vector z with cost $c(z;\pmb{x})$ where $c : \mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{X}\to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ . In general, function c can be an arbitrary non-negative cost function. In our study of strategic linear classification, we assume the cost functions are induced by seminorms. We will consider the following two types of cost functions, with increasing generality.

1. Instance-invariant cost functions: A cost function c is instance-invariant if there is a common function l such that $c(z;\pmb{x})=l(\pmb{z}-\pmb{x})$ for any point $(x,y,r)$ .

2. Instance-wise cost functions: With instance-wise cost functions, each data point is allowed to possess its own loss function. To capture this situation, we need to augment each data point's representation from $(x,y,r)$ to $({\pmb x},y,r,l)$ , where l is a function depending on x such that $c ({\boldsymbol{z}};{\pmb x}) = l ({\boldsymbol{z}}-{\pmb x})$ for some semi-norm l. For notational convenience, we often refer to function l associated with this data point as $l_{x}$ though we emphasize that this is a slight abuse of notation because $l_{x}$ is determined not just by the data point's feature x but rather by the data point itself.4

Both cases have been considered in previous works. For instance, the separable cost function studied in (Hardt et al., 2016) is instance-wise, and the cost function induced by a seminorm as assumed by the main theorem of (Cullina et al., 2018) is instance-invariant. We shall prove later that the choice among these two types of cost functions will largely affect the efficient learnability of the problem.

context.name: Eq. (1): data point best response and tie-breaking
context.statement:
Given a classifier h, the strategic test data point $(x,y,r)$ may shift its feature vector to z and would like to pick the best such z by solving the following optimization problem:

Data Point Best Response:

$$
\Delta_{c}(\pmb{x},r;h)=\arg\operatorname*{max}_{\pmb{\mathrm{z}}\in\mathcal{X}}\big [\mathbb{I}(h(\pmb{z})=1)\cdot r-c(\pmb{z};\pmb{x})\big].\tag{1}
$$

where $\mathbb{I}(S)$ is the indicator function and $[\mathbb{I}(h(z)=1)\cdot r-c(z;\pmb{x})]$ is the quasi-linear utility function of data point $(x,y,r)$ . We call $\Delta_{c}({\pmb x},r;h)$ the manipulated feature. When there are multiple best responses, we assume the data point may choose any best response and thus will adopt the standard worst-case analysis. Note that the test data's strategic behaviors do not change its true label. Such strategic gaming behaviors differ from strategic improvements (see (Miller et al., 2019) for more discussions on their differences). We also point out that the preference r is assumed to be known for any training data (though no need to be known for testing data). While this may appear a strong assumption at the first glance, we believe this parameter can be estimated in real applications (e.g., how much it matters to someone for being admitted to a university, for receiving a loan or for being tested COVID positive). An interesting future direction may be to understand how robust the strategic classifier is to the estimation error of r in the training data.

context.name: StraC problem and Eq. (2): strategic 0-1 loss (Section 2.1)
context.statement:
A STRAC problem is described by a hypothesis class H, the set of preferences R and a manipulation cost function c. We thus denote it as $\mathrm{STRAC}\langle\mathcal{H},R,c\rangle$ . Adopting the standard statistical learning framework, the input to our learning task is n uncontaminated training data points $({\pmb x}_{1},y_{1},r_{1}),\dots,({\pmb x}_{n},y_{n},r_{n})$ drawn independently and identically (i.i.d.) from distribution D. Given these training data, we look to learn a classifier $h \in \mathcal H$ which minimizes the basic 0-1 loss, defined as follows:

Strategic 0-1 Loss of classifier h :

$$
L_{c}(h;\mathcal{D})=\operatorname*{Pr}_{(\mathbf{x},y,r)\sim\mathcal{D}}\big [h(\Delta_{c}(\mathbf{x},r;h))\neq y\big].\tag{2}
$$

Notably, the classifier h in the above loss definition takes the manipulated feature $\textstyle\Delta_{c}({\pmb x},r;h)\big)$ as input and, nevertheless, looks to correctly predict the true label y. For notational convenience, we sometimes omit c when it is clear from the context and simply write $\Delta({\pmb x},r;h)$ and $L(h;\mathcal{D})$ .

context.name: Definition 1 (Strategic Shattering Coefficients)
context.statement:
In this section, we introduce the notion of strategic VC-dimension (SVC) and show that it properly captures the behaviors of a hypothesis class in the strategic setup introduced above. We then show the connection of SVC with previous studies on both strategic and adversarial learning. Before formally introducing SVC, we first define the shattering coefficients in strategic setups.

Definition 1 (Strategic Shattering Coefficients) The n-th shattering coefficient of any strategic classification problem $\mathrm{STRAC}\langle\mathcal{H},R,c\rangle$ is defined as

$$
\sigma_{n}(\mathcal{H},R,c)=\operatorname*{max}_{(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{r})\in\mathcal{X}^{n}\times R^{n}}~|\{(h(\Delta_{c}(\boldsymbol{x}_{1},\boldsymbol{r}_{1};h)),\cdots,h(\Delta_{c}(\boldsymbol{x}_{n},\boldsymbol{r}_{n};h)):h\in\mathcal{H}\}|,
$$

where $\Delta_{c}(\pmb{x}_{i},r_{i};h)$ defined in Eq. (1) is a best response of data point $({\pmb x}_{i}, y_{i}, r_{i})$ to classifier h under cost function c.

That is, $\sigma_{n}(\mathcal{H},R,c)$ captures the maximum number of classification behaviors/outcomes (among all choices of data points) that classifiers in H can possibly induce by using manipulated features as input. Like classic definition of shattering coefficient, the $\sigma_{n}(\mathcal{H},R,c)$ here does not involve the labels of the data points at all. In contrast, in the shattering coefficient definition for adversarial VC-dimension of (Cullina et al., 2018), the "max" is allowed to be over data labels as well. This is an important difference compared to our setting. Given the definition of the strategic shattering coefficients, the definition of strategic VC-dimension is standard.

context.name: Definition 2 (Strategic VC-dimension), Eq. (3)
context.statement:
Definition 2 The Strategic VC-dimension (SVC) for strategic classification problem $\mathrm{STRAC}\langle\mathcal{H},R,c\rangle$ is defined as

$$
S V C(\mathcal{H},R,c)=\operatorname*{sup}\{n\in\mathbb{N}:\sigma_{n}(\mathcal{H},R,c)=2^{n}\}.\tag{3}
$$

context.name: SERM, Eq. (4)
context.statement:
We show that the SVC defined above correctly characterizes the learnability of any strategic classification problem $\mathrm{STRAC}\langle\mathcal{H},R,c\rangle$ . We consider the standard Empirical risk minimization (ERM) paradigm for strategic classification, but take into account training data's manipulation behaviors. Specifically, given any cost function c, any n uncontaminated training data points $(\mathbf{x}_{1},y_{1},r_{1}),\cdot\cdot\cdot,(\mathbf{x}_{n},y_{n},r_{n})$ drawn independently and identically (i.i.d.) from the same distribution $\mathcal{D}.$ , the strategic empirical risk minimization (SERM) problem computes a classifier $h \in \mathcal H$ that minimizes the empirical strategic 0-1 loss in Eq. (2). Formally, the SERM for $\mathrm{STRAC}\langle\mathcal{H},R,c\rangle$ is defined as follows:

$$
\mathrm{SERM}:\quad\mathrm{argmin}_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\ L_{c}(h,\{(x_{i},y_{i},r_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{I}\big [h(\Delta_{c}(\mathbf{x}_{i},r_{i};h))\neq y_{i}\big]\tag{4}
$$

where $L_{c}(h,\{(x_{i},y_{i},r_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n})$ is the empirical loss (compared to the expected loss $L_{c}(h,\mathcal{D})$ defined in Eq. (2)). Unlike the standard (non-strategic) ERM problem and similar in spirit to the "incentive-aware ERM" in (Zhang and Conitzer, 2021), classifiers in the SERM problem take each data point's strategic response $\Delta_{c}~({\bf x}_{i},r_{i};h)$ as input, while not the original feature vector $\pmb{x}_{i}$

context.name: Definition 3 (PAC-Learnability)
context.statement:
Given the definition of strategic VC-dimension and the SERM framework, we state the sample complexity result for PAC-learning in our strategic setup:

Definition 3 (PAC-Learnability) In a strategic classification problem $\mathrm{STRAC}\langle\mathcal{H},R,c\rangle$ the hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}\subseteq(\mathcal{X}\to\{+1,-1\})$ is Probably Approximately Correctly (PAC) learnable by an algorithm A if there is a function $m_{\mathcal{H},R,c}:(0,1)^{2}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that $\forall(\delta,\epsilon)\in$ $(0,1)^{2}$ , for any $n\ge m_{\mathcal{H},R,c}(\delta,\epsilon)$ and any distribution D for $({\pmb x},y,r)$ , with at least probability $1 - \delta$ , we have $L_{c}(h^{\ast},\mathcal{D})\leq\epsilon$ where $h^{*}$ is the output of the algorithm A with n i.i.d. samples from D as input. The problem is agnostic PAC learnable if $\begin{array}{r}{L_{c}(h^{*},\mathcal{D})-\operatorname*{inf}_{h\in\mathcal{H}}L_{c}(h,\mathcal{D})\leq\epsilon}\end{array}$

### Theorem 4
NOTE (Theorem 4) — The Lean assumes the hypothesis class H is countable (`_hH_ctble`); the paper states no such condition (H ⊆ (X → {±1}) is otherwise arbitrary). Without it the theorem is not provable in ZFC: under CH, a class built from the initial segments of a well-order of [0,1] of type ω₁ satisfies every other hypothesis, yet with probability → 1 every SERM output has excess risk 0.75. This is the usual countability / admissibility convention for uniform convergence over a hypothesis class.

namespace ResearchLevel

def stratUtil {X : Type*} (c : X → X → ℝ) (h : X → Bool) (x : X) (r : ℝ) (z : X) : ℝ :=
  (if h z then r else 0) - c z x

def IsBestResponse {X : Type*} (c : X → X → ℝ) (h : X → Bool) (x : X) (r : ℝ) (z : X) :
    Prop :=
  ∀ z' : X, stratUtil c h x r z' ≤ stratUtil c h x r z

def StrategicShatters {X : Type*} (H : Set (X → Bool)) (R : Set ℝ) (c : X → X → ℝ)
    (Δ : (X → Bool) → X → ℝ → X) (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ x : Fin n → X, ∃ r : Fin n → ℝ, (∀ i, r i ∈ R) ∧

    (Δ : (X → Bool) → X → ℝ → X) (h : X → Bool)
    (D : MeasureTheory.Measure (X × Bool × ℝ)) : ℝ :=
  (D {p : X × Bool × ℝ | h (Δ h p.1 p.2.2) ≠ p.2.1}).toReal

def empStrategicLoss {X : Type*} (c : X → X → ℝ) (Δ : (X → Bool) → X → ℝ → X)

  (Finset.univ.filter (fun i => h (Δ h (s i).1 (s i).2.2) ≠ (s i).2.1)).card

def SeparableCost {X : Type*} (c : X → X → ℝ) : Prop :=

def dotp {d : ℕ} (w u : Fin d → ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ i, w i * u i

theorem strategic_agnostic_PAC :
    ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧
      ∀ (X : Type*) [MeasurableSpace X]
        (H : Set (X → Bool)) (_hH : H.Nonempty) (_hH_ctble : H.Countable)
        (R : Set ℝ) (c : X → X → ℝ) (_hc : ∀ x y : X, 0 ≤ c x y)
    (_hc0 : ∀ x : X, c x x = 0)
        (Δ : (X → Bool) → X → ℝ → X)
        (_hΔ : ∀ h ∈ H, ∀ x, ∀ r ∈ R, IsBestResponse c h x r (Δ h x r))
        (_hmeas : ∀ h ∈ H, Measurable (fun p : X × Bool × ℝ => h (Δ h p.1 p.2.2)))
        (d : ℕ) (_hd : SVC H R c Δ = (d : ℕ∞)),
      ∃ m : ℝ → ℝ → ℕ,
        (∀ δ ε : ℝ, 0 < δ → δ < 1 → 0 < ε → ε < 1 →

        ∃ A : (N : ℕ) → (Fin N → X × Bool × ℝ) → (X → Bool),

  sorry

    (Δ : (X → Bool) → X → ℝ → X)

context.name: Setup: data points, preferences, classifiers (Section 2)
context.statement: Basic Setup. We consider binary classification, where each data point is characterized by a tuple $(x,y,r)$ . Like classic classification setups, $\mathbf{\boldsymbol{x}}\in \mathcal{X}$ is the feature vector and $y \in$ $\{+1,-1\}$ is its label. The only difference of our setup from classic classification problems is the additional $r \in R \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ , which is the data point's (positive or negative) preference/reward of being labeled as +1. The data point's reward for label −1 is, without loss of generality, normalized to be 0. A classifier is a mapping $h:\mathcal{X}\to\{+1,-1\}$ . Our model is essentially the same as that of (Hardt et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2019), except that the r in our model can be any real value from set R whereas the aforementioned works assume $r = 1$ for all data points. Notably, we also allow r to be negative, which means some data points prefer to be classified as label $-1$. This generalization is natural and very useful because it allows much richer agent preferences. For instance, it casts the adversarial/robust classification problem as a special case of our model as well (see discussions later). Intuitively, the set R captures the richness of agents' preferences. As we will prove, how rich it is will affect both the statistical learnability and computational tractability of the learning problem.

context.name: Setup: strategic manipulation and cost functions (Section 2)
context.statement:
The Strategic Manipulation of Test Data. We consider strategic behaviors during the test phase and assume that the training data is unaltered/uncontaminated. An illustration of the setup can be found in Figure 1. A generic test data point is denoted as $(x,y,r)$ . The test data point is strategic and may shift its feature to vector z with cost $c(z;\pmb{x})$ where $c : \mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{X}\to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ . In general, function c can be an arbitrary non-negative cost function. In our study of strategic linear classification, we assume the cost functions are induced by seminorms. We will consider the following two types of cost functions, with increasing generality.

1. Instance-invariant cost functions: A cost function c is instance-invariant if there is a common function l such that $c(z;\pmb{x})=l(\pmb{z}-\pmb{x})$ for any point $(x,y,r)$ .

2. Instance-wise cost functions: With instance-wise cost functions, each data point is allowed to possess its own loss function. To capture this situation, we need to augment each data point's representation from $(x,y,r)$ to $({\pmb x},y,r,l)$ , where l is a function depending on x such that $c ({\boldsymbol{z}};{\pmb x}) = l ({\boldsymbol{z}}-{\pmb x})$ for some semi-norm l. For notational convenience, we often refer to function l associated with this data point as $l_{x}$ though we emphasize that this is a slight abuse of notation because $l_{x}$ is determined not just by the data point's feature x but rather by the data point itself.4

Both cases have been considered in previous works. For instance, the separable cost function studied in (Hardt et al., 2016) is instance-wise, and the cost function induced by a seminorm as assumed by the main theorem of (Cullina et al., 2018) is instance-invariant. We shall prove later that the choice among these two types of cost functions will largely affect the efficient learnability of the problem.

context.name: Eq. (1): data point best response and tie-breaking
context.statement:
Given a classifier h, the strategic test data point $(x,y,r)$ may shift its feature vector to z and would like to pick the best such z by solving the following optimization problem:

Data Point Best Response:

$$
\Delta_{c}(\pmb{x},r;h)=\arg\operatorname*{max}_{\pmb{\mathrm{z}}\in\mathcal{X}}\big [\mathbb{I}(h(\pmb{z})=1)\cdot r-c(\pmb{z};\pmb{x})\big].\tag{1}
$$

where $\mathbb{I}(S)$ is the indicator function and $[\mathbb{I}(h(z)=1)\cdot r-c(z;\pmb{x})]$ is the quasi-linear utility function of data point $(x,y,r)$ . We call $\Delta_{c}({\pmb x},r;h)$ the manipulated feature. When there are multiple best responses, we assume the data point may choose any best response and thus will adopt the standard worst-case analysis. Note that the test data's strategic behaviors do not change its true label. Such strategic gaming behaviors differ from strategic improvements (see (Miller et al., 2019) for more discussions on their differences). We also point out that the preference r is assumed to be known for any training data (though no need to be known for testing data). While this may appear a strong assumption at the first glance, we believe this parameter can be estimated in real applications (e.g., how much it matters to someone for being admitted to a university, for receiving a loan or for being tested COVID positive). An interesting future direction may be to understand how robust the strategic classifier is to the estimation error of r in the training data.

context.name: StraC problem and Eq. (2): strategic 0-1 loss (Section 2.1)
context.statement:
A STRAC problem is described by a hypothesis class H, the set of preferences R and a manipulation cost function c. We thus denote it as $\mathrm{STRAC}\langle\mathcal{H},R,c\rangle$ . Adopting the standard statistical learning framework, the input to our learning task is n uncontaminated training data points $({\pmb x}_{1},y_{1},r_{1}),\dots,({\pmb x}_{n},y_{n},r_{n})$ drawn independently and identically (i.i.d.) from distribution D. Given these training data, we look to learn a classifier $h \in \mathcal H$ which minimizes the basic 0-1 loss, defined as follows:

Strategic 0-1 Loss of classifier h :

$$
L_{c}(h;\mathcal{D})=\operatorname*{Pr}_{(\mathbf{x},y,r)\sim\mathcal{D}}\big [h(\Delta_{c}(\mathbf{x},r;h))\neq y\big].\tag{2}
$$

Notably, the classifier h in the above loss definition takes the manipulated feature $\textstyle\Delta_{c}({\pmb x},r;h)\big)$ as input and, nevertheless, looks to correctly predict the true label y. For notational convenience, we sometimes omit c when it is clear from the context and simply write $\Delta({\pmb x},r;h)$ and $L(h;\mathcal{D})$ .

context.name: Definition 1 (Strategic Shattering Coefficients)
context.statement:
In this section, we introduce the notion of strategic VC-dimension (SVC) and show that it properly captures the behaviors of a hypothesis class in the strategic setup introduced above. We then show the connection of SVC with previous studies on both strategic and adversarial learning. Before formally introducing SVC, we first define the shattering coefficients in strategic setups.

Definition 1 (Strategic Shattering Coefficients) The n-th shattering coefficient of any strategic classification problem $\mathrm{STRAC}\langle\mathcal{H},R,c\rangle$ is defined as

$$
\sigma_{n}(\mathcal{H},R,c)=\operatorname*{max}_{(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{r})\in\mathcal{X}^{n}\times R^{n}}~|\{(h(\Delta_{c}(\boldsymbol{x}_{1},\boldsymbol{r}_{1};h)),\cdots,h(\Delta_{c}(\boldsymbol{x}_{n},\boldsymbol{r}_{n};h)):h\in\mathcal{H}\}|,
$$

where $\Delta_{c}(\pmb{x}_{i},r_{i};h)$ defined in Eq. (1) is a best response of data point $({\pmb x}_{i}, y_{i}, r_{i})$ to classifier h under cost function c.

That is, $\sigma_{n}(\mathcal{H},R,c)$ captures the maximum number of classification behaviors/outcomes (among all choices of data points) that classifiers in H can possibly induce by using manipulated features as input. Like classic definition of shattering coefficient, the $\sigma_{n}(\mathcal{H},R,c)$ here does not involve the labels of the data points at all. In contrast, in the shattering coefficient definition for adversarial VC-dimension of (Cullina et al., 2018), the "max" is allowed to be over data labels as well. This is an important difference compared to our setting. Given the definition of the strategic shattering coefficients, the definition of strategic VC-dimension is standard.

context.name: Definition 2 (Strategic VC-dimension), Eq. (3)
context.statement:
Definition 2 The Strategic VC-dimension (SVC) for strategic classification problem $\mathrm{STRAC}\langle\mathcal{H},R,c\rangle$ is defined as

$$
S V C(\mathcal{H},R,c)=\operatorname*{sup}\{n\in\mathbb{N}:\sigma_{n}(\mathcal{H},R,c)=2^{n}\}.\tag{3}
$$

context.name: Separable cost functions (Section 3.2)
context.statement:
Not only restricting the set R of preference values can reduce the SVC. This subsection shows that restricting to special classes of cost functions can also lead to a small SVC. One special class of cost functions studied in many previous works is the separable cost functions (Hardt et al., 2016; Milli et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2019a). Formally, a cost function $c(z;\pmb{x})$ is separable if there exists function $c_{1}, c_{2}: \mathcal{X}\to \mathbb{R}$ such that $c(\pmb{z};\pmb{x})=\operatorname*{max}\left\{c_{2}(\pmb{z})-c_{1}(\pmb{x}),0\right\}$

The following Proposition 9 shows that when the cost function is separable, SVC is at most 2 for any hypothesis class H and any class of preference set $R .^{5}$ Therefore, separable cost function essentially reduces any classification problem to a problem in lower dimension. Together with Theorem 4, Proposition 9 also recovers the PAC-learnability result of (Hardt et al., 2016) in their strategic-robust learning model (specifically, Theorem 1.8 of (2016)) and, moreover, generalizes their learnability from homogeneous agent preferences to the case with arbitrary agent preference values.

context.name: Remark after Proposition 9: role of 0 not in R
context.statement: The assumption $0 \notin R$ implies that each agent must strictly prefer either label +1 or $- 1$ . This assumption is necessary since if $0\in R,$ SVC will be at least the classic VC dimension of H and thus Proposition 9 cannot hold. We remark that the above SVC upper bound 2 holds for any hypothesis class H. This bound 2 is tight for some classes of hypothesis, e.g., linear classifiers.

nl_notes:
### Proposition 9
REPAIRED STATEMENT (Proposition 9) — Proposition 9 as published is FALSE under the paper's own §2 convention that agents break ties in the worst case for the learner: there are instances in which three points are shattered, so SVC ≥ 3. The paper's Eq. (16) and Appendix A.4 instead break ties toward the agent's preferred label. This target is the repaired version: the bound must hold for every best-response selector Δ (`hΔ`) that breaks ties toward the agent's preferred label whenever such a best response exists (`htie`), with the strategic VC dimension defined through Δ.
