context.name: Stochastic dominance and risk-measure properties (M), (TI), (DI) (Section 2.3)
context.statement:
Consider two random variables $X \sim F$ and $Y \sim G$ . We assert that Y dominates $X,$ and correspondingly, G dominates $F,$ denoted as $Y \succeq X$ and $G \succeq F$ , if and only if for every real number x, the inequality $F(x)\geq G(x)$ holds true. A risk measure, $\rho,$ is a function mapping a set of random variables, denoted as $\mathcal{X}$ , to the real numbers. This mapping adheres to several crucial properties:

• Monotonicity (M): $X\preceq Y\Rightarrow\rho(X)\leq\rho(Y),\forall X,Y\in{\mathcal{X}}$

Translation-invariance $(\mathbf{TI})\colon\rho(X+c)=\rho(X)+c,\forall X\in{\mathcal{X}},\forall c\in\mathbb{R},$

Distribution-invariance (DI): $F_{X_{1}}=F_{X_{2}}\Rightarrow\rho(X_{1})=\rho(X_{2})$

A mapping $\rho : \mathcal{X}\to \mathbb{R}$ qualifies as a risk measure if it satisfies both (M) and (TI). Additionally, a risk measure that also adheres to (DI) is termed a distribution-invariant risk measure. Distribution-invariant risk measure allows us to simplify notation by denoting $\rho(F_{X})$ as $\rho(X)$

context.name: Supremum distance, l1 distance, norm balls B_infty(F,c) and B_1(P,c)
context.statement: We begin by establishing additional notations. For two Cumulative Distribution Functions (CDFs) F and G, the supremum distance between them is defined as $\| F - G \|_{\infty}\triangleq$ $\begin{array}{r}{\operatorname*{sup}_{x}|F(x)-G(x)|}\end{array}$ We define the $\ell_{1}$ distance between two Probability Mass Functions $(\mathrm{PMFs})$ with the same support P and $Q$ as $\begin{array}{r}{\| P - Q \|_{1}\triangleq \sum_{i}| P_{i}- Q_{i}|}\end{array}$ . Furthermore, the set $B_{\infty}(F,c): =\{G\in\mathcal{D}|\|G-F\|_{\infty}\leq c\}$ denotes the supremum norm ball of CDFs centered at F with radius c. Analogously, $B_{1}(P,c)$ represents the $\ell_{1}$ norm ball of PMFs centered at P with radius c.

context.name: Definition 7 and the distributional optimism operator O_c^infty (Section 4.2)
context.statement:
Definition 7 Given two CDFs F and G, we say that F is more optimistic than G if $F \geq G$

This definition aligns with the intuitive notion that a more optimistic distribution should possess a larger EntRM value. Given that the exponential transformation preserves order, F is more optimistic than G if and only if $E_{\beta}(F)\ge E_{\beta}(G)$ . Following the methodology of Keramati et al. (2020), we introduce the distributional optimism operator $\mathrm{O}_{c}^{\infty}:\mathcal{D}(a,b)\mapsto$ $\mathcal{D}(a,b)$ for a level $c\in(0,1)$ as

$$
(\mathrm{O}_{c}^{\infty}F)(x)\triangleq [F(x)-c\mathbb{I}_{[a,b)}(x)]^{+}.
$$

This operator shifts the distribution F down by a maximum of c over $[a,b)$ , ensuring that the resulting function ${\mathrm{O}}_{c}^{\infty}F$ remains a valid CDF in $\mathcal{D}(a,b)$ and optimistically dominates all other CDFs within the confidence ball $B_{\infty}(F,c)^{3}$ . In particular, ${\mathrm{O}}_{c}^{\infty}F$ represents maximum permissible downward adjustment under the constraints of the infinity ball, ensuring that for any distribution $G\in B_{\infty}(F,c)$

$$
(\mathrm{O}_{c}^{\infty}F)(x)\leq G(x),\forall x\in\mathbb{R}.
$$

context.name: Lemma 11
context.statement:
Lemma 11 For any $F_{i}\in \mathcal{D}$ and any $\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\Delta_{n}$ with any $n \geq 2$ , it holds that

$$
\left\| \sum_{i = 1}^{n}\theta_{i}F_{i}- \sum_{i = 1}^{n}\theta_{i}^{\prime}F_{i}\right\|_{\infty}\leq \left\| \theta - \theta^{\prime}\right\|_{1}.
$$

context.statement: We begin by establishing additional notations. For two Cumulative Distribution Functions (CDFs) F and G, the supremum distance between them is defined as $\| F - G \|_{\infty}\triangleq$ $\begin{array}{r}{\operatorname*{sup}_{x}|F(x)-G(x)|}\end{array}$ We define the $\ell_{1}$ distance between two Probability Mass Functions $(\mathrm{PMFs})$ with the same support P and $Q$ as $\begin{array}{r}{\| P - Q \|_{1}\triangleq \sum_{i}| P_{i}- Q_{i}|}\end{array}$ . Furthermore, the set $B_{\infty}(F,c): =\{G\in\mathcal{D}|\|G-F\|_{\infty}\leq c\}$ denotes the supremum norm ball of CDFs centered at F with radius c. Analogously, $B_{1}(P,c)$ represents the $\ell_{1}$ norm ball of PMFs centered at P with radius c.

context.name: Definition 7 and the distributional optimism operator O_c^infty (Section 4.2)
context.statement:
Definition 7 Given two CDFs F and G, we say that F is more optimistic than G if $F \geq G$

This definition aligns with the intuitive notion that a more optimistic distribution should possess a larger EntRM value. Given that the exponential transformation preserves order, F is more optimistic than G if and only if $E_{\beta}(F)\ge E_{\beta}(G)$ . Following the methodology of Keramati et al. (2020), we introduce the distributional optimism operator $\mathrm{O}_{c}^{\infty}:\mathcal{D}(a,b)\mapsto$ $\mathcal{D}(a,b)$ for a level $c\in(0,1)$ as

$$
(\mathrm{O}_{c}^{\infty}F)(x)\triangleq [F(x)-c\mathbb{I}_{[a,b)}(x)]^{+}.
$$

This operator shifts the distribution F down by a maximum of c over $[a,b)$ , ensuring that the resulting function ${\mathrm{O}}_{c}^{\infty}F$ remains a valid CDF in $\mathcal{D}(a,b)$ and optimistically dominates all other CDFs within the confidence ball $B_{\infty}(F,c)^{3}$ . In particular, ${\mathrm{O}}_{c}^{\infty}F$ represents maximum permissible downward adjustment under the constraints of the infinity ball, ensuring that for any distribution $G\in B_{\infty}(F,c)$

$$
(\mathrm{O}_{c}^{\infty}F)(x)\leq G(x),\forall x\in\mathbb{R}.
$$

context.name: Empirical Rademacher complexity
context.statement:
Given a dataset \(S = \{z_1, \dots, z_n\}\), the empirical Rademacher complexity is defined as
\[
R_S(\mathcal{F}) \stackrel{\Delta}{=} \mathbb{E}_{\sigma_1,\dots, \sigma_n} \left[ \sup_{f\in \mathcal{F}} \frac{1}{n} \sum^n_{i=1} \sigma_i f(z_i) \right].
\]
\(R_S(\mathcal{F})\) is a function of both the function class \(\mathcal{F}\) and the dataset \(S\).

context.name: definition 4.14
context.statement: \(\mathcal{C}\) is an \(\epsilon\)-cover of \(\mathcal{Q}\) with respect to metric \(\rho\) if for all \(v' \in \mathcal{Q}\), there exists \(v \in \mathcal{C}\) such that \(\rho(v,v')\le \epsilon\).

context.name: definition 4.15
context.statement:
The covering number is defined as the minimum size of an \(\epsilon\)-cover, or explicitly:
\[
N(\epsilon, \mathcal{Q}, \rho) \stackrel{\Delta}{=} (\text{min size of } \epsilon\text{-cover of } \mathcal{Q} \text{ w.r.t. metric } \rho).
\]

context.name: proposition 4.12
context.statement:
Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a collection of functions mapping \(Z \mapsto \mathbb{R}\) and let \(\mathcal{Q}\) be defined as in the referenced equation. Assume that \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \|v\|_2 \le M < \infty\) for all \(v \in \mathcal{Q}\). Then,
\[
R_S(\mathcal{F}) \leq \sqrt{\frac{2 M^2 \log |\mathcal{Q}|}{n}}.
\]

context.name: Output space \(\mathcal{Q}\) and the \(L_2(P_n)\) metric
context.statement:
Given a dataset \(S = \{z_1, \dots, z_n\}\), define the output space
\[
\mathcal{Q} \triangleq \left\{ \left(f(z_1), \dots, f(z_n)\right)^\top : f \in \mathcal{F} \right\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Correspondingly, the empirical Rademacher complexity can be rewritten as a maximization over the output space \(\mathcal{Q}\) instead of the function space \(\mathcal{F}\):
\[
R_S(\mathcal{F}) = \mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[ \sup_{v \in \mathcal{Q}} \frac{1}{n} \langle \sigma, v \rangle \right].
\]
We use the metric \(\rho(v, v') = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \|v - v'\|_2\). In the literature, an \(\epsilon\)-cover of \(\mathcal{Q}\) with respect to \(\rho\) is also referred to as an \(\epsilon\)-cover of the function class \(\mathcal{F}\) under the \(L_2(P_n)\) metric, where \(P_n\) denotes the empirical distribution, i.e. the uniform distribution over the observations \(z_1, \dots, z_n\). In particular,
\[
L_2(P_n)(f, f') = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (f(z_i) - f'(z_i))^2}.
\]
We can write a trivial correspondence between both the output and function class points of view as follows:
\[
N(\epsilon, \mathcal{F}, L_2(P_n)) = N\left(\epsilon, \mathcal{Q}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \|\cdot\|_2\right).
\]

context.statement:
Suppose that the hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\) is finite and the loss function \(\ell\) is bounded in \([0,1]\), i.e. \(0 \leq \ell((x,y),h) \leq 1\). Then for all \(\delta\) with \(0 < \delta < \tfrac{1}{2}\), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\),
\[
|L(h) - \widehat{L}(h)| \leq \sqrt{\frac{\ln|\mathcal{H}| + \ln(2/\delta)}{2n}} \qquad \forall h \in \mathcal{H}.
\]
As a corollary,
\[
L(\hat{h}) - L(h^{*}) \leq \sqrt{\frac{2(\ln|\mathcal{H}| + \ln(2/\delta))}{n}}.
\]

context.name: Risk and empirical-risk minimizer setup for finite hypothesis classes
context.statement:
Let \(\mathcal{H}\) be a finite hypothesis class and let \(\ell\) be a loss function with \(0 \leq \ell((x,y),h) \leq 1\). For \(h \in \mathcal{H}\), define the population risk
\[
L(h) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim \mathcal{D}}[\ell((x,y),h)].
\]
Given \(n\) iid samples \((x^{(1)},y^{(1)}), \dots, (x^{(n)},y^{(n)})\) from \(\mathcal{D}\), define the empirical risk
\[
\widehat{L}(h) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell((x^{(i)},y^{(i)}),h).
\]
Let \(\hat{h} \in \arg\min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \widehat{L}(h)\) be an empirical-risk minimizer and let \(h^* \in \arg\min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} L(h)\) be a population-risk minimizer.

context.name: Talagrand's lemma
context.statement:
Let \(\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be a \(\kappa\)-Lipschitz function. Then
\[

context.name: Rademacher complexity
context.statement:
Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a family of functions mapping \(Z \mapsto \mathbb{R}\), and let \(P\) be a distribution over \(Z\). The (average) Rademacher complexity of \(\mathcal{F}\) is defined as
\[
R_n(F) \triangleq \mathbb{E}_{z_1, \dots, z_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} P} \left[ \mathbb{E}_{\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\{ \pm 1 \}} \left[ \sup_{f\in F} \frac{1}{n} \sum^n_{i=1} \sigma_i f(z_i) \right] \right],
\]
where \(\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n\) are independent Rademacher random variables, i.e. each taking on the value of \(1\) or \(-1\) with probability \(1/2\).

\[

\]

\[
\frac{d}{d\lambda}\Lambda_{X_{1}}(\lambda)=\frac{\int x e^{\lambda x}d\Pr(X_{1}\leq x)}{\int e^{\lambda x}d\Pr(X_{1}\leq x)}=\mathbb{E}_{X_{1}^{\prime}}X_{1}^{\prime}.

\[
\lambda=\arg\max_{\lambda^{\prime}>0}\left[\lambda^{\prime}(\mu+\epsilon^{\prime})-\Lambda_{X_{1}}(\lambda^{\prime})\right].

\[
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\Pr(\bar{X}_{n}^{\prime}-\mu\in [\epsilon,\epsilon^{\prime\prime}])=1.\tag{2.5}

\[

context.name: VC-dimension
context.statement:
Let \(\mathcal{G} = \{\phi(w,z) : w \in \Omega\}\) be a \(\{0,1\}\) valued binary function class of \(z \in \mathcal{Z}\) indexed by \(w \in \Omega\). Given an arbitrary set of \(n\) samples \(\mathcal{S}_n = \{Z_1, \ldots, Z_n\} \in \mathcal{Z}^n\), we are interested in the number of functions (uniform \(L_\infty\) cover of the function class at \(\epsilon = 0\)) that \(\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n) = \{[\phi(w,Z_1), \ldots, \phi(w,Z_n)] : w \in \Omega\}\) can achieve.
We say that \(\mathcal{G}\) shatters \(S_{n}\) if the number of elements \(|\mathcal{G}(S_n)|\) is \(2^{n}\). That is, we can always find \(w\in \Omega\) so that \(\phi (w,z)\) matches any arbitrary possible choice of \(\{0,1\} ^n\) values at the \(n\) points. The maximum \(n\) such that \(\mathcal{G}\) shatters at least one instance of \(S_{n}\in \mathcal{Z}^{n}\), denoted by \(\mathrm{vc}(\mathcal{G})\), is called the VC-dimension of \(\mathcal{G}\).
Note that the maximum number of functions in \(\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n)\) is \(2^n\). If \(n > d\), then for any \(n\) samples \(\mathcal{S}_n\), \(\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n)\) contains fewer than \(2^n\) elements. Surprisingly, if a binary-valued function class \(\mathcal{G}\) has VC dimension \(d\), then when \(n > d\), the size of set \(\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{S}_n)\) can grow only polynomially in \(n\). This gives an \(O(d\ln n)\) upper bound on the uniform entropy of the function class \(\mathcal{G}\) with a finite VC-dimension (see Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1968, 1971; Sauer, 1972).

(Symmetrization) Consider a real valued function family \(F = \{f : Z \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\}\). Assume there exists a function \(\psi : F \times Z^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) and \(\epsilon_{n} : (0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) so that with probability at least \(1-\delta\):
\[
\forall f \in F, \qquad f(\sigma, S_{n}) \leq \psi(f, S_{n}) + \epsilon_{n}(\delta),
\]
where the randomness is over both \(S_{n} \sim D^{n}\) and \(\sigma\). If there exists \(\tilde{\psi}(f, S_{n} \cup S_{n}^{\prime})\) so that the following superadditive inequality holds for all \((S_{n}, S_{n}^{\prime})\)
\[
\psi(f, S_{n}) + \psi(f, S_{n}^{\prime}) \leq \tilde{\psi}(f, S_{n} \cup S_{n}^{\prime}),
\]
then with probability at least \(1-\delta\) over independent random data \((S_{n}, S_{n}^{\prime}) \sim D^{2n}\):
\[
\forall f \in F, \qquad f(S_{n}^{\prime}) \leq f(S_{n}) + \tilde{\psi}(f, S_{n} \cup S_{n}^{\prime}) + 2\epsilon_{n}(\delta/2).
\]

\[
\Pr\left(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}a_{i}\geq\epsilon\right)\leq\exp\left[-\frac{n\epsilon^{2}}{2 n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}^{2}}\right].

context.name: definition 4.7
context.statement:
Consider a real-valued function family \(\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{Z}\to \mathbb{R}\). Consider \(n\) iid Bernoulli random variables \(\sigma_{i}\in \{\pm 1\}\), where \(\operatorname*{Pr}(\sigma_i=1)=\operatorname*{Pr}(\sigma_i= -1)=0.5\). The symmetrized empirical process is
\[
f(\sigma,\mathcal{S}_{n})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}f(Z_{i})\qquad f\in\mathcal{F},
\]
where the randomness is with respect to both \(S_{n} = \{Z_{i}\}\) and \(\sigma = \{\sigma_{i}\}\).
Note that in order to bound the symmetrized empirical process, we only need a covering number result on \( S_{n} \). Therefore the symmetrization analysis allows us to work with empirical covering numbers. Next we will show that a bound on the symmetrized empirical process can be used to obtain uniform convergence of the empirical process \( \{f(S_{n}): f \in \mathcal{F}\} \) to the corresponding result on the validation data. Since one can relate the validation loss of a learning algorithm to its generalization error on the test data, we can use this result to obtain generalization bounds.
The following lemma shows that if we can obtain an upper bound on the symmetrized empirical process \(\{f(\sigma, S_n) : f \in \mathcal{F}\}\), and the upper bound satisfies a superadditive property, then we can obtain the uniform convergence of the empirical process \(\{f(S_n) : f \in \mathcal{F}\}\) on the training data \(S_n\) to the corresponding result on the validation data \(S_n'\).

context.name: Union Bound
context.statement:
(Union Bound) Consider \(m\) events \(E_1, \ldots, E_m\). The following probability inequality holds:
\[
\Pr (E_1 \cup \cdots \cup E_m) \leq \sum_{j=1}^{m} \Pr(E_j).
\]

The union bound has an alternative expression, which is often used in the learning theory analysis. If each \(E_j\) occurs with probability at least \(1-\delta_j\) for \(j=1, \ldots, m\), then with probability at least \(1-\sum_{j=1}^{m} \delta_j\), all of events \(\{E_j\}\) occur simultaneously for \(j=1, \ldots, m\).

\[
\epsilon_{n}^{h}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{n}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}\sup_{w\in\Omega}[\phi(w,\mathcal{D})-\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})-h(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})].\tag{6.2}
\]
This quantity measures the one-sided expected uniform convergence of function class \(\mathcal{G}\) with offset function \(h(w, S_n)\).
We note that
\[
\epsilon_{n}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})=\epsilon_{n}^{h}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D}),\qquad \text{w i t h} h=0.

context.name: definition 6.11
context.statement:
Consider a function class \(\mathcal{G} = \{\phi(w, Z) : w \in \Omega\}\), and let \(h\) be an offset function of the following form
\[
h(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}h(w,Z_{i}),\quad h(w,z)=h_{0}(w)+h_{1}(w,z).\tag{6.3}
\]
Given \( S_{n}=\{Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{n}\} \), the (one-sided) empirical Rademacher complexity of \( \mathcal{G} \) with offset \( h \) decomposition (6.3) is defined as
\[
R^{h}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{S}_{n})=\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\sup_{w\in\Omega}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}[\phi(w,Z_{i})+0. 5h_{1}(w,Z_{i})]-0. 5h(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})\right],
\]
where \(\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_n\) are independent uniform \(\{\pm 1\}\)-valued Bernoulli random variables. Moreover, the expected Rademacher complexity is
\[
R_{n}^{h}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{n}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}R^{h}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{S}_{n}).
\]
We note that the standard Rademacher complexity can be regarded as a special case of the offset Rademacher complexity with \( h(\cdot) = h_0(\cdot) = h_1(\cdot) = 0 \):
\[
R(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{S}_{n})=R^{0}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{S}_{n}),\quad R_{n}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})=R_{n}^{0}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D}).
\]
It should be pointed out that the decomposition of \( h \) in (6.3) may not be unique, and the offset Rademacher complexity relies on the specific decomposition used.

Consider a finite family of distributions \(\mathcal{P} = \{\mathcal{D}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{D}_N\}\). Given a loss function \(Q\) on \(\Theta \times \mathcal{P}\), let
\[
m=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\left|\left\{k:Q(\theta,\mathcal{D}_{k})<\epsilon\right\}\right|.
\]
Assume that \(j\) is a random variable that is uniformly distributed in \(\{1, \dots, N\}\), and conditioned on \(j\), \(Z \sim \mathcal{D}_j\). Given any (possibly random) estimator \(\mathcal{A}(Z)\). Then
\[
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\operatorname*{Pr}_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}_{j}}(Q(\mathcal{A}(Z),\mathcal{D}_{j})<\epsilon)\leq\max\left(\frac{m}{N},\frac{I(j,Z)+\ln 2}{\ln(N/m)}\right),
\]
where \( I(j,Z) \) is the mutual information of \( j \) and \( Z \). The probability includes possible randomization in \( \mathcal{A} \).

context.statement:
Consider a distribution family \(\mathcal{P}\) on sample space \(\mathcal{Z}\), a parameter space \(\Theta\). A learning algorithm \(\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{Z}^n\to \Theta\), a loss function \(Q:\Theta \times \mathcal{P}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\). Then the worst case expected risk of a learning algorithm (i.e., a statistical estimator) \(\mathcal{A}\) with respect to \(\mathcal{P}\) is given by
\[
r_{n}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},Q)=\sup_{\mathcal{D}\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{n}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{A}}Q(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}_{n}),\mathcal{D}),
\]
where \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{A}}\) is the expectation over any internal randomization of \(\mathcal{A}\). Moreover, the minimax risk is defined as:
\[
r_{n}(\mathcal{P},Q)=\inf_{\mathcal{A}}r_{n}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},Q).
\]

\]
where

The ridge regression method defines, for each \(n\),
\[
\hat{w}(\mathcal{S}_{n})=\arg\min_{w}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_{i}-w^{\top}\psi(X_{i}))^{2}+\|w\|_{\Lambda_{0}}^{2}\right].

\[

context.name: definition 16.1
context.statement:
In the multi-armed bandit (or MAB) problem, we consider \(K\) arms. The environment generates a sequence of reward vectors for time steps \(t \geq 1\) as \(r_t = [r_t(1), \ldots, r_t(K)]\). Each \(r_t(a)\) is associated with an arm \(a \in \{1, \ldots, K\}\). In the literature, an arm \(a\) is also referred to as an action. At each time step \(t = 1, 2, \ldots, T\),
- The player pulls one of the arms \( a_{t} \in \{1, \dots, K\} \).
- The environment returns the reward \( r_t(a_t) \), but does not reveal information on any other arm \( a \neq a_t \).
At each time \( t \), a (randomized) bandit algorithm takes the historic observations observed so far, and maps it to a distribution \( \hat{\pi}_{t-1} \) over actions \( a \in \{1, \ldots, K\} \). We then draw a random action \( a_t \) (arm) from \( \hat{\pi}_{t-1} \). Here \( \hat{\pi}_{t-1} \) is referred to as policy.
In the adversarial bandit problem, we are given an arbitrary reward sequence \(\{[r_1(1),\ldots,r_t(K)]:t\geq 1\}\) before hand. The adversary in this setting is called oblivious, who decides the rewards of all the rounds before the game starts (but may take advantage of the bandit algorithm's weakness). For this reward se
quence, the expected cumulative reward of a randomized bandit algorithm is
\[
\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a_{t}),
\]
where the randomization is over the internal randomization of the bandit algorithm. The expected regret is defined as
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}=\max_{a}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a)-\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}\left(a_{t}\right).\tag{16.1}
\]
If the bandit algorithm is deterministic: i.e. pulling a single arm \(a_{t}\) only at any time step, then the regret is
\[
\mathrm{REG}_{T}=\max_{a}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a_{t}).
\]
In the adversarial bandit problem, our goal is to minimize the expected regret \(\mathrm{REG}_T\) (and the expectation is with respect to the internal randomization of the algorithm instead of the data).
Another form of bandit problem, called stochastic bandit, assumes that the reward \( r_t(a) \) is drawn independently from a distribution \( \mathcal{D}_a \), with mean \( \mu(a) = \mathbb{E}_{r_t(a) \sim \mathcal{D}_a} [r_t(a)] \). In this setting, the goal of bandit is to find \( a \) that maximizes the expected reward \( \mu(a) \). We are interested in the expected regret defined as:
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}=T\max_{a}\mu(a)-\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu\left(a_{t}\right).\tag{16.2}
\]
Again, this regret is defined for each realization of the stochastic rewards, and the expectation is with respect to the randomness of the algorithm. If algorithm is deterministic and outputs \( a_{t} \) at each time \( t \), then
\[
\mathrm{REG}_{T}=T\max_{a}\mu(a)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu(a_{t}).
\]
We can further include randomization over data into the regret of stochastic bandit, by considering expected regret as follows:
\[
\mathbb{E}\operatorname{REG}_{T}=T\max_{a}\mu(a)-\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu(a_{t}),
\]
where the expectation is with respect to both the data and the internal randomization of the learning algorithm.

context.name: Empirical Rademacher complexity
context.statement:
Given a dataset \(S = \{z_1, \dots, z_n\}\), the empirical Rademacher complexity is defined as
\[
R_S(\mathcal{F}) \stackrel{\Delta}{=} \mathbb{E}_{\sigma_1,\dots, \sigma_n} \left[ \sup_{f\in \mathcal{F}} \frac{1}{n} \sum^n_{i=1} \sigma_i f(z_i) \right].
\]
\(R_S(\mathcal{F})\) is a function of both the function class \(\mathcal{F}\) and the dataset \(S\).
As the name suggests, the expectation of the empirical Rademacher complexity is the Rademacher complexity:
\[
R_n(\mathcal{F}) = \mathbb{E}_{\substack{z_1, \dots, z_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} P \\ S = \{z_1, \dots, z_n\}}}\left[ R_S(\mathcal{F}) \right].
\]

\mathbb{E}_{z_1, \dots, z_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} P} \left[ \sup_{f\in F} \left[ \frac{1}{n} \sum^n_{i=1} f(z_i) - \mathbb{E}_{z\sim P} [f(z)] \right]\right] \leq 2 R_n(\mathcal{F}).

context.name: McDiarmid's inequality
context.statement:
Suppose \(f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) satisfies the bounded difference condition: there exist constants \(c_1, \ldots, c_n \in \mathbb{R}\) such that for all real numbers \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) and \(x_i'\),
\[
|f(x_1, \ldots, x_n) - f(x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, x_i', x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_n)| \leq c_i.
\]
Then, for any independent random variables \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\),
\[
\mathbb{P}\left[f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) - \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, \ldots, X_n)] \geq t\right] \leq \exp\left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2}\right).
\]
Moreover, \(f(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is \(O\!\left(\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2}\right)\)-sub-Gaussian.

context.name: Output space \(\mathcal{Q}\) and the \(L_2(P_n)\) metric
context.statement:
Given a dataset \(S = \{z_1, \dots, z_n\}\), define the output space
\[
\mathcal{Q} \triangleq \left\{ \left(f(z_1), \dots, f(z_n)\right)^\top : f \in \mathcal{F} \right\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Correspondingly, the empirical Rademacher complexity can be rewritten as a maximization over the output space \(\mathcal{Q}\) instead of the function space \(\mathcal{F}\):
\[
R_S(\mathcal{F}) = \mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[ \sup_{v \in \mathcal{Q}} \frac{1}{n} \langle \sigma, v \rangle \right].
\]
We use the metric \(\rho(v, v') = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \|v - v'\|_2\). In the literature, an \(\epsilon\)-cover of \(\mathcal{Q}\) with respect to \(\rho\) is also referred to as an \(\epsilon\)-cover of the function class \(\mathcal{F}\) under the \(L_2(P_n)\) metric, where \(P_n\) denotes the empirical distribution, i.e. the uniform distribution over the observations \(z_1, \dots, z_n\). \[
L_2(P_n)(f, f') = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (f(z_i) - f'(z_i))^2}.
\]
We can write a trivial correspondence between both the output and function class points of view as follows:
\[
N(\epsilon, \mathcal{F}, L_2(P_n)) = N\left(\epsilon, \mathcal{Q}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \|\cdot\|_2\right).
\]

\]
and suppose \(\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|x\right\|_2^2\right] \leq C^2\). Then
\[
R_n(\mathcal{H}) \le 2 B_w B_u C\sqrt{\frac{m}{n}}.

context.name: Removing the absolute value in Rademacher complexity
context.statement:
Let \(\sigma = (\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n)\) and \(f_{\theta}(x) = \left(f_{\theta}\left(x^{(1)}\right), \dots, f_{\theta}\left(x^{(n)}\right)\right)\). Suppose that for any \(\sigma \in \{\pm 1\}^n\), \(\sup_{\theta} \langle \sigma, f_{\theta}(x) \rangle \geq 0\). Then,
\[
\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[ \sup_{\theta} \left| \langle \sigma, f_{\theta}(x) \rangle \right| \right] \leq 2\, \mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[ \sup_{\theta} \langle \sigma, f_{\theta}(x) \rangle \right].
\]

context.name: Talagrand's lemma
context.statement:
Let \(\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be a \(\kappa\)-Lipschitz function. Then
\[
R_S(\phi\circ \mathcal{H})\leq \kappa R_S(\mathcal{H}),
\]
where \(\phi\circ\mathcal{H} = \{z\mapsto \phi(h(z))\mid h\in\mathcal{H}\}\).

context.name: Rademacher complexity of l2-bounded linear functions
context.statement:
Let \(\mathcal{H} = \{x \mapsto \langle w,x \rangle \mid w \in \mathbb{R}^d,\, \|w\|_2 \le B\}\) for some constant \(B > 0\). Moreover, assume \(\mathbb{E}_{x \sim P}[\|x\|_2^2] \leq C^2\), where \(P\) is some distribution and \(C > 0\) is a constant. Then
\[
R_S(\mathcal{H}) \le \frac{B}{n} \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n \|x^{(i)}\|_2^2},
\]
and
\[
R_n(\mathcal{H}) \le \frac{BC}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]

context.name: Rademacher complexity
context.statement:
Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a family of functions mapping \(Z \mapsto \mathbb{R}\), and let \(P\) be a distribution over \(Z\). The (average) Rademacher complexity of \(\mathcal{F}\) is defined as
\[
R_n(F) \triangleq \mathbb{E}_{z_1, \dots, z_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} P} \left[ \mathbb{E}_{\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\{ \pm 1 \}} \left[ \sup_{f\in F} \frac{1}{n} \sum^n_{i=1} \sigma_i f(z_i) \right] \right],
\]
where \(\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n\) are independent Rademacher random variables, i.e. each taking on the value of \(1\) or \(-1\) with probability \(1/2\).

context.name: Two-layer ReLU network
context.statement:
Given a width \(m\), let \(w_1,\dots,w_m \in \mathbb{R}\), \(u_1,\dots,u_m \in \mathbb{R}^d\), and let \(\phi\) denote the ReLU activation. For \(\theta=(w_1,\dots,w_m,u_1,\dots,u_m)\), define the two-layer ReLU network
\[
f_{\theta}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m w_j \phi\left(u_j^\top x\right).
\]
Throughout this section, we use the following notation: \(\theta = (w, U)\) are the parameters of the model with \(w \in \mathbb{R}^m\) and \(U \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times d}\), where \(m\) denotes the number of hidden units. We use \(u_i \in \mathbb{R}^d\) to denote the \(i\)-th row of \(U\) (written as a column vector). \(\phi(z) = \max(z,0)\) is the ReLU activation function applied element-wise. \(f_\theta(x) = \langle w, \phi(Ux)\rangle = w^\top \phi(Ux)\) is the model. \(\{(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^n\) is the training set, with \(x^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) and \(y^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}\).

context.name: Lemma 4.8
context.statement:
(Symmetrization) Consider a real valued function family \(F = \{f : Z \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\}\). Assume there exists a function \(\psi : F \times Z^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) and \(\epsilon_{n} : (0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) so that with probability at least \(1-\delta\):
\[
\forall f \in F, \qquad f(\sigma, S_{n}) \leq \psi(f, S_{n}) + \epsilon_{n}(\delta),
\]
where the randomness is over both \(S_{n} \sim D^{n}\) and \(\sigma\). If there exists \(\tilde{\psi}(f, S_{n} \cup S_{n}^{\prime})\) so that the following superadditive inequality holds for all \((S_{n}, S_{n}^{\prime})\)
\[
\psi(f, S_{n}) + \psi(f, S_{n}^{\prime}) \leq \tilde{\psi}(f, S_{n} \cup S_{n}^{\prime}),
\]
then with probability at least \(1-\delta\) over independent random data \((S_{n}, S_{n}^{\prime}) \sim D^{2n}\):
\[
\forall f \in F, \qquad f(S_{n}^{\prime}) \leq f(S_{n}) + \tilde{\psi}(f, S_{n} \cup S_{n}^{\prime}) + 2\epsilon_{n}(\delta/2).
\]

context.name: lemma 4.11
context.statement:
Let \(\psi_{\mathrm{trn}}: \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{Z}^n \to \mathbb{R}\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{val}}: \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{Z}^n \to \mathbb{R}\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{tst}}: \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{D} \to \mathbb{R}\) be appropriately training (where \(\mathcal{D}\) denotes probability distributions on \(\mathcal{Z}\)), validation, and test statistics. Assume that for any \(\delta_1 \in (0,1)\), the following uniform convergence result holds. With probability at least \(1 - \delta_1\) over randomly drawn training and validation sets \((S_n, S_n') \sim \mathcal{D}^{2n}\):
\[
\forall f\in\mathcal{F}:\psi_{\mathrm{val}}(f,\mathcal{S}_{n}^{\prime})\leq\psi_{\mathrm{trn}}(f,\mathcal{S}_{n})+\epsilon_{n}^{1}(\delta_{1}).
\]
Moreover, assume \(\forall f\in \mathcal{F}\), we have with probability \(1 - \delta_{2}\) over randomly drawn \(\mathcal{S}_n^\prime \sim \mathcal{D}\):
\[
\psi_{\mathrm{tst}}(f,\mathcal{D})\leq\psi_{\mathrm{val}}(f,\mathcal{S}_{n}^{\prime})+\epsilon_{n}^{2}(\delta_{2}).
\]
Then the following uniform convergence statement holds. With probability at least \(1 - \delta_1 - \delta_2\),
\[
\forall f\in\mathcal{F}:\psi_{\mathrm{tst}}(f,\mathcal{D})\leq\psi_{\mathrm{trn}}(f,\mathcal{S}_{n})+\epsilon_{n}^{1}(\delta_{1})+\epsilon_{n}^{2}(\delta_{2}).
\]

context.name: Union Bound
context.statement:
(Union Bound) Consider \(m\) events \(E_1, \ldots, E_m\). The following probability inequality holds:
\[
\Pr (E_1 \cup \cdots \cup E_m) \leq \sum_{j=1}^{m} \Pr(E_j).
\]

The union bound has an alternative expression, which is often used in the learning theory analysis. If each \(E_j\) occurs with probability at least \(1-\delta_j\) for \(j=1, \ldots, m\), then with probability at least \(1-\sum_{j=1}^{m} \delta_j\), all of events \(\{E_j\}\) occur simultaneously for \(j=1, \ldots, m\).

context.name: definition 4.1
context.statement:
Let \((\mathcal{V},d)\) be a pseudometric space with metric \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\). A finite
set \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon) \subset \mathcal{V}\) is an \(\epsilon\)-cover (or \(\epsilon\)-net) of \(\mathcal{G} \subset \mathcal{V}\) if, for all \(\phi \in \mathcal{G}\), there exists \(\phi' \in \mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\) so that \(d(\phi', \phi) \leq \epsilon\). The \(\epsilon\)-covering number of \(\mathcal{G}\) with metric \(d\) is the smallest cardinality \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) of such \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\). The number \(\ln N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) is called the \(\epsilon\)-entropy.
For a function class \(\mathcal{G}\) with seminorm \(L_{p}(\mathcal{D})\) in (3.19), we denote the corresponding \(L_{p}(\mathcal{D})\)-covering number as \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, L_{p}(\mathcal{D}))\). When \(1 \leq p \leq q\), we have
\[
N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{p}(\mathcal{D}))\leq N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{q}(\mathcal{D})).
\]

context.name: definition 3.8
context.statement:
We define
\[
\phi(w,z)=L\left(f(w,x),y\right)-L_{*}(x,y),\tag{3.4}
\]
for \( w \in \Omega \) and \( z = (x, y) \in \mathcal{Z} = \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \), and a pre-chosen \( L_{*}(x, y) \) of \( z = (x, y) \) that does not depend on \( w \).
For training data \( S_{n}=\{Z_{i}=(X_{i},Y_{i}):i=1,\ldots,n\} \), we define the training loss for \( w\in \Omega \) as
\[
\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi(w,Z_{i}).\tag{3.5}
\]
Moreover, for a distribution \(\mathcal{D}\) on \(\mathcal{Z}\), we define the test loss for \(w \in \Omega\) as:
\[
\phi(w,\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}}\phi(w,Z).\tag{3.6}
\]
Since \( L_{*}(x,y) \) does not depend on \( w \), the ERM solution with respect to the loss \( L(\cdot) \) is equivalent to the ERM solution with respect to \( \phi (w,\cdot) \). Therefore with the simplified notations, the approximate ERM method (3.3) is a special case of the following method:
\[
\phi(\hat{w},\mathcal{S}_{n})\leq\inf_{w\in\Omega}\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})+\epsilon^{\prime}.\tag{3.7}
\]
In general, we may simply take \( L_{*}(x,y) = 0 \) in (3.4). However, for some applications, we may choose a non-zero \( L_{*}(x,y) \) so that
\[
L(f(w,x),y)-L_{*}(x,y)
\]
has a small variance. For least squares loss, this can be achieved with \( L_{*}(x,y) = L(f_{*}(x),y) \) where \( f_{*}(x) \) is the optimal prediction function that minimizes the test loss as shown in Example 3.9. The smaller variance, combined with Bernstein's inequality, implies better generalization bound (see Section 3.6 for more details).

context.name: Empirical and Uniform Covering Number
context.statement:
Given an empirical distribution \( S_{n}=\{Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{n}\} \), we define the pseudometric \( d = L_{p}(S_{n}) \) as
\[
d(\phi,\phi^{\prime})=\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\phi(Z_{i})-\phi^{\prime}(Z_{i})|^{p}\right]^{1/p}.
\]
The corresponding metric covering number \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, L_p(\mathcal{S}_n))\) is referred to as the
empirical \( L_{p} \) covering number. Given \( n \), the largest \( L_{p} \) covering number over empirical distribution \( S_{n} \) is referred to as the uniform \( L_{p} \) covering number
\[
N_{p}(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},n)=\sup_{\mathcal{S}_{n}}N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{p}(\mathcal{S}_{n})).
\]

context.name: Bracketing Number
context.statement:
Let \(\mathcal{G} = \{\phi(w, \cdot) : w \in \Omega\}\) be a real-valued function class, equipped with a pseudometric \(d\). We say
\[
\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)=\left\{\left[\phi_{1}^{L}(z),\phi_{1}^{U}(z)\right],\dots,\left[\phi_{N}^{L}(z),\phi_{N}^{U}(z)\right]\right\}
\]
is an \(\epsilon\)-bracket of \(\mathcal{G}\) under metric \(d\) if for all \(w \in \Omega\), there exists \(j = j(w)\) such that \(\forall z\):
\[
\phi_{j}^{L}(z)\leq\phi(w,z)\leq\phi_{j}^{U}(z),\quad d(\phi_{j}^{L},\phi_{j}^{U})\leq\epsilon .
\]
The \(\epsilon\)-bracketing number is the smallest cardinality \(N_{\mathbb{I}}(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) of such \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\). The quantity \(\ln N_{\mathbb{I}}(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) is called \(\epsilon\) bracketing entropy.
In particular, given a distribution \(\mathcal{D}\) and \(p \geq 1\), we define \(L_{p}\)-seminorm in function space as
\[
\left\|f-f^{\prime}\right\|_{L_{p}(\mathcal{D})}=\left[\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}}|f(Z)-f^{\prime}(Z)|^{p}\right]^{1/p}.\tag{3.19}
\]
It induces a pseudometric, denoted as \( d = L_{p}(\mathcal{D}) \), and the corresponding bracketing number is \( N_{\parallel}(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, L_{p}(\mathcal{D})) \).
For \(p = \infty\), the \(L_{\infty}(\mathcal{D})\)-seminorm is defined as the essential supremum seminorm, which leads to the pseudometric
\[
d(f,f^{\prime})=\inf\left\{\omega:\Pr_{\mathcal{D}}[|f(Z)-f^{\prime}(Z)|\leq\omega]=1\right\}.
\]
However, when \( p = \infty \), instead of using the \( L_{\infty} \) bracketing number, it is more conventional to use the equivalent notion of \( L_{\infty} \) covering number (see Proposition 4.3).

This is the usual countability / permissibility convention for uniform bounds over a function class.

namespace GraduateLevel

noncomputable def empLoss {𝒵 : Type*} {Ωp : Type*} {n : ℕ}
    (φ : Ωp → 𝒵 → ℝ) (Z : Fin n → 𝒵) (w : Ωp) : ℝ :=
  (1 / (n : ℝ)) * ∑ i : Fin n, φ w (Z i)

noncomputable def testLoss {𝒵 : Type*} [MeasurableSpace 𝒵] {Ωp : Type*}
    (φ : Ωp → 𝒵 → ℝ) (D : Measure 𝒵) (w : Ωp) : ℝ :=
  ∫ z, φ w z ∂D

def IsUnifL1Cover {𝒵 : Type*} [MeasurableSpace 𝒵] {Ωp : Type*}
    (D : Measure 𝒵)
    (C : Finset (𝒵 → ℝ)) (φ : Ωp → 𝒵 → ℝ) (𝒲 : Set Ωp) (ε : ℝ) {m : ℕ}
    (S : Fin m → 𝒵) : Prop :=
  (∀ g ∈ C, (∀ z, g z ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) ∧ AEMeasurable g D) ∧
  (∀ w ∈ 𝒲, ∃ g ∈ C,
    (1 / (m : ℝ)) * ∑ j : Fin m, |φ w (S j) - g (S j)| ≤ ε)

def IsUnifL1CoveringNumber {𝒵 : Type*} [MeasurableSpace 𝒵] {Ωp : Type*}
    (D : Measure 𝒵)
    (N : ℕ) (φ : Ωp → 𝒵 → ℝ) (𝒲 : Set Ωp) (ε : ℝ) (m : ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ S : Fin m → 𝒵, ∃ C : Finset (𝒵 → ℝ),
      C.card ≤ N ∧ IsUnifL1Cover D C φ 𝒲 ε S) ∧
  (∀ M : ℕ,
    (∀ S : Fin m → 𝒵, ∃ C : Finset (𝒵 → ℝ),
        C.card ≤ M ∧ IsUnifL1Cover D C φ 𝒲 ε S) →
      N ≤ M)

context.name: Martingale Sub-Gaussian Inequality
context.statement:
Consider a sequence of random functions \(\xi_1(S_1),\ldots,\xi_t(S_t),\ldots\) Assume each \(\xi_{i}\) is sub-Gaussian with respect to \(Z_{i}^{(y)}\):
\[
\ln\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}e^{\lambda\xi_{i}}\leq\lambda\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}\xi_{i}+\frac{\lambda^{2}\sigma_{i}^{2}}{2}
\]
for some \(\sigma_{i}\) that may depend on \(S_{i - 1}\) and \(Z_{i}^{(x)}\). Then for all \(\sigma >0\), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\)
\[
\forall n>0:\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{i}^{(y)}}\xi_{i}<\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}+\left(\sigma+\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}^{2}}{\sigma}\right)\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2}}.
\]

context.name: lemma 16.2
context.statement:
Let \(a_* \in \arg \max_a \mu(a)\). Let
\[
\delta_{1}=\Pr [\exists t>K:\mu(a_{*})>\hat{\mu}_{t-1}(a_{*})+\hat{c}_{t-1}(a_{*})]
\]
be the probability that the upper confident bound fails on \( a_* \). Let
\[
\delta_{2}=\Pr\left[\exists t>K\&a\in\{1,\dots,K\}\backslash\left\{a_{*}\right\}:\mu(a)<\hat{\mu}_{t-1}(a)-\hat{c}_{t-1}^{\prime}(a)\right]
\]
be the probability that the lower confident bound fails on \( a \neq a_* \). Then for Algorithm 16.1, we have with probability at least \( 1 - \delta_1 - \delta_2 \):
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}\leq\sum_{a=1}^{K}[\mu(a_{*})-\mu(a)]+\sum_{t=K+1}^{T}[\hat{c}_{t-1}(a_{t})+\hat{c}_{t-1}^{\prime}(a_{t})]\mathbb{1}(a_{t}\neq a_{*}).
\]

context.name: definition 16.1
context.statement:
In the multi-armed bandit (or MAB) problem, we consider \(K\) arms. The environment generates a sequence of reward vectors for time steps \(t \geq 1\) as \(r_t = [r_t(1), \ldots, r_t(K)]\). Each \(r_t(a)\) is associated with an arm \(a \in \{1, \ldots, K\}\). In the literature, an arm \(a\) is also referred to as an action. At each time step \(t = 1, 2, \ldots, T\),
- The player pulls one of the arms \( a_{t} \in \{1, \dots, K\} \).
- The environment returns the reward \( r_t(a_t) \), but does not reveal information on any other arm \( a \neq a_t \).
At each time \( t \), a (randomized) bandit algorithm takes the historic observations observed so far, and maps it to a distribution \( \hat{\pi}_{t-1} \) over actions \( a \in \{1, \ldots, K\} \). We then draw a random action \( a_t \) (arm) from \( \hat{\pi}_{t-1} \). Here \( \hat{\pi}_{t-1} \) is referred to as policy.
In the adversarial bandit problem, we are given an arbitrary reward sequence \(\{[r_1(1),\ldots,r_t(K)]:t\geq 1\}\) before hand. The adversary in this setting is called oblivious, who decides the rewards of all the rounds before the game starts (but may take advantage of the bandit algorithm's weakness). For this reward se
quence, the expected cumulative reward of a randomized bandit algorithm is
\[
\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a_{t}),
\]
where the randomization is over the internal randomization of the bandit algorithm. The expected regret is defined as
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}=\max_{a}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a)-\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}\left(a_{t}\right).\tag{16.1}
\]
If the bandit algorithm is deterministic: i.e. pulling a single arm \(a_{t}\) only at any time step, then the regret is
\[
\mathrm{REG}_{T}=\max_{a}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a_{t}).
\]
In the adversarial bandit problem, our goal is to minimize the expected regret \(\mathrm{REG}_T\) (and the expectation is with respect to the internal randomization of the algorithm instead of the data).
Another form of bandit problem, called stochastic bandit, assumes that the reward \( r_t(a) \) is drawn independently from a distribution \( \mathcal{D}_a \), with mean \( \mu(a) = \mathbb{E}_{r_t(a) \sim \mathcal{D}_a} [r_t(a)] \). In this setting, the goal of bandit is to find \( a \) that maximizes the expected reward \( \mu(a) \). We are interested in the expected regret defined as:
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}=T\max_{a}\mu(a)-\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu\left(a_{t}\right).\tag{16.2}
\]
Again, this regret is defined for each realization of the stochastic rewards, and the expectation is with respect to the randomness of the algorithm. If algorithm is deterministic and outputs \( a_{t} \) at each time \( t \), then
\[
\mathrm{REG}_{T}=T\max_{a}\mu(a)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu(a_{t}).
\]
We can further include randomization over data into the regret of stochastic bandit, by considering expected regret as follows:
\[
\mathbb{E}\operatorname{REG}_{T}=T\max_{a}\mu(a)-\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu(a_{t}),
\]
where the expectation is with respect to both the data and the internal randomization of the learning algorithm.

context.name: UCB Algorithm
context.statement:
Algorithm 16.1: UCB Algorithm
Input: \(K\) and \(T\geq K\)   
1 for \(a=1,\dots,K\) do   
2 Let \(\hat{n}_0(a) = 0\)   
3 Let \(\hat{\mu}_0(a) = 0\)   
4 for \(t=1,2,\ldots,T\) do   
5 if \(t\leq K\) then   
6 Let \(a_{t} = t\)   
7 else   
8 Let \(a_{t}\in \arg \max_{a}[\hat{\mu}_{t - 1}(a) + \hat{c}_{t - 1}(a)]\) according to (16.3)   
9 Pull arm \(a_{t}\) and observe reward \(r_t(a_t)\)

context.name: equation 16.3
context.statement:
For each arm \(a\), define the number of pulls up to time \(t\) and the corresponding empirical mean by
\[
\hat n_t(a)=\sum_{s=1}^{t}\mathbb{1}(a_s=a), \qquad
\hat\mu_t(a)=\frac{1}{\hat n_t(a)}\sum_{s=1}^{t} r_s(a_s)\mathbb{1}(a_s=a),
\]
with the initialization \(\hat n_0(a)=0\) and \(\hat\mu_0(a)=0\). In the UCB algorithm, after the initialization rounds, the arm is selected according to
\[
a_t\in\arg\max_a\left[\hat\mu_{t-1}(a)+\hat c_{t-1}(a)\right]. \tag{16.3}
\]
Here \(\hat c_t(a)\) denotes the confidence width used by the algorithm.

import Mathlib

open MeasureTheory ProbabilityTheory Real Finset
open scoped ENNReal NNReal

namespace GraduateLevel

lemma measurable_encode {α : Type*} {_ : MeasurableSpace α} [Encodable α]
    [MeasurableSingletonClass α] :
    Measurable (Encodable.encode (α := α)) := by
  refine measurable_to_nat fun a ↦ ?_
  have : Encodable.encode ⁻¹' {Encodable.encode a} = {a} := by ext; simp
  rw [this]
  exact measurableSet_singleton _

lemma measurableEmbedding_encode (α : Type*) {_ : MeasurableSpace α} [Encodable α]
    [MeasurableSingletonClass α] :
    MeasurableEmbedding (Encodable.encode (α := α)) where
  injective := Encodable.encode_injective
  measurable := measurable_encode
  measurableSet_image' _ _ := .of_discrete

section Finite

variable {𝓧 𝓨 α : Type*} {m𝓧 : MeasurableSpace 𝓧} {m𝓨 : MeasurableSpace 𝓨}
  {mα : MeasurableSpace α} [TopologicalSpace α] [LinearOrder α]
  [OpensMeasurableSpace α] [OrderClosedTopology α] [SecondCountableTopology α]

lemma measurableSet_isMax [Countable 𝓨]
    {f : 𝓧 → 𝓨 → α} (hf : ∀ y, Measurable (fun x ↦ f x y)) (y : 𝓨) :
    MeasurableSet {x | ∀ z, f x z ≤ f x y} := by
  rw [show {x | ∀ y', f x y' ≤ f x y} = ⋂ y', {x | f x y' ≤ f x y} by ext; simp]
  exact MeasurableSet.iInter fun z ↦ measurableSet_le (by fun_prop) (by fun_prop)

lemma exists_isMaxOn' {α : Type*} [LinearOrder α]
    [Nonempty 𝓨] [Finite 𝓨] [Encodable 𝓨] (f : 𝓧 → 𝓨 → α) (x : 𝓧) :
    ∃ n : ℕ, ∃ y, n = Encodable.encode y ∧ ∀ z, f x z ≤ f x y := by
  obtain ⟨y, h⟩ := Finite.exists_max (f x)
  exact ⟨Encodable.encode y, y, rfl, h⟩

noncomputable
def measurableArgmax [Nonempty 𝓨] [Finite 𝓨] [Encodable 𝓨] [MeasurableSingletonClass 𝓨]
    (f : 𝓧 → 𝓨 → α)
    [∀ x, DecidablePred fun n ↦ ∃ y, n = Encodable.encode y ∧ ∀ (z : 𝓨), f x z ≤ f x y]
    (x : 𝓧) :
    𝓨 :=
  (measurableEmbedding_encode 𝓨).invFun (Nat.find (exists_isMaxOn' f x))

lemma measurable_measurableArgmax [Nonempty 𝓨] [Finite 𝓨] [Encodable 𝓨]
    [MeasurableSingletonClass 𝓨]
    {f : 𝓧 → 𝓨 → α}
    [∀ x, DecidablePred fun n ↦ ∃ y, n = Encodable.encode y ∧ ∀ (z : 𝓨), f x z ≤ f x y]
    (hf : ∀ y, Measurable (fun x ↦ f x y)) :
    Measurable (measurableArgmax f) := by
  refine (MeasurableEmbedding.measurable_invFun (measurableEmbedding_encode 𝓨)).comp ?_
  refine measurable_find _ fun n ↦ ?_
  have : {x | ∃ y, n = Encodable.encode y ∧ ∀ (z : 𝓨), f x z ≤ f x y}
      = ⋃ y, ({x | n = Encodable.encode y} ∩ {x | ∀ z, f x z ≤ f x y}) := by ext; simp
  rw [this]
  refine MeasurableSet.iUnion fun y ↦ (MeasurableSet.inter (by simp) ?_)
  exact measurableSet_isMax (by fun_prop) y

end Finite

structure Algorithm (𝓐 𝓨 : Type*) [MeasurableSpace 𝓐] [MeasurableSpace 𝓨] where

  policy : (n : ℕ) → Kernel (Iic n → 𝓐 × 𝓨) 𝓐
  [h_policy : ∀ n, IsMarkovKernel (policy n)]

  p0 : Measure 𝓐
  [hp0 : IsProbabilityMeasure p0]

attribute [instance] Algorithm.h_policy Algorithm.hp0

structure Environment (𝓐 𝓨 : Type*) [MeasurableSpace 𝓐] [MeasurableSpace 𝓨] where

  feedback : (n : ℕ) → Kernel ((Iic n → 𝓐 × 𝓨) × 𝓐) 𝓨
  [h_feedback : ∀ n, IsMarkovKernel (feedback n)]

  ν0 : Kernel 𝓐 𝓨
  [hp0 : IsMarkovKernel ν0]

attribute [instance] Environment.h_feedback Environment.hp0

section Traj

variable {𝓐 𝓨 : Type*} [MeasurableSpace 𝓐] [MeasurableSpace 𝓨]

noncomputable
def stepKernel (alg : Algorithm 𝓐 𝓨) (env : Environment 𝓐 𝓨) (n : ℕ) :
    Kernel (Iic n → 𝓐 × 𝓨) (𝓐 × 𝓨) :=
  alg.policy n ⊗ₖ env.feedback n

instance (alg : Algorithm 𝓐 𝓨) (env : Environment 𝓐 𝓨) (n : ℕ) :
    IsMarkovKernel (stepKernel alg env n) := by
  rw [stepKernel]; infer_instance

noncomputable
def trajMeasure (alg : Algorithm 𝓐 𝓨) (env : Environment 𝓐 𝓨) :
    Measure (ℕ → 𝓐 × 𝓨) :=
  Kernel.trajMeasure (alg.p0 ⊗ₘ env.ν0) (stepKernel alg env)

def action (n : ℕ) (h : ℕ → 𝓐 × 𝓨) : 𝓐 := (h n).1

end Traj

noncomputable
def regret {𝓐 Ω : Type*} [MeasurableSpace 𝓐] (ν : Kernel 𝓐 ℝ) (A : ℕ → Ω → 𝓐) (t : ℕ) (ω : Ω) :
    ℝ :=
  (t : ℝ) * (⨆ a, (ν a)[id]) - ∑ s ∈ range t, (ν (A s ω))[id]

section History

variable {𝓐 R : Type*} [DecidableEq 𝓐] {n : ℕ}

noncomputable def pullCount' (n : ℕ) (h : Iic n → 𝓐 × R) (a : 𝓐) : ℕ :=
  #(univ.filter (fun s ↦ (h s).1 = a))

lemma pullCount'_eq_sum (n : ℕ) (h : Iic n → 𝓐 × R) (a : 𝓐) :
    pullCount' n h a = ∑ s : Iic n, if (h s).1 = a then 1 else 0 := by
  rw [pullCount', Finset.card_filter]

noncomputable def sumRewards' (n : ℕ) (h : Iic n → 𝓐 × ℝ) (a : 𝓐) : ℝ :=
  ∑ s, if (h s).1 = a then (h s).2 else 0

noncomputable def empMean' (n : ℕ) (h : Iic n → 𝓐 × ℝ) (a : 𝓐) : ℝ :=
  sumRewards' n h a / pullCount' n h a

variable [MeasurableSpace 𝓐] [MeasurableSingletonClass 𝓐] [MeasurableSpace R]

@[fun_prop]
lemma measurable_pullCount' (n : ℕ) (a : 𝓐) :
    Measurable (fun h : Iic n → 𝓐 × R ↦ pullCount' n h a) := by
  simp_rw [pullCount'_eq_sum]
  have h_meas s : Measurable (fun (h : Iic n → 𝓐 × R) ↦ if (h s).1 = a then 1 else 0) := by
    refine Measurable.ite ?_ (by fun_prop) (by fun_prop)
    exact (measurableSet_singleton _).preimage (by fun_prop)
  fun_prop

@[fun_prop]
lemma measurable_sumRewards' (n : ℕ) (a : 𝓐) :
    Measurable (fun h : Iic n → 𝓐 × ℝ ↦ sumRewards' n h a) := by
  simp_rw [sumRewards']
  have h_meas s : Measurable (fun (h : Iic n → 𝓐 × ℝ) ↦ if (h s).1 = a then (h s).2 else 0) := by
    refine Measurable.ite ?_ (by fun_prop) (by fun_prop)
    exact (measurableSet_singleton _).preimage (by fun_prop)
  fun_prop

@[fun_prop]
lemma measurable_empMean' (n : ℕ) (a : 𝓐) :
    Measurable (fun h : Iic n → 𝓐 × ℝ ↦ empMean' n h a) := by
  unfold empMean'; fun_prop

end History

def RoundRobin.nextAction {K : ℕ} (hK : 0 < K) (n : ℕ) : Fin K := ⟨(n + 1) % K, Nat.mod_lt _ hK⟩

section Interaction

variable {𝓐 𝓨 : Type*} [MeasurableSpace 𝓐] [MeasurableSpace 𝓨]

noncomputable def detAlgorithm (nextA : (n : ℕ) → (Iic n → 𝓐 × 𝓨) → 𝓐)
    (h_next : ∀ n, Measurable (nextA n)) (action0 : 𝓐) : Algorithm 𝓐 𝓨 where
  policy n := Kernel.deterministic (nextA n) (h_next n)
  p0 := Measure.dirac action0

noncomputable def stationaryEnv (ν : Kernel 𝓐 𝓨) [IsMarkovKernel ν] : Environment 𝓐 𝓨 where
  feedback _ := ν.comap Prod.snd measurable_snd
  ν0 := ν

end Interaction

noncomputable def ucbWidthNL {K : ℕ} (δ : ℝ) (n : ℕ) (h : Iic n → Fin K × ℝ) (a : Fin K) : ℝ :=
  Real.sqrt (Real.log (2 * ((pullCount' n h a : ℝ) + 1) ^ 2 / δ) / (2 * pullCount' n h a))

@[fun_prop]
lemma measurable_ucbWidthNL {K : ℕ} (δ : ℝ) (n : ℕ) (a : Fin K) :
    Measurable (fun h : Iic n → Fin K × ℝ ↦ ucbWidthNL δ n h a) := by
  unfold ucbWidthNL; fun_prop

open Classical in

noncomputable def nextArmNL {K : ℕ} (hK : 0 < K) (δ : ℝ) (n : ℕ) (h : Iic n → Fin K × ℝ) : Fin K :=
  have : Nonempty (Fin K) := Fin.pos_iff_nonempty.mp hK
  if n < K - 1 then RoundRobin.nextAction hK n else
  measurableArgmax (fun h a ↦ empMean' n h a + ucbWidthNL δ n h a) h

open Classical in
@[fun_prop]
lemma measurable_nextArmNL {K : ℕ} (hK : 0 < K) (δ : ℝ) (n : ℕ) :
    Measurable (nextArmNL hK δ n) := by
  have : Nonempty (Fin K) := Fin.pos_iff_nonempty.mp hK
  unfold nextArmNL
  split_ifs with hc
  · exact measurable_const
  · refine measurable_measurableArgmax fun a ↦ ?_
    fun_prop

noncomputable def ucbAlgorithmNL {K : ℕ} (hK : 0 < K) (δ : ℝ) : Algorithm (Fin K) ℝ :=
  detAlgorithm (nextArmNL hK δ) (measurable_nextArmNL hK δ) ⟨0, hK⟩

\left|\phi_{i}(\theta)-\phi_{i}\left(\theta^{\prime}\right)\right|\leq\gamma_{i}\left|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\right|.
\]
Then for any real valued function \( h: \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{Z}^n \to \mathbb{R} \), and \( S_n = \{Z_1, \ldots, Z_n\} \subset \mathcal{Z}^n \), we have

Given \(\mathcal{D}\) and \(\mathcal{F}\), and consider a localization function \(h: \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}\) such that \(b_0 = \inf_{f \in \mathcal{F}} h(f) > -\infty\). Define localized function class \(\mathcal{F}^h(b) = \{f \in \mathcal{F}: h(f) \leq b\}\) for all \(b > b_0\). For any \(\alpha > 0\), the rate function with respect to localization \(h\) is defined as
\[
\bar{r}_{n}^{h}(\alpha,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{D})=\sup\left\{r:r\leq\inf_{r^{\prime}>\max(r,\alpha b_{0})}\epsilon_{n}\left(\mathcal{F}^{h}\big(r^{\prime}/\alpha\big),\mathcal{D}\right)\right\}.
\]
We note that the requirement of \( r' > \alpha b_0 \) in Definition 6.35 is only to make sure that \( \mathcal{F}^h(r'/\alpha) \) is always non-empty, and thus \( \epsilon_n(\mathcal{F}^h(r'/\alpha), \mathcal{D}) \) is well-defined.

context.name: definition 6.1
context.statement:
Given an empirical process \(\{\phi(w, S_n) : w \in \Omega\}\), with \(S_n \sim \mathcal{D}^n\). Define the expected supremum of this empirical process as
\[
\epsilon_{n}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{n}}\sup_{w\in\Omega}\left[\phi(w,\mathcal{D})-\phi(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})\right],
\]
which will be referred to as the uniform convergence complexity of the function class \(\mathcal{G}\).
The smaller this quantity is, the closer the gap between the training error and the test error is, which implies that we have less overfitting. In Chapter 3, we
obtained large probability uniform convergence results for empirical processes, and then derived oracle inequalities in large probabilities. In the following, we show that if average convergence can be obtained, then we can derive oracle inequalities in expectation directly.

context.name: definition 6.3
context.statement:
Given \(S_{n}=\{Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{n}\}\), the (one-sided) empirical Rademacher complexity of \(\mathcal{G}\) is defined as
\[
R(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{S}_{n}) = \mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\sup_{w\in \Omega}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i = 1}^{n}\sigma_{i}\phi (w,Z_{i}),
\]
where \(\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_n\) are independent uniform \(\{\pm 1\}\)-valued Bernoulli random variables. Moreover, the expected Rademacher complexity is
\[
R_{n}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{n}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}R(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{S}_{n}).
\]

context.name: Variance Condition
context.statement:
Given a function class \(\mathcal{G}\). We say it satisfies the variance condition if there exists \(c_0, c_1 > 0\) such that for all \(\phi(z) \in \mathcal{G}\):
\[
\operatorname{Var}_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}}(\phi(Z))\leq c_{0}^{2}+c_{1}\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}}\phi(Z),\tag{3.13}
\]
where we require that \(\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim \mathcal{D}}\phi (Z)\geq -c_0^2 /c_1\) for all \(\phi \in \mathcal{G}\)
In applications, the following modification of the variance condition is often more convenient to employ
\[
\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}}[\phi(Z)^{2}]\leq c_{0}^{2}+c_{1}\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}}\phi(Z).\tag{3.14}
\]
It is easy to see that (3.14) implies (3.13). If \(\phi(Z)\) is bounded, then the two conditions are equivalent.
In general, if the variance condition (3.13) only holds for \( c_{1} = 0 \), then we can only obtain a convergence rate that is \( O(1 / \sqrt{n}) \) at the best. When the variance condition holds for \( c_{1} > 0 \) and \( c_{0} = 0 \), then we may be able to obtain a convergence rate faster than \( O(1 / \sqrt{n}) \) by using Bernstein's inequality. The ability to achieve faster convergence is the main reason to study this condition.

context.name: Union Bound
context.statement:
(Union Bound) Consider \(m\) events \(E_1, \ldots, E_m\). The following probability inequality holds:
\[
\Pr (E_1 \cup \cdots \cup E_m) \leq \sum_{j=1}^{m} \Pr(E_j).
\]

The union bound has an alternative expression, which is often used in the learning theory analysis. If each \(E_j\) occurs with probability at least \(1-\delta_j\) for \(j=1, \ldots, m\), then with probability at least \(1-\sum_{j=1}^{m} \delta_j\), all of events \(\{E_j\}\) occur simultaneously for \(j=1, \ldots, m\).

context.name: definition 8.1
context.statement:
Consider a loss function \(\phi(f, z): \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{Z} \to \mathbb{R}\), and a model family \(\{\mathcal{A}(\theta, S_n): \Theta \times \mathcal{Z}^n \to \mathcal{F}, n \geq 0\}\). Consider \(N \geq n \geq 0\), and iid dataset \(S_n \subset S_N \sim \mathcal{D}^N\). A model selection algorithm \(\bar{\mathcal{A}}\) maps \(S_N\) to \(\hat{\theta} = \hat{\theta}(S_N) \in \Theta\),
and then train a model \(\hat{f} = \mathcal{A}(\hat{\theta}(\mathcal{S}_N), \mathcal{S}_n) = \bar{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{S}_N)\). It satisfies an \(\epsilon_{n,N}(\cdot, \cdot)\) oracle inequality if there exists \(\epsilon_{n,N}(\theta, \delta)\), such that for all \(\delta \in (0,1)\), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) over \(\mathcal{S}_N\):
\[
\phi(\mathcal{A}(\hat{\theta}(\mathcal{S}_{N}),\mathcal{S}_{n}),\mathcal{D})\leq\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{n}}\phi(\mathcal{A}(\theta,\mathcal{S}_{n}),\mathcal{D})+\epsilon_{n,N}(\theta,\delta)].
\]
More generally, a learning algorithm \(\bar{\mathcal{A}}: S_N \to \mathcal{F}\) is \(\epsilon_{n,N}(\cdot, \cdot)\) adaptive to the model family \(\{\mathcal{A}(\theta, \cdot): \theta \in \Theta\}\) if there exists \(\epsilon_{n,N}(\theta, \delta)\), such that for all \(\delta \in (0,1)\), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) over \(S_N\):
\[
\phi(\bar{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{S}_{N}),\mathcal{D})\leq\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{n}}\phi(\mathcal{A}(\theta,\mathcal{S}_{n}),\mathcal{D})+\epsilon_{n,N}(\theta,\delta)\right].
\]
Note that we have used a slightly different notation \(\phi(f, Z)\), instead of \(\phi(w, Z)\) as in earlier chapters, to emphasize that in model selection, the prediction function \(f(w, \cdot)\) from different models can be compared, but the parameter \(w\) of the functions may not be comparable when different models have different functional forms such as decision trees versus neural networks. Without causing confusion, one may consider \(f\) to be the function represented by \(w\), so that \(\phi(f, Z) = L(f(X), Y)\) and \(\phi(w, Z) = L(f(w, X), Y)\). Similar to Definition 3.8, we use the simplified notation
\[
\phi(f,\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}}\phi(f,Z),\quad\phi(f,\mathcal{S}_{n})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{Z\in\mathcal{S}_{n}}\phi(f,Z).
\]
The concept adaptivity is more general than model selection, as the algorithm does not need to choose a specific model \(\mathcal{A}(\theta,\cdot)\) indexed by \(\theta\). For example, a commonly used method to achieve adaptivity is model averaging, where we take the average of several different model outputs \(\hat{f}_{\theta_j} = \mathcal{A}(\theta_j,\mathcal{S}_n)\) as
\[
\hat{f}_{\mathrm{avg}}(x)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\hat{f}_{\theta_{j}}(x).
\]
If different models have the same functional form, with a vector model parameter \( w \in \mathbb{R}^d \): \( \hat{f}_{\theta_j}(x) = f(\hat{w}_j, x) \). Then one may also average the model parameters as follows:
\[
\hat{w}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\hat{w}_{j}.
\]
In general, the training data \( S_{n} \) is a subset of \( S_{N} \), and we allow \( n < N \) in order to analyze validation methods which are commonly used in practice. In addition to the large probability bounds in Definition 8.1, one may also derive bounds that hold for expectation over \( S_{N} \).

context.name: equation (8.2)
context.statement:
Given training data \(S_n\) and validation data \(\bar{S}_m\), define the validation objective
\[
Q(\theta, f, \bar{\mathcal{S}}_m) = \phi(f, \bar{\mathcal{S}}_m) + r_m(q(\theta)).
\]
We select \(\hat{\theta}\) by approximate minimization:
\[
Q(\hat{\theta}, \mathcal{A}(\hat{\theta}, \mathcal{S}_n), \bar{\mathcal{S}}_m) \leq \inf_{\theta} Q(\theta, \mathcal{A}(\theta, \mathcal{S}_n), \bar{\mathcal{S}}_m) + \tilde{\epsilon}. \tag{8.2}
\]
Here \(\tilde{\epsilon}\) is the additive slack in the validation-based model-selection rule.

context.name: equation (8.1)
context.statement:
Let \(q(\theta)\geq 0\) for \(\theta = 1,2,\ldots\) satisfy
\[
\sum_{\theta=1}^{\infty} q(\theta) \leq 1. \tag{8.1}
\]

context.name: lemma 2.15
context.statement:
Consider a random variable \(X \in [0,1]\) and \(\mathbb{E}X = \mu\). We have the following inequality:
\[
\ln\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda X}\leq\ln [(1-\mu)e^{0}+\mu e^{\lambda}]\leq\lambda\mu+\lambda^{2}/8.
\]

context.name: proposition 7.16
context.statement:
Given any function \(U(w)\), we have
\[
\min_{p\in\Delta(\Omega)}\left[\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p}U(w)+\mathrm{KL}(p| |p_{0})\right]= -\ln\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{0}}\exp(-U(w)),
\]
and the solution is achieved by the Gibbs distribution \( q(w) \propto p_0(w) \exp(-U(w)) \). Here \( \Delta(\Omega) \) denotes the set of probability distributions on \( \Omega \).

context.name: proposition 14.14
context.statement:
Consider \(\Omega = \{w_0, w_1, \ldots, w_T\}\) that contains \(T\) members. Given any deterministic online learning algorithm \(\mathcal{A}\) that returns a model parameter \(w_{t-1}\) based on \(\{\ell_s : s = 1, \ldots, t-1\}\), there exists a loss sequence \(\ell_t(w) \in \{0, 1\}\) so that
\[
\inf_{w}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}(w)=0,\qquad\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}(w_{t-1})=T.
\]

context.name: definition 5.12
context.statement:
The convex hull of a function class \(\mathcal{F} = \{f(\theta, x) : \theta \in \Theta\}\) is defined as
\[
\operatorname{CONV}(\mathcal{F})=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_{j}f\left(\theta_{j},x\right):m>0,\|w\|_{1}=1,w_{j}\geq 0,\theta_{j}\in\Theta\right\}.
\]
We also include the closure of the finite sum functions above with respect to an appropriate topology in the convex hull.

context.name: definition 4.1
context.statement:
Let \((\mathcal{V},d)\) be a pseudometric space with metric \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\). A finite
set \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon) \subset \mathcal{V}\) is an \(\epsilon\)-cover (or \(\epsilon\)-net) of \(\mathcal{G} \subset \mathcal{V}\) if, for all \(\phi \in \mathcal{G}\), there exists \(\phi' \in \mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\) so that \(d(\phi', \phi) \leq \epsilon\). The \(\epsilon\)-covering number of \(\mathcal{G}\) with metric \(d\) is the smallest cardinality \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) of such \(\mathcal{G}(\epsilon)\). The number \(\ln N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, d)\) is called the \(\epsilon\)-entropy.
For a function class \(\mathcal{G}\) with seminorm \(L_{p}(\mathcal{D})\) in (3.19), we denote the corresponding \(L_{p}(\mathcal{D})\)-covering number as \(N(\epsilon, \mathcal{G}, L_{p}(\mathcal{D}))\). When \(1 \leq p \leq q\), we have
\[
N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{p}(\mathcal{D}))\leq N(\epsilon,\mathcal{G},L_{q}(\mathcal{D})).
\]

\hat{\Lambda}\left(\mathcal{S}_{n}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi\left(X_{i}\right)\psi\left(X_{i}\right)^{\top}+\Lambda_{0}.
\]
Given \( x \), the posterior distribution of \( y \) is
\[
\hat{p}(y|x,\mathcal{S}_{n})=N\left(\hat{w}(\mathcal{S}_{n})^{\top}\psi(x),\sigma^{2}+\sigma^{2}\psi(x)^{\top}\hat{\Lambda}(\mathcal{S}_{n})^{-1}\psi(x)\right).

context.name: equation (15.3)
context.statement:
The ridge regression method defines, for each \(n\),
\[
\hat{w}(\mathcal{S}_{n})=\arg\min_{w}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_{i}-w^{\top}\psi(X_{i}))^{2}+\|w\|_{\Lambda_{0}}^{2}\right].
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\hat{w}(\mathcal{S}_{n})=\Lambda_{n}^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi(X_{i})Y_{i},\quad\Lambda_{n}=\Lambda_{0}+\sum_{s=1}^{n}\psi(X_{s})\psi(X_{s})^{\top}.
\]

context.name: theorem 15.3
context.statement:
We have
\[
\begin{array}{l}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ln\hat{p}\left(Y_{t}\mid X_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t-1}\right)= -\ln\mathbb{E}_{w\sim p_{0}}\prod_{t=1}^{T}p\left(Y_{t}\mid w,X_{t}\right)\\ =\inf_{q\in\Delta(\Omega)}\left[-\mathbb{E}_{w\sim q}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ln p(Y_{t}|w,X_{t})+\mathbb{E}_{w\sim q}\ln\frac{q(w)}{p_{0}(w)}\right],\\ \end{array}
\]
where \(\Delta (\Omega)\) is the set of probability distributions over \(\Omega\)

context.name: Equations (15.1)-(15.2) (posterior and Bayesian posterior averaging estimator)
context.statement:
In the Bayesian setting, the optimal statistical estimation of posterior density for log-loss is the Bayesian posterior averaging estimator. Here we consider a prior \(p_{0}(w)\) on \(\Omega\). Given the training data \(\mathcal{S}_n = \{Z_1, \ldots, Z_n\}\), the posterior distribution is
\[
p(w|\mathcal{S}_{n})=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n}p(Y_{i}|w,X_{i})p_{0}(w)}{\int_{\Omega}\prod_{i=1}^{n}p(Y_{i}|w^{\prime},X_{i})p_{0}(w^{\prime})d w^{\prime}}.\tag{15.1}
\]
Unlike ERM, the Bayesian posterior averaging method does not use \(p(y|\hat{w}, x)\) for a specific \(\hat{w} \in \Omega\) that is estimated from the training data, but instead use the averaged probability estimate over the posterior as follows:
\[
\hat{p}(y|x,\mathcal{S}_{n})=\int_{\Omega}p(y|w,x)p(w|\mathcal{S}_{n})d w.\tag{15.2}
\]

nl_statement:
Consider a countable family of approximate ERM algorithms \(\{\mathcal{A}(\theta, \cdot): \theta = 1, 2, \ldots\}\), each characterized by its model space \(\mathcal{F}(\theta)\), and returns a function \(\hat{f}_{\theta} \in \mathcal{F}(\theta)\) such that
\[
\phi(\hat{f},\mathcal{S}_{n})\leq\inf_{f\in\mathcal{F}(\theta)}\phi(f,\mathcal{S}_{n})+\epsilon^{\prime},
\]
where we use the notation of Definition 8.1.
Assume further that \(\sup_{Z,Z'}[\phi(f,Z) - \phi(f,Z')]\leq M\) for all \(f\), and we use (8.2) to select the best model \(\hat{\theta}\) on the validation data \(\bar{S}_m\), with the choice
\[
r_{m}(q)=M\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/q)}{2 m}}.
\]
Then the following result holds with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) over random selection
of \(S_{n}\) and \(\bar{S}_m\) ..
\[
\begin{array}{l}\phi(\mathcal{A}(\hat{\theta},\mathcal{S}_{n}),\mathcal{D})\leq\inf_{\theta}\left[\inf_{f\in\mathcal{F}(\theta)}\phi(f,\mathcal{D})+2 R_{n}(\mathcal{G}(\theta),\mathcal{D})+r_{m}(q(\theta))\right]\\ +\tilde{\epsilon}+\epsilon^{\prime}+M\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(4/\delta)}{n}}+M\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(4/\delta)}{m}},\\ \end{array}
\]
where \( R_{n}(\mathcal{G}(\theta),\mathcal{D}) \) is the Rademacher complexity of \( \mathcal{G}(\theta) = \{\phi (f,\cdot):f\in \mathcal{F}(\theta)\} \) and \( q(\theta) \) satisfies (8.1).

context.name: definition 8.1
context.statement:
Consider a loss function \(\phi(f, z): \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{Z} \to \mathbb{R}\), and a model family \(\{\mathcal{A}(\theta, S_n): \Theta \times \mathcal{Z}^n \to \mathcal{F}, n \geq 0\}\). Consider \(N \geq n \geq 0\), and iid dataset \(S_n \subset S_N \sim \mathcal{D}^N\). A model selection algorithm \(\bar{\mathcal{A}}\) maps \(S_N\) to \(\hat{\theta} = \hat{\theta}(S_N) \in \Theta\),
and then train a model \(\hat{f} = \mathcal{A}(\hat{\theta}(\mathcal{S}_N), \mathcal{S}_n) = \bar{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{S}_N)\). It satisfies an \(\epsilon_{n,N}(\cdot, \cdot)\) oracle inequality if there exists \(\epsilon_{n,N}(\theta, \delta)\), such that for all \(\delta \in (0,1)\), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) over \(\mathcal{S}_N\):
\[
\phi(\mathcal{A}(\hat{\theta}(\mathcal{S}_{N}),\mathcal{S}_{n}),\mathcal{D})\leq\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{n}}\phi(\mathcal{A}(\theta,\mathcal{S}_{n}),\mathcal{D})+\epsilon_{n,N}(\theta,\delta)].
\]
More generally, a learning algorithm \(\bar{\mathcal{A}}: S_N \to \mathcal{F}\) is \(\epsilon_{n,N}(\cdot, \cdot)\) adaptive to the model family \(\{\mathcal{A}(\theta, \cdot): \theta \in \Theta\}\) if there exists \(\epsilon_{n,N}(\theta, \delta)\), such that for all \(\delta \in (0,1)\), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) over \(S_N\):
\[
\phi(\bar{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{S}_{N}),\mathcal{D})\leq\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{n}}\phi(\mathcal{A}(\theta,\mathcal{S}_{n}),\mathcal{D})+\epsilon_{n,N}(\theta,\delta)\right].
\]
Note that we have used a slightly different notation \(\phi(f, Z)\), instead of \(\phi(w, Z)\) as in earlier chapters, to emphasize that in model selection, the prediction function \(f(w, \cdot)\) from different models can be compared, but the parameter \(w\) of the functions may not be comparable when different models have different functional forms such as decision trees versus neural networks. Without causing confusion, one may consider \(f\) to be the function represented by \(w\), so that \(\phi(f, Z) = L(f(X), Y)\) and \(\phi(w, Z) = L(f(w, X), Y)\). Similar to Definition 3.8, we use the simplified notation
\[
\phi(f,\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}}\phi(f,Z),\quad\phi(f,\mathcal{S}_{n})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{Z\in\mathcal{S}_{n}}\phi(f,Z).
\]
The concept adaptivity is more general than model selection, as the algorithm does not need to choose a specific model \(\mathcal{A}(\theta,\cdot)\) indexed by \(\theta\). For example, a commonly used method to achieve adaptivity is model averaging, where we take the average of several different model outputs \(\hat{f}_{\theta_j} = \mathcal{A}(\theta_j,\mathcal{S}_n)\) as
\[
\hat{f}_{\mathrm{avg}}(x)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\hat{f}_{\theta_{j}}(x).
\]
If different models have the same functional form, with a vector model parameter \( w \in \mathbb{R}^d \): \( \hat{f}_{\theta_j}(x) = f(\hat{w}_j, x) \). Then one may also average the model parameters as follows:
\[
\hat{w}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\hat{w}_{j}.
\]
In general, the training data \( S_{n} \) is a subset of \( S_{N} \), and we allow \( n < N \) in order to analyze validation methods which are commonly used in practice. In addition to the large probability bounds in Definition 8.1, one may also derive bounds that hold for expectation over \( S_{N} \).

context.name: Model Selction on Validation Data
context.statement:
Assume \(\sup_{Z,Z'}[\phi(f,Z) - \phi(f,Z')] \leq M\) for all \(f\), and the validation data \(\bar{S}_m\) contains \(m\) iid samples from \(\mathcal{D}\). Given training data \(S_n\), consider (8.2) with
\[
r_{m}(q)=M\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/q)}{2 m}}.
\]
Then with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) over the random selection of \(S_{m}\):
\[
\phi(\mathcal{A}(\hat{\theta},\mathcal{S}_{n}),\mathcal{D})\leq\inf_{\theta}Q(\theta,\mathcal{A}(\theta,\mathcal{S}_{n}),\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{m})+\tilde{\epsilon}+M\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2 m}}.
\]
This implies the following oracle inequality. With probability at least \(1 - \delta\) over the random sampling of \(\bar{S}_m\):
\[
\phi(\mathcal{A}(\hat{\theta},\mathcal{S}_{n}),\mathcal{D})\leq\inf_{\theta}[\phi(\mathcal{A}(\theta,\mathcal{S}_{n}),\mathcal{D})+r_{m}(q(\theta))]+\tilde{\epsilon}+M\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(2/\delta)}{m}},
\]
where \(q(\theta)\) satisfies (8.1).

context.name: corollary 6.21
context.statement:
Assume that for some \(M \geq 0\):
\[
\sup_{w\in\Omega}\left[\sup_{z,z^{\prime}}[\phi(w,z)-\phi(w,z^{\prime})]+\Delta_{n}h(w)\right]\leq M.
\]
Then the approximate ERM method (6.1) satisfies the following oracle inequality. With probability at least \( 1 - \delta - \delta' \):
\[
\begin{array}{l}\phi(\hat{w},\mathcal{D})\leq\inf_{w\in\Omega}\left[\phi(w,\mathcal{D})+\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{n}}h(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})+\Delta_{n}h(w)\sqrt{\frac{\ln\left(1/\delta^{\prime}\right)}{2 n}}\right]\\ +\epsilon^{\prime}+\epsilon_{n}^{h}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})+2 M\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2 n}}.\\ \end{array}
\]
If \( h(\cdot) \) has the decomposition (6.3), then
\[
\begin{array}{l}\phi(\hat{w},\mathcal{D})\leq\inf_{w\in\Omega}\left[\phi(w,\mathcal{D})+\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{n}}h(w,\mathcal{S}_{n})+\Delta_{n}h(w)\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta^{\prime})}{2 n}}\right]\\ +\epsilon^{\prime}+2 R_{n}^{h}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})+2 M\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2 n}}.\\ \end{array}
\]

context.name: Union Bound
context.statement:
(Union Bound) Consider \(m\) events \(E_1, \ldots, E_m\). The following probability inequality holds:
\[
\Pr (E_1 \cup \cdots \cup E_m) \leq \sum_{j=1}^{m} \Pr(E_j).
\]

The union bound has an alternative expression, which is often used in the learning theory analysis. If each \(E_j\) occurs with probability at least \(1-\delta_j\) for \(j=1, \ldots, m\), then with probability at least \(1-\sum_{j=1}^{m} \delta_j\), all of events \(\{E_j\}\) occur simultaneously for \(j=1, \ldots, m\).

context.name: definition 6.3
context.statement:
Given \(S_{n}=\{Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{n}\}\), the (one-sided) empirical Rademacher complexity of \(\mathcal{G}\) is defined as
\[
R(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{S}_{n}) = \mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\sup_{w\in \Omega}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i = 1}^{n}\sigma_{i}\phi (w,Z_{i}),
\]
where \(\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_n\) are independent uniform \(\{\pm 1\}\)-valued Bernoulli random variables. Moreover, the expected Rademacher complexity is
\[
R_{n}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{n}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}R(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{S}_{n}).
\]

context.name: equation (8.1)
context.statement:
Let \(q(\theta)\geq 0\) for \(\theta = 1,2,\ldots\) satisfy
\[
\sum_{\theta=1}^{\infty} q(\theta) \leq 1. \tag{8.1}
\]

context.name: equation (8.2)
context.statement:
Given training data \(S_n\) and validation data \(\bar{S}_m\), define the validation objective
\[
Q(\theta, f, \bar{\mathcal{S}}_m) = \phi(f, \bar{\mathcal{S}}_m) + r_m(q(\theta)).
\]
We select \(\hat{\theta}\) by approximate minimization:
\[
Q(\hat{\theta}, \mathcal{A}(\hat{\theta}, \mathcal{S}_n), \bar{\mathcal{S}}_m) \leq \inf_{\theta} Q(\theta, \mathcal{A}(\theta, \mathcal{S}_n), \bar{\mathcal{S}}_m) + \tilde{\epsilon}. \tag{8.2}
\]
Here \(\tilde{\epsilon}\) is the additive slack in the validation-based model-selection rule.

Assume that rewards \(r_t(a) \in [0,1]\). Let \(a_* \in \arg \max_a \mu(a)\). With a choice of
\[
\hat{c}_{t}(a)=\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2(\hat{n}_{t}(a)+1)^{2}/\delta)}{2\hat{n}_{t}(a)}},

\[
\mathrm{REG}_{T}\leq(K-1)+\sqrt{8\ln(2 K T^{2}/\delta)(T-K)K}.

context.name: lemma 16.6
context.statement:
Let \(a_* \in \arg \max_a \mu(a)\). Let
\[
\delta_{1}=\Pr\left[\exists t>K:\mu\left(a_{*}\right)>\hat{\mu}_{t-1}\left(a_{*}\right)+\hat{c}_{t-1}\left(a_{*}\right)\right],
\]
\[
\delta_{2}=\Pr\left[\exists t>K,a\in\{1,\dots,K\}\backslash\{a_{*}\}:\mu(a)<\hat{\mu}_{t-1}(a)-\hat{c}_{t-1}^{\prime}(a)\right].
\]
Define \(\Delta(a) = \mu(a_{*}) - \mu(a)\), and
\[
T(a)=\max\left\{m:\Delta(a)\leq\hat{c}_{t-1}(a)+\hat{c}_{t-1}^{\prime}(a),\hat{n}_{t-1}(a)=m,K<t\leq T\right\}\cup\{0\}.
\]
Then for Algorithm 16.1, we have with probability at least \(1 - \delta_{1} - \delta_{2}\):
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}\leq\inf_{\Delta_{0}>0}\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}T(a)\Delta(a)\mathbb{1}(\Delta(a)>\Delta_{0})+(T-K)\Delta_{0}\right]+\sum_{a=1}^{K}\Delta(a).
\]

context.name: definition 16.1
context.statement:
In the multi-armed bandit (or MAB) problem, we consider \(K\) arms. The environment generates a sequence of reward vectors for time steps \(t \geq 1\) as \(r_t = [r_t(1), \ldots, r_t(K)]\). Each \(r_t(a)\) is associated with an arm \(a \in \{1, \ldots, K\}\). In the literature, an arm \(a\) is also referred to as an action. At each time step \(t = 1, 2, \ldots, T\),
- The player pulls one of the arms \( a_{t} \in \{1, \dots, K\} \).
- The environment returns the reward \( r_t(a_t) \), but does not reveal information on any other arm \( a \neq a_t \).
At each time \( t \), a (randomized) bandit algorithm takes the historic observations observed so far, and maps it to a distribution \( \hat{\pi}_{t-1} \) over actions \( a \in \{1, \ldots, K\} \). We then draw a random action \( a_t \) (arm) from \( \hat{\pi}_{t-1} \). Here \( \hat{\pi}_{t-1} \) is referred to as policy.
In the adversarial bandit problem, we are given an arbitrary reward sequence \(\{[r_1(1),\ldots,r_t(K)]:t\geq 1\}\) before hand. The adversary in this setting is called oblivious, who decides the rewards of all the rounds before the game starts (but may take advantage of the bandit algorithm's weakness). For this reward se
quence, the expected cumulative reward of a randomized bandit algorithm is
\[
\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a_{t}),
\]
where the randomization is over the internal randomization of the bandit algorithm. The expected regret is defined as
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}=\max_{a}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a)-\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}\left(a_{t}\right).\tag{16.1}
\]
If the bandit algorithm is deterministic: i.e. pulling a single arm \(a_{t}\) only at any time step, then the regret is
\[
\mathrm{REG}_{T}=\max_{a}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}(a_{t}).
\]
In the adversarial bandit problem, our goal is to minimize the expected regret \(\mathrm{REG}_T\) (and the expectation is with respect to the internal randomization of the algorithm instead of the data).
Another form of bandit problem, called stochastic bandit, assumes that the reward \( r_t(a) \) is drawn independently from a distribution \( \mathcal{D}_a \), with mean \( \mu(a) = \mathbb{E}_{r_t(a) \sim \mathcal{D}_a} [r_t(a)] \). In this setting, the goal of bandit is to find \( a \) that maximizes the expected reward \( \mu(a) \). We are interested in the expected regret defined as:
\[
\operatorname{REG}_{T}=T\max_{a}\mu(a)-\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu\left(a_{t}\right).\tag{16.2}
\]
Again, this regret is defined for each realization of the stochastic rewards, and the expectation is with respect to the randomness of the algorithm. If algorithm is deterministic and outputs \( a_{t} \) at each time \( t \), then
\[
\mathrm{REG}_{T}=T\max_{a}\mu(a)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu(a_{t}).
\]
We can further include randomization over data into the regret of stochastic bandit, by considering expected regret as follows:
\[
\mathbb{E}\operatorname{REG}_{T}=T\max_{a}\mu(a)-\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu(a_{t}),
\]
where the expectation is with respect to both the data and the internal randomization of the learning algorithm.

context.name: UCB Algorithm
context.statement:
Algorithm 16.1: UCB Algorithm
Input: \(K\) and \(T\geq K\)   
1 for \(a=1,\dots,K\) do   
2 Let \(\hat{n}_0(a) = 0\)   
3 Let \(\hat{\mu}_0(a) = 0\)   
4 for \(t=1,2,\ldots,T\) do   
5 if \(t\leq K\) then   
6 Let \(a_{t} = t\)   
7 else   
8 Let \(a_{t}\in \arg \max_{a}[\hat{\mu}_{t - 1}(a) + \hat{c}_{t - 1}(a)]\) according to (16.3)   
9 Pull arm \(a_{t}\) and observe reward \(r_t(a_t)\)

context.name: equation 16.3
context.statement:
For each arm \(a\), define the number of pulls up to time \(t\) and the corresponding empirical mean by
\[
\hat n_t(a)=\sum_{s=1}^{t}\mathbb{1}(a_s=a), \qquad
\hat\mu_t(a)=\frac{1}{\hat n_t(a)}\sum_{s=1}^{t} r_s(a_s)\mathbb{1}(a_s=a),
\]
with the initialization \(\hat n_0(a)=0\) and \(\hat\mu_0(a)=0\). In the UCB algorithm, after the initialization rounds, the arm is selected according to
\[
a_t\in\arg\max_a\left[\hat\mu_{t-1}(a)+\hat c_{t-1}(a)\right]. \tag{16.3}
\]
Here \(\hat c_t(a)\) denotes the confidence width used by the algorithm.
